lessons.title: What Is Software Engineering?
lessons.content:
Imagine two people who both want a house. The first one buys some bricks, cement and tin, and starts building with his cousin on a Friday. No drawing, no plan, no budget. It works for a small shed. But if he tries to build a ten-storey building in Dhaka this way, the walls will crack, the stairs will end in the wrong place and the money will finish halfway. The second person hires an engineer. There is a plan, a drawing, a soil test, a budget, a schedule, inspections at each floor and a team where everyone knows their job. Software engineering is the second way of building, but for software.

What it is: Software engineering is the disciplined, systematic way of building, testing, delivering and maintaining software, so that it works correctly, is finished on time and within budget, and can be changed safely later. The IEEE defines it as the application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software. The key words are systematic (there is an order of steps), disciplined (people follow agreed rules) and quantifiable (we measure things like effort, size and defects).

Program vs software product: A program is a piece of code that solves a problem, often written by one person for themselves. Your C assignment that calculates GPA is a program. A software product is much bigger. It has many users who are not the programmers, it has documentation, installation steps, a user interface, error handling, security, tests, updates and support. The software includes the code, the documents and the data that come with it. A rough rule often quoted is that turning a working program into a real product that other people can rely on takes several times more effort than writing the program itself.

The problem it solved: In the 1960s computers became powerful enough to run very large programs, like airline booking systems and operating systems. Teams grew from a few people to hundreds. Projects started to fail badly: they finished years late, cost far more than planned, and were full of bugs. People called this the software crisis. In 1968, NATO organised a conference in Garmisch, Germany, with the title "Software Engineering". The name was chosen on purpose, to say that building software should be as disciplined as building bridges or aeroplanes.

Before and after: Before software engineering, programming was treated like a personal craft. A clever programmer wrote code in his own style, tested it a little and moved on. There were few written requirements, few designs and no common way to estimate time. After the idea of software engineering spread, teams started using process models, written requirements, design documents, structured testing, version control and project management. Today we also have agile methods, automated testing and cloud deployment, but the goal is the same: build the right thing, build it right, and keep it working.

Why projects fail: Software fails for surprisingly human reasons. The requirements were unclear or kept changing. The team underestimated the work. Nobody tested properly. Communication between the client and the developers was poor. Some famous failures teach this well. In 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket exploded about 40 seconds after launch because a piece of reused software from Ariane 4 converted a 64-bit floating point number into a 16-bit integer, and the value was too big. In the 1980s the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine gave some patients massive overdoses because of a software race condition and weak safety design. These are not just bugs; they are engineering failures of process, testing and review.

Software is different from hardware: A chair or a car engine wears out with use. Software does not wear out; running the same code a million times does not rub it away. But software does deteriorate. Each time someone changes it to fix a bug or add a feature, there is a chance of adding new bugs and making the design messier. Over years a clean system can become a tangled one. This is why maintenance and good design matter so much. Also, software is developed, not manufactured: copying a finished app costs almost nothing, so nearly all of the cost is in the thinking, designing, coding and testing.

More characteristics: Software is invisible. You cannot walk around it like a building site and see that the third floor is half done, which makes progress hard to measure. Software is also easy to change in theory, which tempts clients to ask for changes all the time. And most software is built from existing parts, like libraries, frameworks and APIs, so engineers spend a lot of time understanding other people's code. These features explain why we need careful processes, reviews and measurements.

Kinds of software: Software engineering applies to many kinds of software. System software such as operating systems and compilers. Application software such as a hospital management system or a payroll system. Embedded software inside washing machines, cars and medical devices. Web and mobile apps such as an online shop or a ride-sharing app. Scientific and engineering software for weather forecasting. AI-based software that learns from data. Each kind needs the same basic engineering ideas, adjusted to its risks. A bug in a game is annoying; a bug in a heart monitor can kill.

The layered view: Roger Pressman, author of a very popular textbook, describes software engineering as four layers. At the bottom is a quality focus: everything rests on a commitment to quality. On top of that is the process layer, the framework that says which activities happen and in what order. Then come methods, the technical how-to for each task, like how to write requirements, how to design, how to test. At the top are tools, the software that supports the methods, like Git, issue trackers, testing frameworks and UML editors. Tools without a process just create a faster mess.

Computer science vs software engineering: Computer science studies the theory: algorithms, data structures, computation, complexity. It asks "what can be computed, and how fast?" Software engineering is about the practical job of building real systems with real people under real limits of time, money and skill. A computer scientist may prove that an algorithm runs in O(n log n). A software engineer decides whether to use it, how to test it, how to document it, and how a team of ten will keep it working for five years. You need both: theory tells you what is possible, engineering tells you how to deliver it reliably.

Who does what: A real software team has many roles. A product owner or business analyst understands what the customer needs. Architects and designers decide the overall structure. Developers write code. Testers or quality assurance engineers find problems. A project manager or Scrum Master keeps work flowing. DevOps or operations engineers deploy and monitor the system. UI/UX designers make it easy to use. In a small startup in Dhaka, one person may wear three of these hats, but all the jobs still need doing.

The cost of fixing bugs late: One of the most important ideas in this course is that a mistake is cheapest to fix early. If a requirement is wrong and you catch it while writing the requirements, you change a sentence. If you only find it after the system is coded, tested and deployed, you may need to change the design, code, tests, documents and the data of real users. Many studies have reported that the cost of fixing a defect grows a lot the later it is found. The exact multiplier varies between studies, so do not memorise one number, but remember the direction: early is cheap, late is expensive.

Software engineering ethics: Because software controls money, health, elections and safety, engineers have a responsibility. The ACM and IEEE published a Software Engineering Code of Ethics. It says, in short, that engineers should act in the public interest, be honest about their skills and estimates, protect confidential data, not hide known defects, and keep improving themselves. If your manager asks you to ship a payment feature you know is unsafe, ethics says you must speak up.

Real life example 1, a mobile banking app: Think of a mobile financial service app like bKash or Nagad. Millions of people send money, pay bills and recharge phones every day. Behind the simple screen, there are requirements (send money only if the balance is enough, limit per day, PIN rules from the central bank), design (servers, databases, security layers), construction (many teams writing code), testing (does a transfer during a network drop lose money?), deployment (releasing updates without stopping service) and maintenance (new features before Eid, fixing bugs, following new regulations). Without software engineering, one bug could lose real people's money.

Real life example 2, a university result system: Suppose your university wants an online result system. A student who can code might build one in a weekend: a form, a database and a page. But then real questions arrive. What happens when 10,000 students check results at the same minute? Who can edit a grade, and is every change logged? What if a teacher enters 95 instead of 59? How will the system change when the grading policy changes next year? Software engineering gives you a way to ask these questions early, write them down, design for them, test them and plan for change.

What this course covers: We start with the software process and process models: waterfall, V-model, incremental, prototyping, spiral and the Unified Process. Then agile methods, Extreme Programming, Scrum and Kanban. Next, requirements essentials (the full analysis side is in the System Analysis and Design course). Then modeling with UML: use case, class, sequence, activity and state diagrams. Then design: fundamentals, architecture styles, SOLID principles and design patterns. Then construction: code quality, refactoring and Git. Then testing: fundamentals, black-box, white-box, automation, TDD, CI/CD. Finally management: scheduling, estimation, risk, quality, maintenance and configuration management.

Common mistakes: Many students think software engineering means just coding. Coding is only one part; requirements, design, testing and maintenance often take more effort. Some think more people always means faster delivery; you will see later that adding people to a late project can make it later. Some believe a process means heavy documents; good processes can be light, like Scrum. Others think a program that runs once on their laptop is finished. A product must work for all users, on all expected inputs, for years.

What exams ask: Define software engineering (IEEE definition is a safe answer). Explain the software crisis and its causes. Differentiate program and software product. List the characteristics of software, especially "software does not wear out but deteriorates". Describe the layered technology view (quality, process, methods, tools). Give an example of a software failure and explain what engineering practice could have prevented it.

Recap: Software engineering is the systematic, disciplined and measurable way to build and maintain software. It was born from the software crisis of the 1960s and named at the 1968 NATO conference. Software is developed, not manufactured, does not wear out but does deteriorate with change, and is invisible and complex. Quality is the base, process gives order, methods give technique, and tools give support. Fix mistakes early, because late fixes are expensive. Next lesson: what a software process is and what activities every project goes through.
key_points: Software engineering is the systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to developing, operating and maintaining software (IEEE).
A software product includes code, documentation and data, and serves users who are not its programmers.
The software crisis of the 1960s (late, over budget, buggy projects) led to the 1968 NATO conference that named the field.
Software does not wear out, but it deteriorates as changes add bugs and messy design.
Pressman's layers: quality focus at the base, then process, methods and tools.
Defects cost much more to fix the later they are found, so catch them early.
Most failures come from unclear requirements, poor estimates, weak testing and poor communication.
Engineers have ethical duties: public interest, honesty, protecting data, not hiding defects.
lessons.tip: For every topic in this course, ask: which problem in real projects does this solve? If you can name the problem, you will remember the solution.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily (bKash, Pathao, Daraz or your university portal). Write down five things that could go wrong in it and, for each, which phase (requirements, design, coding, testing, maintenance) should have caught it.

quiz.q: Which statement about software is correct?
options: Software wears out with use like a car engine
Software does not wear out but can deteriorate as it is changed
Copying software costs as much as building it
Software never needs maintenance once it works
quiz.explain: Software has no physical parts to rub away, but each change can introduce bugs and messy design.

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of the 1968 NATO conference titled Software Engineering?
options: To launch the first programming language
To respond to the software crisis by calling for a disciplined, engineering approach
quiz.explain: Projects were late, over budget and buggy; the name was chosen to push for engineering discipline.

quiz.q: In Pressman's layered view, what is at the base of software engineering?
quiz.explain: Quality focus is the bedrock; process, methods and tools are built on it.

quiz.q: Why is it important to find a requirements mistake early?
options: Because the cost of fixing a defect usually grows the later it is found
Because testers are not allowed to report requirement errors
Because requirements cannot be changed after coding
Because compilers detect requirement errors automatically
quiz.explain: A wrong requirement found early means changing a sentence; found late it means changing design, code, tests and data.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of a software product compared with a program?
options: A program has more users than a product
A product is only the source code
A product includes code, documentation, data and support for many users
A product never has a user interface
quiz.explain: A product is built for others to rely on, so it needs documents, data, testing, installation and support.

lessons.title: Software Process and the SDLC
lessons.content:
Think about how your family prepares for a wedding. Nobody just wakes up and starts cooking biryani for 500 guests. First the families talk about what they want: date, budget, number of guests. Then someone makes a plan: which community centre, which caterer, who handles the invitation cards. Then the details are designed: the menu, the stage decoration, the seating. Then the actual work happens: cooking, decorating, receiving guests. Finally the event is delivered, and afterwards there is the cleanup and the paying of bills. Along the whole way, an uncle keeps checking the budget and an aunt keeps checking quality. Building software follows a very similar pattern, and that pattern is called a software process.

What a software process is: A software process is a structured set of activities, actions and tasks that a team carries out to produce a software product. It answers questions like: what do we do first, what do we produce at each step, who checks it, and when do we move on? A process is not a rigid recipe that must be followed word by word. It is a framework that the team adapts to the project. A two-person app for a local restaurant needs a lighter process than banking software used by millions.

Why we need one: Without a process, every developer works in their own way. One starts coding before anyone knows what the client wants. Another writes no tests. Nobody knows how much is done. Problems are found at the last moment. A defined process gives predictability (we can plan and estimate), visibility (we can see progress), quality (checks are built in) and repeatability (a team can do the next project in the same proven way). It also helps new team members, because they can learn "how we work here" quickly.

Activities, actions and tasks: Pressman describes a process as a hierarchy. A framework activity is a big area of work, like modeling. An action is a set of tasks that produce one major work product, like "architectural design". A task is a small, concrete piece of work with a clear result, like "draw the deployment diagram" or "review the database schema with the senior developer". Breaking work down this way makes it possible to assign, track and estimate it.

The five generic framework activities: Pressman lists five activities found in almost every software project. Communication: talk with the customer and other stakeholders to understand goals and gather requirements. Planning: create a project plan, which describes the tasks, risks, resources, schedule and work products. Modeling: create models (sketches, diagrams, designs) that help understand the requirements and the design before building. Construction: write the code and test it. Deployment: deliver the software to the customer, who evaluates it and gives feedback. In small projects these may happen in a few days; in large ones each can take months.

Umbrella activities: Some activities do not belong to one phase. They run over the whole project, like an umbrella covering everything. Pressman lists: project tracking and control (are we on schedule?), risk management (what could go wrong?), software quality assurance (are we following quality practices?), technical reviews (checking work products to find errors early), measurement (collecting numbers like effort and defects), software configuration management (managing versions and changes), reusability management (deciding what can be reused) and work product preparation (creating documents, models, logs). Many of these have their own lessons later in this course.

Sommerville's view: Another famous textbook, by Ian Sommerville, groups the work into four fundamental activities. Software specification: defining what the system should do and its constraints. Software design and implementation: designing the structure and writing the code. Software validation: checking that the system does what the customer wants, mostly by testing. Software evolution: changing the software as needs change. The two views are compatible; they just cut the same cake into different slices. In an exam, say which author's model you are using.

The SDLC: SDLC stands for Software Development Life Cycle. It is the sequence of stages that software goes through from the first idea to its retirement. A common version has these stages: planning and feasibility, requirements analysis, design, implementation (coding), testing, deployment, and maintenance. Some books add a final stage, retirement, when the old system is switched off and data is moved to a new one. The word "cycle" is important: after deployment, feedback and new needs often start the loop again for the next version.

A small walk through the SDLC: Imagine a coaching centre in Rajshahi wants an app for attendance and fees. Planning: is it worth building, what is the budget, when is it needed? Requirements: teachers mark attendance, parents receive an SMS if a student is absent, the accountant records fees. Design: a mobile app for teachers, a web page for the office, one database, an SMS gateway. Implementation: developers code the screens and the server. Testing: does an absent mark really trigger the SMS? Deployment: install it on the teachers' phones and train them. Maintenance: next year they ask for online fee payment, and the loop begins again.

Work products: Each stage produces something you can see, review and keep. These are called work products or artifacts. Planning produces a project plan and maybe a feasibility report. Requirements produce a requirements document or a product backlog. Design produces architecture diagrams, UML models and database designs. Implementation produces source code. Testing produces test plans, test cases and bug reports. Deployment produces release notes and user manuals. Having concrete artifacts makes it possible to review them and to measure progress.

Entry and exit criteria: A mature process also says when a stage can start and when it is finished. For example, design may start only when the main requirements are reviewed and approved (entry criterion). Testing of a feature may be considered done only when all planned test cases have run and no critical bugs remain open (exit criterion). These criteria stop the team from rushing ahead with half-finished work, which is a very common cause of late surprises.

What a process model is: A process model (also called a life cycle model) is a simplified description of how these activities are arranged in time. Do we do each stage once, in a straight line? Do we repeat all stages in small loops? Do we build a quick prototype first? Different arrangements give different models: waterfall, V-model, incremental, prototyping, spiral, Unified Process, and agile methods such as Scrum. The activities are almost the same in all of them. What changes is the order, the overlap and how often they repeat.

Process flow: Pressman names four ways activities can flow. Linear flow: each activity once, in sequence. Iterative flow: one or more activities are repeated before moving on. Evolutionary flow: the whole set of activities runs in circles, each circle producing a more complete version. Parallel flow: some activities run at the same time, like designing one part while coding another. Recognising the flow helps you understand any model you meet.

Prescriptive vs agile: Process models are often split into two families. Prescriptive (or plan-driven) models define activities, order and documents in advance and expect the team to follow the plan. Waterfall and the V-model are classic examples. Agile models put working software, customer collaboration and quick response to change first, using short iterations and lighter documentation. Neither family is always better. Plan-driven processes suit stable, safety-critical or contract-heavy projects; agile suits projects where requirements are uncertain and fast feedback is possible. Many real companies mix the two.

Tailoring a process: No textbook process fits every project exactly, so teams tailor it. Tailoring means deciding which activities, documents and reviews this particular project really needs. Things that push towards a heavier process: a large team, many locations, legal contracts, safety risks, strict regulators. Things that allow a lighter one: a small team sitting together, a customer who is available every day, low risk, and requirements that are still being discovered. For example, a medical device team may keep detailed review records by law, while a three-person team building an internal tool may use a simple board and weekly demos. Both are following a process; one is just thicker than the other.

Process assessment and improvement: How do you know if a team's process is good? Organisations use assessment models such as CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) and standards such as ISO 9001 to evaluate and improve their processes. A team at a low maturity level depends on heroes working late nights; a team at a high level has defined, measured processes and keeps improving them. We will look at CMMI levels in the quality lesson. For now, remember that a process itself can be measured and improved, just like a product.

Real life example 1, a garment factory ERP: A large garment factory in Gazipur wants software to track orders from buyers, raw material, production lines and shipments. Communication: meetings with merchandisers, production managers and accounts. Planning: a ten-month plan with three releases. Modeling: data models for orders and materials, screen mock-ups for the floor supervisors. Construction: coding and testing module by module. Deployment: first the order module, then production, then shipment. Umbrella activities run all the time: the project manager tracks the schedule, the QA team reviews each module, and every change to requirements is logged.

Real life example 2, a student project: Your final year project is a small software project too. Communication is your talk with the supervisor. Planning is your timeline for the semester. Modeling is your diagrams in the proposal. Construction is coding plus testing. Deployment is the demo and the final report. The umbrella activities are there as well: you track progress every week, you manage risk (what if the dataset is not available?), and you keep your code in Git. Thinking in terms of a process will make your project calmer and better.

Common mistakes: Students often confuse the SDLC (the stages software passes through) with a process model (one particular way to arrange those stages). Another mistake is thinking a process means lots of paperwork; a process can be very light. Some believe testing is one stage at the end; in good processes, reviews and testing happen throughout. Finally, many forget maintenance, even though it often takes more than half of the total lifetime cost of a system.

What exams ask: Define software process. List and explain the five generic framework activities. What are umbrella activities? Give examples. Describe the phases of the SDLC with a diagram. Differentiate a software process and a process model. Compare prescriptive and agile process models. Explain linear, iterative, evolutionary and parallel process flows.

Recap: A software process is a framework of activities, actions and tasks for producing software. The five generic activities are communication, planning, modeling, construction and deployment, supported by umbrella activities like tracking, risk management, quality assurance, reviews and configuration management. The SDLC is the life journey of software from idea to retirement. A process model decides how these activities are arranged in time. Next lesson: the first and most famous model, waterfall, and its testing-focused cousin, the V-model.
key_points: A software process is a framework of activities, actions and tasks used to build a software product.
Pressman's five generic activities: communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment.
Umbrella activities (tracking, risk management, SQA, reviews, measurement, SCM) run across the whole project.
Sommerville's four activities: specification, design and implementation, validation, evolution.
The SDLC is the journey from planning to requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment, maintenance and retirement.
A process model describes how the activities are arranged in time: linear, iterative, evolutionary or parallel.
Prescriptive models plan everything in advance; agile models use short iterations and embrace change.
Each stage produces work products that can be reviewed, and entry/exit criteria control moving forward.
lessons.tip: Draw the five framework activities as five boxes and the umbrella activities as a big umbrella over them. That one picture answers half the exam questions on this lesson.
lessons.task: Think of a recent event you organised (a class trip, a programme, a birthday). Map what you did onto communication, planning, modeling, construction and deployment, and name one umbrella activity you did along the way.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Pressman's five generic framework activities?
quiz.explain: The five are communication, planning, modeling, construction and deployment.

quiz.q: Software configuration management and risk management are examples of:
quiz.explain: They run across the whole project rather than belonging to one phase.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between the SDLC and a process model?
options: They are exactly the same thing
The SDLC lists the stages; a process model describes one way of arranging them in time
A process model is only used for hardware
The SDLC has no testing stage
quiz.explain: Waterfall, spiral and Scrum are different arrangements of the same life cycle stages.

quiz.q: In which process flow does the whole set of activities run in circles, each producing a more complete version?
quiz.explain: Evolutionary flow repeats all activities in loops, growing the product each time.

quiz.q: Which of Sommerville's activities is mainly about checking the system meets the customer's needs?
quiz.explain: Validation checks, mostly by testing, that the system does what the customer wants.

lessons.title: The Waterfall Model and the V-Model
lessons.content:
Picture building the Padma Bridge. First the engineers studied the river, the soil and the traffic. Then they finalised the design: where each pillar stands, how deep the piles go, how the deck is joined. Only then did construction start, pillar by pillar. You cannot change your mind about pillar positions after half of them are in the river. Each step had to be finished and approved before the next could safely begin. The waterfall model brings exactly this way of thinking to software: finish one phase completely, sign it off, then flow down to the next, like water falling down steps.

What it is: The waterfall model, also called the classic life cycle or linear sequential model, arranges the software activities in a fixed sequence. A typical version has these phases: requirements analysis and definition, system and software design, implementation and unit testing, integration and system testing, and operation and maintenance. The output of each phase becomes the input of the next. In principle, a phase begins only when the previous one is finished and its documents are approved.

A bit of history: The model is usually traced to a 1970 paper by Winston W. Royce about managing large software projects. Interestingly, Royce himself pointed out that the pure one-way version is risky and recommended feedback between phases and doing parts of the work twice. Later, the simple one-directional diagram became famous anyway, partly because it fitted the way governments and large companies managed contracts in those days. The name "waterfall" came from the diagram, where the phases look like steps of falling water.

Phase 1, requirements: The team collects and documents everything the system must do and the constraints it must respect. The result is a Software Requirements Specification (SRS). In waterfall, the SRS is expected to be complete and stable, because everything later depends on it. The customer reviews and signs it. This sign-off is like a contract: later changes are possible but need formal change requests, extra time and often extra money.

Phase 2, design: Designers turn the requirements into a plan for the software. Architectural design decides the major components and how they talk to each other. Detailed design describes each module: its data structures, algorithms and interfaces. The database design is fixed. The output is a design document that programmers can follow. A good design document lets a new programmer understand the system without reading all the code.

Phase 3, implementation and unit testing: Programmers write code for each module according to the design. Each module is tested on its own, which is called unit testing, to check that it does what its design says. In a big project many programmers work in parallel on different modules, which is possible because the design already fixed the interfaces between them.

Phase 4, integration and system testing: The separate modules are joined together and tested as a whole system. Integration testing checks that modules talk to each other correctly. System testing checks the complete system against the requirements, including performance, security and usability. Only after this is the software delivered to the customer, often with an acceptance test where the customer confirms it meets the agreed requirements.

Phase 5, operation and maintenance: The system is installed and used. Over time, users find bugs that testing missed, the environment changes (a new operating system, a new tax rule) and users want new features. Maintenance handles all of these. For long-lived systems, this phase is often the longest and most expensive of all.

Feedback in practice: In real projects, almost nobody runs waterfall in a perfectly straight line. When designers find a gap in the requirements, they go back and fix the SRS. When testers find a design flaw, the design is changed. So many diagrams show small arrows going back up one step. This is sometimes called the iterative waterfall model. The key difference from agile is that going back is treated as an exception to be controlled, not a normal part of every cycle.

Managing change in waterfall: Because the SRS is signed, a change cannot just be slipped in. The usual path is a formal change request: someone writes what should change and why, the team estimates the impact on design, code, tests, schedule and cost, and a change control board (customer and project leaders) approves or rejects it. If approved, all affected documents are updated so they stay consistent. This protects the project from chaos, but it is slow. A small change like "add a mobile number field to the form" may take days of paperwork in a strict waterfall project.

Overlapping phases: Some teams soften waterfall by letting neighbouring phases overlap a little, for example starting the design of well-understood parts while the rest of the requirements are still being finished. This variation is sometimes called the sashimi model, because the phases overlap like slices of fish on a plate. It saves time, but it also means a late requirement change can affect work that has already started.

Advantages: Waterfall is simple to understand and to manage. Each phase has clear deliverables and milestones, so a manager can say "design is 100 percent done and approved". It produces thorough documentation, which helps with maintenance, audits and handing the system to another team. It works well with fixed-price contracts, because the scope is agreed at the start. And it forces the team to think carefully about requirements and design before writing code.

Disadvantages: The biggest problem is that working software appears very late. The customer may see the real system only after many months, and only then realises that something important is missing or misunderstood. Changes are expensive, because a change in requirements can ripple through design, code and tests. Real customers rarely know all their requirements at the start, but waterfall assumes they do. Testing comes at the end, so serious problems can be discovered when there is no time left. And the model gives little visible progress to the users during development.

When waterfall fits: Waterfall is a reasonable choice when requirements are well understood, stable and unlikely to change; when the technology is familiar to the team; when the project is short or is a new version of a well-known system; or when external rules demand heavy documentation and formal sign-offs, as in some government, defence, aviation and medical projects. For example, rewriting an existing, well-documented payroll system on a new platform, with the same rules, can work well with waterfall.

Worked comparison of timing: Suppose a 12-month project has 2 months of requirements, 2 of design, 4 of coding, 3 of testing and 1 of deployment. With waterfall, the customer first uses the real system around month 11 or 12. If the customer then says "the report screen is not what we meant", the fix must go back through design, code and testing, maybe adding two or three months. In an iterative model, the same report screen might have been shown in month 3, and the misunderstanding fixed in days.

The V-model: The V-model is a version of waterfall that puts strong focus on testing. Draw the development phases going down the left side of a letter V: requirements, system design, architectural design, module (detailed) design. At the bottom of the V is coding. Then the testing phases go up the right side: unit testing, integration testing, system testing and acceptance testing. Each left-side phase is paired with a right-side testing phase straight across from it.

The pairs: Module design is paired with unit testing: the unit tests check that each module does what its detailed design promised. Architectural design is paired with integration testing: the integration tests check that modules connect as the architecture said. System design (or system requirements) is paired with system testing: the whole system is tested against the system specification. User requirements are paired with acceptance testing: the customer checks that the system meets their real needs. The important trick is that the test plans are written during the matching left-side phase, long before coding, so testing is planned early even if it runs later.

Verification and validation: The V-model is often used to explain two important words. Verification asks "are we building the product right?", meaning does each phase's output correctly follow from the previous phase's specification. Reviews of design documents and unit testing against the design are verification. Validation asks "are we building the right product?", meaning does the final system meet the user's real needs. Acceptance testing with the customer is validation. This phrasing comes from Barry Boehm and is a very common exam question.

V-model strengths and weaknesses: Its strengths are that testing is planned from the start, every requirement has a matching test, and defects in specifications can be spotted while writing test plans. It is popular in safety-critical areas such as automotive and medical software, where traceability from requirement to test is required. Its weaknesses are the same as waterfall: it is rigid, working software appears late, and it handles changing requirements poorly.

Real life example 1, a bank's interest calculation module: A bank in Dhaka needs a module that calculates interest on fixed deposits according to rules set by the central bank and the bank's own policy. The rules are written down clearly, they rarely change, and errors could cost a lot of money. A V-model approach works well: the business rules are documented and approved, acceptance test cases are written from the rules on day one (for example, 1,00,000 Taka for 1 year at 8 percent should earn 8,000 Taka before tax), the design is reviewed, the code is unit tested, and finally the bank's officers run the acceptance tests.

Real life example 2, where waterfall hurt: Imagine a ministry that ordered an online service for citizens with a two-year waterfall contract. Requirements were written in the first months by officials, without testing ideas on real citizens. When the system finally launched, people found the forms too long, the Bangla text confusing and the mobile view broken. Fixing these needed new contracts and months of work. This kind of story, seen in many countries, is a big reason agile and iterative methods became popular for user-facing systems.

Common mistakes: Students often say waterfall has "no feedback at all"; most practical versions allow going back, but it is costly. Some confuse the V-model with a totally different idea; it is waterfall with testing levels mapped to development phases. Many swap verification and validation; remember "product right" vs "right product". Another mistake is saying testing happens only at the end in the V-model; execution comes later, but test planning happens early.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the waterfall model. List its advantages and disadvantages, and when it is appropriate. Draw the V-model and explain which testing phase pairs with which development phase. Differentiate verification and validation with examples. Compare waterfall with the iterative or incremental model.

Recap: Waterfall arranges requirements, design, implementation, testing and maintenance in a strict sequence with sign-offs. It is simple, well documented and good for stable, well-understood projects, but working software appears late and change is expensive. The V-model pairs each development phase with a testing phase and plans tests early. Verification checks we built the product right; validation checks we built the right product. Next lesson: models that deliver software in pieces, incremental and prototyping.
key_points: Waterfall runs requirements, design, implementation, testing and maintenance in a fixed sequence with sign-offs.
It is usually traced to Royce's 1970 paper, which itself warned about the purely one-way version.
Strengths: simple, clear milestones, strong documentation, suits fixed and stable requirements.
Weaknesses: working software appears late, changes are expensive, testing comes at the end.
The V-model pairs requirements with acceptance tests, system design with system tests, architecture with integration tests, module design with unit tests.
In the V-model, test plans are written early in the matching development phase.
Verification: are we building the product right? Validation: are we building the right product?
Use plan-driven models for stable, well-understood or safety-critical systems.

Are we building the right product?

lessons.title: Incremental, Iterative and Prototyping Models
lessons.content:
Think about how a new family builds a house in a village in Bangladesh. They rarely build the full two-storey house at once. First they build one room and a kitchen so they can move in. A year later, when there is more money, they add two more rooms. Later a veranda, then the second floor. At each step the family lives in a house that works, and every addition is shaped by what they learned living there. This is the spirit of incremental development: deliver a useful part first, then grow it step by step.

The problem with doing everything at once: In the last lesson we saw that waterfall delivers working software only at the end. If the requirements were wrong or the market changed, the team finds out too late. Customers also have to wait a long time before they get any value. Incremental, iterative and prototyping models were designed to fix this: show something real early, learn from it, and adjust.

The incremental model: In the incremental model, the system is split into pieces called increments. Each increment is a working, deliverable part of the system. The first increment usually contains the core features, the minimum that is useful. Each later increment adds more features on top. Inside each increment, the team still does a small version of analysis, design, coding and testing, often in a waterfall-like way. Pressman describes it as linear sequences applied in a staggered fashion over time.

How increments are chosen: The customer and team list all the requirements and rank them by priority. The highest-priority requirements go into the first increment. For a word processor, Pressman's classic example is: increment 1 delivers basic file management, editing and document production; increment 2 adds more advanced editing; increment 3 adds spelling and grammar checking; increment 4 adds advanced page layout. Each increment is delivered to users, who start benefiting immediately.

Worked example, a release plan: A pharmacy chain in Chattogram wants a point-of-sale system. Requirements ranked by value: sell medicines and print receipts, manage stock, alert when stock is low, handle supplier orders, generate monthly reports, offer a loyalty card. Increment 1 (month 2): sales and receipts, with a simple stock count. Increment 2 (month 4): full stock management and low-stock alerts. Increment 3 (month 6): supplier orders. Increment 4 (month 8): reports and loyalty cards. After two months the shops are already selling with the new system, and feedback from the counters shapes the next increments.

Advantages of incremental delivery: Customers get value early. The most important features are delivered first, so they get the most testing and use. Risk is lower, because if the project is stopped, there is still a working system. Feedback from real users guides later increments. It is often easier to test and debug a smaller increment. And the staff can be added gradually; an early increment can be built with a small team.

Disadvantages: The overall architecture must be planned well enough at the start, or later increments may not fit cleanly. Adding features repeatedly can make the structure messy unless time is spent on refactoring. Some systems need a lot of shared basic infrastructure (security, database, communication) before any useful feature works, which makes a small first increment hard. Contracts and budgets are harder to fix in advance, because the later increments may change.

Minimum viable product: Startups often call the first increment a minimum viable product, or MVP. It is the smallest version that real users can use and that lets the team learn whether the idea is worth continuing. The word "viable" is important: an MVP is small but must still work reliably for what it does. A food delivery MVP might only cover one area of Dhaka, a few restaurants and cash payment. If people love it, the team invests in more areas and features; if nobody uses it, the team has lost weeks, not years.

Planning the skeleton first: Before the first increment, a good team spends a short time on the overall architecture: the main components, the database approach, how security will work, how the app will talk to the server. This skeleton does not need every detail, but it must leave room for the later increments. Without it, increment 3 might require tearing down what increments 1 and 2 built. Think of the village house again: if the first room was built with a weak foundation, the second floor cannot be added later.

Iterative development: Iterative means repeating a cycle to refine something. In iterative development, the team builds a rough version of the whole system or a feature, gets feedback, then improves it in the next iteration, and repeats. Each iteration produces a better version. Think of drawing a portrait: first a rough outline of the whole face, then the eyes and nose more clearly, then shading. Incremental is like adding new parts; iterative is like improving the parts you have.

Incremental vs iterative together: In practice most modern methods are both. Each iteration (say two weeks) adds a new increment of features and also improves what exists based on feedback. Agile methods such as Scrum are iterative and incremental. A common picture: incremental builds a painting one square at a time, each square finished; iterative paints the whole canvas roughly and refines it again and again. Real teams usually do a mix.

The prototyping model: A prototype is an early, simplified version of the system, built quickly to answer a question. It is used when the customer cannot clearly say what they want, or when the developers are unsure whether an idea or a technology will work. The steps are: listen to the customer and gather basic requirements, build a quick prototype (often just screens), let the customer try it, collect feedback, refine the prototype, and repeat until the requirements are clear. Then the real system is built.

Throwaway prototyping: In throwaway (rapid) prototyping, the prototype is built only to learn and is then thrown away. It might be made with paper sketches, a design tool like Figma, or quick code that ignores security, performance and error handling. Once the requirements are clear, the real system is designed and built properly from scratch. The danger is that the customer sees a working-looking prototype and says "great, it is almost done, just give us this". The team must explain clearly that the prototype is not the product.

Evolutionary prototyping: In evolutionary prototyping, the prototype is not thrown away. It is built with reasonable quality from the start and keeps being refined until it becomes the final system. This is closer to iterative development. It suits projects where requirements are discovered gradually, such as a new kind of app. The risk is that early quick-and-dirty decisions remain in the final product and become hard to fix.

Kinds of prototypes: A low-fidelity prototype is rough, like paper sketches or wireframes; it is cheap and good for discussing layout and flow. A high-fidelity prototype looks and behaves much like the real product, with real colours, buttons and maybe some fake data; it is good for usability testing. A horizontal prototype shows many screens with little behind them, to explore the user interface broadly. A vertical prototype implements one feature deeply, through all layers, to test a technical risk, for example whether an SMS gateway can send 10,000 messages per minute.

Advantages of prototyping: Users see something concrete early, which makes it much easier for them to say what they really want. Misunderstandings are caught before expensive coding. User interfaces improve a lot through quick feedback. Technical risks can be tested with vertical prototypes. Users feel involved, which increases acceptance of the final system.

Deciding when to stop: Every prototyping loop needs an exit rule, or it can go on forever. Useful rules are: stop when the customer has approved the key screens and flows, stop when a fixed number of rounds (say three) is reached, or stop when the technical question the prototype was built to answer has a clear yes or no. Writing down what was learned at each round, even as short notes, turns the prototype into useful requirements for the real build.

Disadvantages of prototyping: Customers may think the prototype is the finished product and push to ship it. Developers may make quick compromises (a slow algorithm, no security) and forget to remove them. Endless prototyping loops can waste time if nobody decides when the requirements are clear enough. Managing cost is harder because the number of iterations is not fixed. A good rule is to agree at the start whether the prototype is throwaway or evolutionary.

Prototyping inside other models: Prototyping is often not a full process model on its own but a technique used inside other models. A waterfall project may build a throwaway prototype during requirements. A Scrum team may sketch screens in Figma before a sprint. The System Analysis and Design course discusses prototyping as a requirements gathering technique; here we focus on its role in the life cycle.

Real life example 1, a ride-sharing app: When a ride-sharing service starts in a city, the first version might only let a rider request a motorbike ride and pay cash. That is increment 1, and it already solves the main problem. Later increments add car rides, digital payments, food delivery, parcel delivery and ratings. Each feature is improved through iterations as the company learns how riders and drivers actually use the app. This growth pattern is typical of successful app companies.

Real life example 2, an upazila health clinic app: Health workers in rural clinics need to record patient visits, but the designers have never worked in a clinic. Instead of writing a 50-page SRS, they make paper prototypes of three screens and visit two clinics. They learn that workers often have no internet, write numbers faster than text, and need large buttons. The prototype is thrown away and the real app is designed for offline use with number pads. A few days of prototyping saved months of building the wrong thing.

Common mistakes: Students mix up incremental (add new pieces, each delivered) with iterative (refine the same thing repeatedly). Another mistake is saying the prototype "is" the final product in all prototyping; that is only true for evolutionary prototyping. Some believe incremental needs no planning; it actually needs a solid architecture and a clear priority list. Finally, prototypes are not only for user interfaces; vertical prototypes test technical risks too.

What exams ask: Explain the incremental model with a diagram and an example. Differentiate incremental and iterative development. Describe the prototyping model and its steps. Differentiate throwaway and evolutionary prototyping. List the advantages and disadvantages of prototyping. When would you choose prototyping over waterfall?

Recap: Incremental development delivers the system in working pieces, highest priority first. Iterative development repeatedly refines what exists. Most modern methods are both. Prototyping builds quick, simplified versions to clarify requirements or test risks; throwaway prototypes are discarded after learning, evolutionary ones grow into the product. These models give early feedback and lower risk, but need good architecture and careful expectation management. Next lesson: the risk-driven spiral model, RAD, the Unified Process, and how to choose a model.
key_points: Incremental: deliver the system in working pieces, highest-priority features first.
Iterative: build a rough version and refine it repeatedly based on feedback.
Most modern methods, including Scrum, are both iterative and incremental.
Prototyping builds a quick, simplified version to clarify requirements or test technical risks.
Throwaway prototypes are discarded after learning; evolutionary prototypes grow into the final system.
Low-fidelity vs high-fidelity, horizontal (many screens) vs vertical (one feature in depth) prototypes.
Risks: customers mistake prototypes for the product; quick hacks remain; architecture may degrade.
Incremental delivery gives early value and lowers the risk of total failure.
lessons.tip: To remember the difference, think of LEGO: incremental adds new bricks, iterative reshapes the model you already built.

lessons.title: Spiral, RAD, the Unified Process and Choosing a Model
lessons.content:
Imagine planning a trip from Dhaka to Bandarban during the rainy season. A careful traveller does not just book everything and go. First she asks: what could go wrong? The road could be flooded, the hotel could be fake, a landslide could block the hill road. For each risk she does something: checks the weather, calls the hotel, keeps a backup route. Then she travels the first part, looks around, and plans the next part with fresh information. Each loop of "plan, check risks, move, review" takes her closer to the goal. The spiral model of software development works exactly like this careful traveller.

Why risk matters: A risk is something that might go wrong and hurt the project, like a new technology not working, a key developer leaving, or requirements being misunderstood. Waterfall and simple incremental models do not make risk the centre of planning. Big, expensive and novel projects needed a model where the most dangerous unknowns are attacked first, before lots of money is spent. That led to the spiral model.

The spiral model: The spiral model was proposed by Barry Boehm in the 1980s. It combines the iterative nature of prototyping with the controlled, systematic steps of waterfall, and puts risk analysis at the centre. The process is drawn as a spiral that starts small in the middle and grows outward. Each loop of the spiral is a phase of the project, and the distance from the centre represents the cumulative cost so far. The angle represents progress within the current loop.

The four quadrants: Each loop of the spiral passes through four quadrants. First, determine objectives, alternatives and constraints for this phase: what do we want, what options do we have, what limits apply? Second, evaluate alternatives and identify and resolve risks: find the biggest risks and reduce them, often by building a prototype, running a simulation or doing a benchmark. Third, develop and verify the next-level product: do the actual development for this loop, such as writing requirements, a design, or code and tests. Fourth, plan the next phase: review the results with stakeholders and decide whether and how to continue into the next loop.

How the loops progress: Early loops might produce a concept of operation and a requirements plan. Middle loops produce a validated design, perhaps supported by more advanced prototypes. Later loops produce detailed design, code, testing and deployment. There is no fixed number of loops; the project keeps spiralling until the product is complete or the risks show it should stop. A very useful property is the review at the end of each loop: management can cancel the project early if the risk analysis shows it is not viable, before most of the money is spent.

Worked example of risk-driven planning: A team must build a system that reads car number plates at Dhaka toll plazas. Loop 1: objective, read plates in real time; biggest risk, can the cameras read Bangla number plates at night in rain? They build a small prototype with sample images. Accuracy is only 70 percent, so they test better cameras and lighting until it reaches 97 percent. Loop 2: risk, can the server handle thousands of cars per hour? They run a load test with simulated traffic. Loop 3: develop the full system. Each loop attacks the scariest unknown first.

Why it is called a meta-model: The spiral is sometimes called a meta-model, a model of models, because it can behave like other models depending on the risks. If the biggest risk is unclear user needs, a loop looks like prototyping. If the requirements and design are well understood and the main risk is just getting the work done, the remaining loops look like waterfall steps. If the product is delivered in parts, the loops look incremental. Risk decides which shape each loop takes.

Strengths and weaknesses of spiral: Strengths: strong focus on risk, good for large, expensive and complex projects, allows changes and prototypes at each loop, and lets management stop early. Weaknesses: it needs real risk assessment skill, which not every team has. It can be costly and complex to manage, and it is overkill for small, low-risk projects. It is also harder to agree on a fixed price contract, because the number of loops is not known at the start.

RAD: Rapid Application Development, or RAD, is an approach that became popular around 1990, associated with James Martin. The goal is to deliver working software very quickly, often within 60 to 90 days, by using heavy user involvement, prototyping, reusable components and powerful tools that generate code (for example form builders and database tools). Work is divided among several teams, each building one part in parallel.

Timeboxing in RAD: A key idea in RAD is the timebox. A timebox is a fixed period, say 60 days, for delivering a set of features. The deadline does not move. If not everything fits, lower-priority features are dropped from this timebox, not the deadline extended. This idea of fixing time and adjusting scope later became central in agile methods too, for example in Scrum's fixed-length sprints.

RAD phases and limits: A common description of RAD includes business modeling, data modeling, process modeling, application generation and testing/turnover. RAD works well when the system can be split into modules, users are available to give quick feedback, and suitable tools and reusable components exist. It works poorly for systems with high technical risk, very high performance needs, or where users cannot be involved often. Without discipline, it can produce a quickly built but poorly designed system.

The Unified Process: The Unified Process (UP) is an iterative and incremental framework that grew out of the work of Ivar Jacobson, Grady Booch and James Rumbaugh, the same three people behind UML. The best-known commercial version is the Rational Unified Process (RUP), later owned by IBM. UP is described as use-case driven (requirements are captured as use cases, which drive design and testing), architecture-centric (a solid architecture is built early) and iterative and incremental (the system grows over many iterations).

The four phases of UP: Inception: define the scope and business case, identify key use cases and major risks, and decide whether the project is worth doing. Elaboration: analyse the problem in more depth, build and validate the core architecture (an executable architectural baseline), and plan the rest of the project. Construction: build the remaining features in a series of iterations, producing a working product. Transition: deliver the product to users, including beta testing, training, data migration and fixing issues found in real use. Each phase ends with a milestone where progress is reviewed.

Disciplines across phases: In UP, the work types (called disciplines or workflows) run across all phases with different intensity. The main ones are business modeling, requirements, analysis and design, implementation, test and deployment, supported by configuration and change management, project management and environment. The famous "hump chart" shows, for example, that requirements work is heaviest in inception and elaboration, while implementation peaks in construction. This shows clearly that UP is not waterfall: all kinds of work happen in every phase, just in different amounts.

Phases are not activities: A common trap is to think inception means requirements, elaboration means design, construction means coding and transition means testing. That is wrong. Phases are time periods with goals and milestones. Inside each phase there can be several iterations, and each iteration may include requirements, design, coding and testing. For example, during elaboration a team codes and tests the riskiest parts of the architecture to prove it works.

Comparing the models: Waterfall: one pass, heavy documents, stable requirements, low flexibility. V-model: waterfall plus early test planning, good for safety-critical. Incremental: early value, priority-ordered delivery. Prototyping: clarify unclear requirements or test risks. Spiral: risk-driven loops for large, risky projects. RAD: speed via tools, reuse and timeboxes. Unified Process: use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative phases. Agile methods (next lessons): short iterations, close customer collaboration, light documentation and embracing change.

How to choose: Ask a few questions. How clear and stable are the requirements? Clear and stable points towards waterfall or V-model; unclear points towards prototyping, iterative or agile. How big and risky is the project? Large and risky suggests spiral or UP; small and low-risk suggests something simple. Is the customer available often? If yes, agile and prototyping work well. Are there legal or safety rules that require documentation and traceability? That pushes towards V-model or a documented process. How soon does the customer need something usable? Urgent value suggests incremental or RAD.

A quick decision example: A government agency needs a land records system with strict legal rules, a fixed budget and audits. A V-model or a carefully documented incremental approach fits. A startup wants a new social app and has no idea what users will like. Prototyping and agile fit. A defence contractor building a new radar control system with unproven hardware should use a risk-driven approach like spiral. A company replacing an old internal tool, with clear rules and tight time, might use RAD-style timeboxes.

Real life example 1, a mobile financial service: Before launching a new nationwide payment service, a company faces big risks: will the system handle millions of transactions on Eid days, will it satisfy central bank rules, will rural users understand the interface? A spiral-like approach makes sense: first loops test transaction throughput and security with prototypes, then regulatory compliance, then usability with pilot users in a few districts, and only then the national rollout.

Real life example 2, a university ERP using UP: A private university wants an ERP for admission, registration, results and accounts. In inception, the team writes key use cases (student registers for courses, teacher submits grades) and a business case. In elaboration, they build the core architecture and test the hardest part, course registration with thousands of students at once. In construction, they add modules in iterations. In transition, they run the old and new systems side by side for one semester and train staff.

Common mistakes: Students often draw the spiral without explaining the four quadrants, or forget that risk analysis is its defining feature. Some think RAD means "no design"; it means fast delivery with tools and reuse, still with modeling. Many map UP phases one-to-one to waterfall stages, which is wrong. And some claim one model is always the best; the right answer always depends on the project.

What exams ask: Draw the spiral model and explain its four quadrants. Why is the spiral model called a risk-driven or meta-model? What is RAD and what is a timebox? Explain the four phases of the Unified Process and its key features (use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative). Compare process models and justify which one you would choose for a given scenario.

Recap: The spiral model loops through objectives, risk analysis, development and planning, attacking the biggest risks first; it suits large, risky projects. RAD delivers quickly using tools, reuse, user involvement and fixed timeboxes. The Unified Process is use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative and incremental, with phases inception, elaboration, construction and transition. Choose a model by looking at requirement stability, risk, size, customer availability, regulation and urgency. Next lesson: the agile revolution and Extreme Programming.
key_points: Boehm's spiral model is risk-driven: each loop sets objectives, analyses and reduces risks, develops, then plans the next loop.
Distance from the spiral's centre shows cumulative cost; management can stop after any loop.
RAD delivers quickly through user involvement, prototyping, reuse, code-generating tools and fixed timeboxes.
A timebox fixes the deadline and drops lower-priority scope instead of slipping the date.
The Unified Process is use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative and incremental.
UP phases: inception, elaboration, construction, transition, each ending in a milestone.
UP disciplines (requirements, design, implementation, test...) run in every phase with different intensity.
Choose a model based on requirement stability, risk, size, customer availability, regulation and urgency.

lessons.title: Agile Development and Extreme Programming
lessons.content:
Imagine a tailor making a wedding sherwani. One tailor takes your measurements once, disappears for two months and hands you the final sherwani the day before the wedding. If the sleeves are too long or the colour looks different in daylight, it is too late. Another tailor asks you to come back every week: first to check the cut on a rough cloth, then the first stitching, then the embroidery. Each visit you say "a bit shorter here, loosen this". The second tailor changes small things often and you end up with exactly what you wanted. Agile software development is the second tailor.

The problem agile solved: By the 1990s many teams felt that heavy, document-driven processes were slowing them down. Projects spent months writing requirements that changed anyway. Customers saw working software too late. Developers spent more time on paperwork than on building and testing. Markets, especially for web and mobile software, were changing faster than a long plan could follow. Several lightweight methods appeared, such as Extreme Programming, Scrum, Crystal, Feature-Driven Development and DSDM, each trying to deliver faster and adapt better.

The Agile Manifesto: In February 2001, seventeen practitioners met at a ski resort in Snowbird, Utah, USA, and wrote the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. It says they have come to value: individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. It ends with a key sentence: while there is value in the items on the right, they value the items on the left more.

Reading the values correctly: The manifesto does not say "no documentation", "no plans" or "no processes". It says when you must choose, prefer the left side. A team still writes documents, but only those that truly help. A team still plans, but expects the plan to change. A team still uses tools, but people talking to each other solves more problems than any tool. Many teams misuse "agile" as an excuse for chaos; that is not what the authors meant.

The twelve principles, in short: The manifesto is supported by twelve principles. In plain words, they say: satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software; welcome changing requirements, even late; deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale; business people and developers work together daily; build projects around motivated individuals and trust them; face-to-face conversation is the most efficient way to share information; working software is the primary measure of progress; keep a sustainable pace that can be maintained indefinitely; pay continuous attention to technical excellence and good design; simplicity, the art of maximising the amount of work not done, is essential; the best designs emerge from self-organising teams; and at regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective and adjusts.

How agile works in practice: Agile teams work in short iterations, usually one to four weeks. At the start of each iteration they choose a small set of the most valuable features. During the iteration they design, code and test those features completely. At the end they show working software to the customer, collect feedback, and reflect on their own way of working. Then the next iteration begins with updated priorities. Requirements are kept as a living, ordered list rather than a frozen document.

The cost of change curve: Traditional thinking says changes get more and more expensive as a project progresses. Agile practitioners argue that with good practices, such as automated tests, continuous integration, simple design and refactoring, the cost of a late change can be kept much lower. That is why agile can "welcome change": not because change is free, but because the team has built safety nets that make change safer and cheaper.

Extreme Programming: Extreme Programming, usually called XP, was developed by Kent Beck in the late 1990s, and he described it in the book Extreme Programming Explained. The name comes from the idea of taking good practices to the extreme: if code review is good, review code all the time through pair programming; if testing is good, write tests before the code; if integration is good, integrate many times a day; if short iterations are good, make them very short.

XP values: XP is built on five values. Communication: team members and customers talk often and openly. Simplicity: do the simplest thing that could possibly work. Feedback: get feedback quickly from tests, from the customer and from the team. Courage: be brave enough to change or throw away code, and to tell the truth about estimates. Respect: team members respect each other's work and opinions. The first edition of the book had four values; respect was added in the second edition.

User stories and the planning game: In XP, requirements are written as user stories, short descriptions of a feature from the user's point of view, often written on cards. A common template is: As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some reason]. For example: as a passenger, I want to see the driver's location on a map so that I know when to go downstairs. In the planning game, customers write and prioritise stories, developers estimate them, and together they choose which stories go into the next release and iteration.

Small releases: XP releases working software to users very often, in small pieces. Each release must deliver real business value. Small releases give quick feedback and reduce the risk of big surprises.

Simple design and refactoring: XP says design only for the current needs, not for imagined future needs, which matches the principle known as YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it). Because the design is kept simple, it must be improved constantly. Refactoring means changing the internal structure of code to make it cleaner without changing its external behaviour, for example renaming unclear variables, splitting a long function or removing duplicated code. Tests make refactoring safe.

Test-driven development: In XP, programmers write an automated unit test before writing the code that makes it pass. The cycle is: write a failing test (red), write the simplest code to pass it (green), then clean up the code (refactor). Customers also define acceptance tests for each story. The result is a large suite of automated tests that run constantly and catch regressions. TDD is covered in more depth in the test automation lesson.

Pair programming: Two programmers sit at one computer. One, the driver, types the code; the other, the navigator, reviews each line, thinks about the bigger picture and spots mistakes. They switch roles often. It looks wasteful, two people for one keyboard, but it gives continuous code review, spreads knowledge across the team, and often reduces defects. It is also tiring, so teams usually mix pairing with solo work.

Continuous integration: In XP, every developer integrates their code into the shared main codebase frequently, at least daily and often several times a day. Each integration triggers a build and runs all the tests. If something breaks, it is fixed immediately. This avoids "integration hell", where weeks of separate work are combined at the end and nothing fits.

Collective ownership, coding standards and sustainable pace: In XP, any pair can change any part of the code; nobody owns a module alone, which avoids bottlenecks when one person is away. A shared coding standard makes all code look as if one person wrote it. Sustainable pace, originally called the 40-hour week, means the team does not rely on constant overtime, because tired programmers make more mistakes. XP also recommended an on-site customer, a real customer representative sitting with the team to answer questions immediately.

Other agile methods briefly: Scrum focuses on how to organise the team and work in sprints; we study it in the next lesson. Kanban focuses on visualising work and limiting work in progress. Crystal is a family of methods adjusted to team size and project criticality. Feature-Driven Development organises work around small client-valued features. DSDM grew out of RAD and emphasises fixed time and cost with flexible features. Lean software development borrows ideas from Toyota's production system, such as eliminating waste.

Where agile fits and where it struggles: Agile fits best when requirements are uncertain or changing, when the customer can be closely involved, and when the team is small to medium and can communicate easily. It struggles with very large teams spread across the world, with strict fixed-price contracts that require full specifications in advance, and with safety-critical systems that legally require extensive documentation, although many such organisations now use adapted, scaled versions of agile.

Real life example 1, a food delivery startup: A small Dhaka startup builds a food delivery app. Every two weeks the team releases a new version to a test group of users. One week they learn that users want to see the restaurant's estimated cooking time; two weeks later it is live. Their tests run automatically on every commit, so they can change the payment screen without fear. They meet the founder every day to clarify stories. This rhythm lets them respond to competitors and customer complaints within days, not months.

Real life example 2, a software outsourcing company: Many software companies in Bangladesh build products for clients in Europe, North America and elsewhere. A typical arrangement is that the client's product owner joins video calls for sprint planning and reviews, while the developers in Dhaka work in two-week iterations. The client sees working software every sprint, changes priorities when their market changes, and the team keeps code quality high with pull request reviews and automated tests. Agile practices help bridge distance and time zones.

Common mistakes: Thinking agile means no documentation or no planning. Thinking agile means no deadlines; in fact iterations have strict deadlines. Doing "agile" only in name: having daily meetings but still delivering everything at the end. Ignoring technical practices; without automated tests and refactoring, frequent change quickly ruins code quality. And believing pair programming means one person watches while the other works; the navigator is actively reviewing and thinking.

What exams ask: State the four values of the Agile Manifesto. Explain several agile principles. What is Extreme Programming? List and explain XP practices such as pair programming, TDD, refactoring, continuous integration and small releases. List the XP values. Compare agile with plan-driven development. Write a user story in the standard format.

Recap: Agile development values people, working software, collaboration and responding to change, as stated in the 2001 Agile Manifesto. Work is done in short iterations with frequent feedback. Extreme Programming, created by Kent Beck, pushes good practices to the extreme: user stories, small releases, simple design, refactoring, test-driven development, pair programming, continuous integration, collective ownership and sustainable pace, guided by communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect. Next lesson: Scrum, the most widely used agile framework, and Kanban.

Agile still values processes, documents, contracts and plans, just less than the items on the left.
Agile teams deliver working software in short iterations and use feedback to reprioritise.
XP was created by Kent Beck; its values are communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect.
XP practices: user stories, planning game, small releases, simple design, refactoring, TDD, pair programming, continuous integration.
Collective code ownership, coding standards and sustainable pace keep XP teams healthy.
User story format: As a [user], I want [goal] so that [reason].
Agile fits uncertain requirements and involved customers; it needs strong technical practices to work.

To give each developer their own private module
