lessons.title: Scrum and Kanban
lessons.content:
Think of a cricket team during a T20 series. Before each match, the captain and coach decide the plan for that match only: batting order, bowlers, field settings. During the match, players talk constantly and adjust. After the match, they sit together: what went well, what went wrong, what will we change next time? The series is won match by match, not by a single plan made months before. Scrum organises software work in the same rhythm: short, fixed-length cycles with a clear goal, daily coordination, a show of results and a team review at the end.

What Scrum is: Scrum is a lightweight framework for developing complex products in short cycles. It was developed by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, who first presented it in the mid-1990s and maintain the official Scrum Guide. Scrum is not a full method that tells you how to code or test; it is a framework of roles, events and artifacts, and teams add their own technical practices, often from XP. Scrum is the most widely used agile framework today.

Empiricism, the idea underneath: Scrum is based on empiricism, meaning knowledge comes from experience and decisions are made based on what is observed. It has three pillars. Transparency: the work and the process are visible to everyone involved. Inspection: the team frequently checks progress and artifacts to detect problems. Adaptation: when something is going wrong, the team adjusts as soon as possible. Every Scrum event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt.

The Scrum Team: A Scrum Team is small, typically 10 or fewer people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies. It is cross-functional, meaning together the members have all the skills needed to create a usable product increment, and self-managing, meaning they decide internally who does what and how. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes three accountabilities: the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers.

The Product Owner: The Product Owner is one person who is accountable for maximising the value of the product. They manage the Product Backlog: writing or approving items, ordering them by value, and making sure everyone understands them. They represent the customers and stakeholders, decide what gets built next, and accept or reject the work. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee, though they may listen to many stakeholders. In a company, this might be a product manager or a business analyst with decision power.

The Scrum Master: The Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness and for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. They are not a traditional boss who assigns tasks. They coach the team in self-management, help remove impediments (blockers like a missing server access or a delayed decision from another department), make sure events happen and stay productive and within their timebox, and help the wider organisation understand Scrum. The Scrum Guide calls them a true leader who serves the team.

The Developers: Developers are the people in the Scrum Team committed to creating a usable increment each Sprint. "Developer" here does not mean only programmers; testers, designers, database specialists and others who build the increment are all Developers. They create the plan for the Sprint (the Sprint Backlog), keep quality by following the Definition of Done, adapt their plan every day, and hold each other accountable as professionals.

The Sprint: The Sprint is the heartbeat of Scrum. It is a fixed-length period of one month or less, commonly two weeks, during which a usable increment is created. A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends. During the Sprint, no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal, quality does not decrease, and the Product Backlog is refined as needed. A Sprint can be cancelled only by the Product Owner, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

Sprint Planning: Sprint Planning starts the Sprint, and for a one-month Sprint it is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours (usually shorter for shorter Sprints). The whole Scrum Team answers three questions. Why is this Sprint valuable? They agree a Sprint Goal. What can be done this Sprint? Developers select items from the Product Backlog, considering their past performance and capacity. How will the chosen work get done? Developers break items into smaller tasks, often of a day or less. The Sprint Goal, the selected items and the plan together form the Sprint Backlog.

The Daily Scrum: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held every working day at the same time and place. Its purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan for the next day. Many teams use three questions: what did I do yesterday toward the goal, what will I do today, and is anything blocking me? The 2020 guide lets teams choose any structure as long as it focuses on progress toward the goal. Detailed problem solving happens after the meeting, with only the people involved.

The Sprint Review: At the end of the Sprint, the Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and discusses progress toward the Product Goal. It is a working session, not a slide show: people see the working increment, give feedback, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted based on what was learned. For a one-month Sprint it is at most four hours.

The Sprint Retrospective: The Sprint Retrospective is the last event of the Sprint. The Scrum Team looks at how the last Sprint went regarding individuals, interactions, processes, tools and their Definition of Done. What went well? What problems happened and how were they solved or not? They identify the most helpful changes to improve their effectiveness, and the most impactful improvements may even be added to the next Sprint Backlog. For a one-month Sprint it is at most three hours. The Review is about the product; the Retrospective is about the way of working.

The Product Backlog: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of everything that might be needed to improve the product. It is the single source of work for the Scrum Team. Items at the top are small, clear and ready to be built; items lower down may be large and vague. Backlog refinement is the ongoing activity of breaking items down, adding detail, estimating and reordering. The Product Backlog's commitment is the Product Goal, a long-term objective for the product.

The Sprint Backlog and the Increment: The Sprint Backlog contains the Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, and the plan for delivering them. It belongs to the Developers and is updated throughout the Sprint. An Increment is a concrete step toward the Product Goal: the sum of all work completed, verified and usable. Several increments may be created in one Sprint. The Increment's commitment is the Definition of Done.

Definition of Done: The Definition of Done is a formal, shared description of the quality an item must meet to be considered part of the Increment. A typical Definition of Done: code written and reviewed, unit tests passing, integrated into the main branch, acceptance criteria met, no known critical bugs, documentation updated, deployed to the test environment. If an item does not meet it, it is not done and goes back to the Product Backlog. This prevents "almost done" work from piling up.

User stories, story points and velocity: Scrum itself does not require these, but most Scrum teams use them. Product Backlog items are often written as user stories with acceptance criteria. Teams estimate effort in story points, a relative measure of size and complexity, commonly using a Fibonacci-like scale such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. A story of 8 points is roughly four times the effort of a 2-point story. Velocity is the number of story points a team completes per Sprint. If a team finished 28, 32 and 30 points in the last three Sprints, its average velocity is 30, so a backlog of 150 points needs about 5 more Sprints.

Burndown charts: A Sprint burndown chart shows the remaining work (in hours or points) on the vertical axis and the days of the Sprint on the horizontal axis. An ideal straight line goes from the total at day 1 to zero on the last day. The actual line shows reality. If the actual line stays above the ideal for days, the team is behind and should talk about scope or blockers early. A release burndown does the same across many Sprints.

Kanban: Kanban comes from the Toyota Production System, where cards (kanban means signboard or card in Japanese) signalled when to make more parts. In software, it was popularised by David J. Anderson in the 2000s. A Kanban board shows columns for the stages of work, for example To Do, In Progress, Testing, Done. Each work item is a card that moves from left to right. Kanban does not use Sprints or fixed roles; work flows continuously.

WIP limits and flow: The key rule in Kanban is limiting work in progress (WIP). For example, the In Progress column may hold at most 3 cards. If it is full, nobody starts a new item; instead, the team helps finish or unblock existing items. This reduces multitasking, exposes bottlenecks (if Testing is always full, testing is the bottleneck) and shortens the time each item takes. Teams measure lead time (from request to delivery) and cycle time (from starting work to finishing it), and try to make flow smooth and predictable.

Scrum vs Kanban: Scrum uses fixed-length Sprints, defined accountabilities and events, and commits to a Sprint Goal; changes are normally made between Sprints. Kanban uses continuous flow, no required roles, and limits WIP per column; priorities can change any time a slot frees up. Scrum suits product development with planned increments. Kanban suits support and maintenance work, where urgent tickets arrive unpredictably. Many teams combine them, sometimes called Scrumban.

Real life example 1, an e-commerce team before a sale: An e-commerce company plans a big Eid sale. The Product Owner orders the backlog: flash-sale countdown page, stock reservation during checkout, discount coupons, SMS notifications. In a two-week Sprint, the team commits to the Sprint Goal "customers can buy flash-sale items without overselling stock". At the Daily Scrum, a developer reports that the payment gateway sandbox is down; the Scrum Master escalates it. At the Review, stakeholders try the flash-sale flow and ask for a "notify me" button, added to the backlog. At the Retrospective, the team agrees to set up load testing earlier next time.

Real life example 2, an IT support team with Kanban: The IT support team of a hospital in Sylhet receives tickets: a printer not working, a doctor locked out of the system, a request for a new report. Work arrives unpredictably, so Sprints would be awkward. They use a Kanban board with columns New, In Progress (limit 4), Waiting for User and Done, with an expedite lane for urgent issues like the emergency ward's system. Measuring cycle time shows that report requests take 9 days on average, so they create a template that cuts it to 3.

Common mistakes: Treating the Scrum Master as a project manager who assigns tasks. Turning the Daily Scrum into a long status report to a boss. Extending Sprints when work is unfinished instead of returning items to the backlog. Comparing velocity between different teams; story points are relative to each team. Skipping retrospectives because "we are busy". In Kanban, drawing a board but not setting WIP limits, which removes most of its benefit.

What exams ask: Describe the Scrum framework: three roles, five events and three artifacts. Explain the purpose of the Sprint Review vs the Sprint Retrospective. What is a Definition of Done? What are story points and velocity? Calculate how many Sprints remain given a velocity. Draw and explain a burndown chart. Explain Kanban and WIP limits. Compare Scrum and Kanban.

Recap: Scrum is a lightweight framework based on transparency, inspection and adaptation. The Scrum Team has a Product Owner (value and backlog), a Scrum Master (effectiveness and coaching) and Developers (building the increment). Events: the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective. Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment, with commitments Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done. Kanban visualises work and limits work in progress to improve flow. Next lesson: requirements engineering essentials.
key_points: Scrum, by Schwaber and Sutherland, is a lightweight framework built on transparency, inspection and adaptation.
Accountabilities: Product Owner (maximises value, owns backlog), Scrum Master (team effectiveness, removes impediments), Developers (build the increment).
The Sprint is one month or less; events inside it are Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15 minutes), Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.
Artifacts: Product Backlog (Product Goal), Sprint Backlog (Sprint Goal), Increment (Definition of Done).
Review inspects the product with stakeholders; Retrospective improves the team's way of working.
Story points estimate relative size; velocity is points completed per Sprint; burndown shows remaining work.
Kanban visualises work on a board and limits work in progress to improve flow; it has no fixed Sprints or roles.
Scrum suits planned product increments; Kanban suits continuous, unpredictable work like support.
lessons.tip: Make a 3-5-3 table: 3 accountabilities, 5 events, 3 artifacts. Write it from memory before every exam.
lessons.task: Make a Kanban board on a sheet of paper or with sticky notes for your own study week: columns To Do, Doing (limit 2), Done. Move cards for a week and note whether the WIP limit helped you finish things.

quiz.explain: The Product Owner manages and orders the Product Backlog to maximise value.

quiz.q: What is the timebox of the Daily Scrum?
quiz.explain: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers.

quiz.q: A team completed 24, 26 and 28 points in the last three Sprints. About how many Sprints are needed for 130 remaining points?
quiz.explain: Average velocity is 26 points per Sprint; 130 / 26 = 5 Sprints.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: To show the product to stakeholders
To improve the team's way of working
quiz.explain: The Retrospective inspects people, processes and tools and plans improvements.

quiz.q: What is the key rule that distinguishes Kanban?
options: Limiting work in progress in each stage
quiz.explain: WIP limits stop new work from starting until current work moves on, improving flow.

lessons.title: Requirements Engineering Essentials
lessons.content:
Imagine you tell a tailor, "make me a nice shirt". You get a shirt, but it has short sleeves, a bright pink colour and a size too small. The tailor did make a nice shirt, by his idea of nice. The problem was not his sewing; it was the requirement. "Nice" meant something different to each of you. Software projects suffer from this all the time. Requirements engineering is the work of finding out, writing down, checking and managing what a system must do, so that the customer's "nice shirt" and the developer's "nice shirt" are the same shirt.

What a requirement is: A requirement is a statement of a service the system must provide or a constraint it must respect. "The system shall let a student download their transcript as a PDF" is a requirement. "The transcript page shall load within 3 seconds" is also a requirement. Requirements describe what the system should do, not how it will be built internally. Choosing the database or the programming language is normally a design decision, unless the customer requires it.

Why requirements matter so much: Many studies and industry reports have found that problems with requirements, such as missing, unclear or changing requirements, are among the most common causes of project failure. As we saw in lesson 1, an error in requirements is cheap to fix when found early and very expensive when found after coding and release. A small investment in clear requirements saves a large amount of rework later.

The requirements engineering process: Requirements engineering usually includes several activities: elicitation (discovering requirements from stakeholders), analysis and negotiation (understanding, organising and resolving conflicts), specification (writing them down clearly), validation (checking they are correct and what stakeholders really want) and management (handling changes over time). Feasibility study often comes before or alongside. The techniques for elicitation, such as interviews, questionnaires, observation and workshops, and the feasibility study are covered in depth in the System Analysis and Design course; here we focus on what a good requirement looks like and how requirements are documented, checked and managed.

Stakeholders: A stakeholder is anyone who affects or is affected by the system. For a university result system, stakeholders include students, teachers, the controller of examinations, department heads, the IT team, and maybe parents and accreditation bodies. Different stakeholders want different things and sometimes conflict: students want results fast, the exam office wants every grade double-checked. Requirements engineering must identify all important stakeholders and balance their needs.

Functional requirements: Functional requirements describe what the system should do: its services, functions and behaviour in specific situations. Examples for a ride-sharing app: the rider shall be able to request a ride by choosing pickup and drop-off points; the system shall show the estimated fare before confirmation; the driver shall be able to accept or reject a request within 15 seconds; the system shall send a receipt by SMS after the trip. Functional requirements are usually tested by checking that given inputs produce the expected behaviour.

Non-functional requirements: Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how well the system must do its job, or constraints on it. They are often called quality attributes. Common types: performance (the search shall return results within 2 seconds for 95 percent of requests), scalability (support 50,000 concurrent users), availability (99.9 percent uptime per month), security (passwords stored hashed; lock the account after 5 wrong attempts), usability (a new user can book a ride within 3 minutes without help), reliability, maintainability, portability (run on Android 8 and above), and legal or regulatory requirements (follow the central bank's rules for digital payments).

Why NFRs are tricky: Non-functional requirements often affect the whole architecture, not one feature. If a system must handle 1 million transactions per day, that decides the database design, caching, servers and much more. Missing an NFR can make a working system useless: an app that does everything correctly but takes 30 seconds per screen will be abandoned. NFRs are also often written vaguely, like "the system should be fast" or "user friendly". These are not testable and must be rewritten with numbers.

Making NFRs measurable: Turn vague words into measurable statements. "Fast" becomes "the home screen loads within 2 seconds on a 4G connection for 95 percent of users". "Secure" becomes specific rules about encryption, authentication and access. "Easy to use" becomes "80 percent of first-time users complete registration without help in under 4 minutes". Once a requirement has a number and a condition, a tester can check whether it is met.

User requirements vs system requirements: Sommerville distinguishes two levels. User requirements are high-level statements, in natural language and diagrams, of what services the system provides and its constraints, written for customers and managers. System requirements are more detailed descriptions of the system's functions, services and constraints, written as a basis for design and sometimes for a contract. For example, a user requirement: "The system shall generate monthly sales reports." Related system requirements: "On the last working day of each month, the system shall generate a report of sales per branch. Only users with the manager role can view it. The report shall be available as PDF and Excel."

Domain requirements: Some requirements come from the application domain itself rather than from a specific user. A pharmacy system must follow drug regulations; a payroll system must apply the current income tax rules; a banking system must follow the regulator's know-your-customer rules. Domain experts may consider these so obvious that they forget to mention them, which makes them easy to miss.

The SRS document: A Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is the official statement of what the developers should build. The classic structure comes from IEEE 830-1998, which was later superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148. A typical SRS includes: introduction (purpose, scope, definitions, references, overview); overall description (product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, constraints, assumptions and dependencies); specific requirements (functional requirements, external interfaces, performance, design constraints, quality attributes); and appendices and an index. Agile teams often keep requirements in a product backlog instead, but the same information still needs to live somewhere.

Qualities of a good requirement: A good requirement is correct (it states something stakeholders actually need), unambiguous (only one interpretation), complete (nothing important is missing), consistent (it does not contradict other requirements), verifiable (it can be tested), feasible (it can be built within constraints), traceable (its origin and links to design and tests are known) and ranked for importance. Many teams use "shall" for mandatory requirements and "should" for desirable ones, and keep each requirement to a single statement.

Spotting bad requirements: Consider "The system should be user friendly and handle a lot of users quickly." It is vague (user friendly?), not measurable (a lot? quickly?) and combines several requirements. Better: "REQ-17: The system shall support at least 5,000 concurrent users. REQ-18: For 95 percent of requests, the response time shall be under 2 seconds with 5,000 concurrent users. REQ-19: A first-time user shall be able to register in under 3 minutes without help." Each is separate, numbered, measurable and testable.

Use cases and user stories: Requirements can also be expressed as use cases, which describe how an actor interacts with the system to achieve a goal (covered in the UML lessons), or as user stories in agile teams. A user story is short on purpose; it is "a promise for a conversation". Its detail lives in acceptance criteria, which define when the story is done.

Acceptance criteria with Given-When-Then: A popular way to write acceptance criteria is the Given-When-Then format from behaviour-driven development. Example for the story "As a customer I want to pay with my mobile wallet so that I do not need cash": Given I have 500 Taka in my wallet and the order total is 350 Taka, when I confirm payment with the correct PIN, then 350 Taka is deducted and I see a payment success message. A second criterion: Given my balance is 200 Taka and the total is 350 Taka, when I try to pay, then the payment is refused with an "insufficient balance" message and nothing is deducted. These criteria are directly testable.

Requirements validation: Validation checks that the requirements describe the system the customer really wants. Techniques include requirements reviews (stakeholders and the team read the document together and look for errors), prototyping (show screens and let users react), test-case generation (if you cannot write a test for a requirement, it is probably unclear), and checking for consistency and completeness. Validation catches errors at the cheapest possible moment.

Traceability: Traceability means being able to follow a requirement forward to the design elements, code and tests that implement it, and backward to its source (a stakeholder, a law, a meeting). A traceability matrix is a simple table with requirements as rows and design items or test cases as columns. It answers questions like: is every requirement tested? If this law changes, which modules are affected? Traceability is required in safety-critical industries and is useful everywhere.

Requirements change: Requirements change because the business changes, users understand their needs better after seeing the system, laws change, or competitors launch new features. Change is normal, but it must be managed. A change management process records each change request, analyses its impact on cost, schedule and other requirements, gets a decision, and updates documents and traceability. In Scrum, this is handled by the Product Owner reordering the backlog between Sprints. Uncontrolled growth of requirements during a project is called scope creep.

Real life example 1, an online train ticket system: Functional requirements: search trains by route and date, choose seats, pay online, receive an e-ticket by SMS and email. Non-functional: handle a huge rush when Eid tickets open (tens of thousands of users at the same minute), keep payment data secure, and prevent the same seat from being sold twice. A system that meets all functional requirements but crashes when Eid booking opens has failed its most important non-functional requirement. Many real ticketing systems around the world have learned this painfully.

Real life example 2, a school fee app: A school asks for "an app where parents can pay fees". After a requirements workshop, the team finds hidden needs: siblings get a discount, late fees apply after the 10th of each month, receipts must show the school's registration number, and the accountant needs a daily collection report. Writing these as numbered, testable requirements with Given-When-Then criteria prevents arguments later about what was promised.

Common mistakes: Writing design instead of requirements ("use MySQL" when the need is "store records for 10 years"). Vague words like fast, easy, flexible and user friendly without numbers. Forgetting non-functional requirements. Mixing many requirements in one sentence. Not involving real users. Treating the SRS as finished forever instead of a living document. Ignoring traceability, so nobody knows which tests cover which requirement.

What exams ask: Define requirements engineering and list its activities. Differentiate functional and non-functional requirements with examples. Differentiate user and system requirements. List the characteristics of a good SRS. Describe the structure of an SRS (IEEE 830). Rewrite a vague requirement into a testable one. What is a traceability matrix? Write acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then format.

Recap: Requirements engineering discovers, analyses, specifies, validates and manages what a system must do. Functional requirements describe behaviour; non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints and must be measurable. User requirements are high-level; system requirements are detailed. A good requirement is correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable, feasible and traceable. Acceptance criteria, validation, traceability and change management keep requirements useful throughout the project. Next lesson: UML and use case modeling.
key_points: Requirements engineering: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management of requirements.
Functional requirements describe what the system does; non-functional requirements describe how well (performance, security, usability, availability...).
Vague NFRs like 'fast' or 'user friendly' must be rewritten with measurable numbers.
User requirements are high-level for customers; system requirements are detailed for developers.
An SRS (IEEE 830, now ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) documents requirements in a standard structure.
Good requirements are correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable, feasible and traceable.
Acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then format make user stories testable.
Traceability links requirements to design and tests; change management controls scope creep.
lessons.tip: For every requirement you write, ask: how would a tester prove this is done? If you cannot answer, the requirement is not finished yet.
lessons.task: Take these vague requirements: 'The app should be fast', 'The app should be secure', 'The app should be easy to use'. Rewrite each as one or two measurable, testable requirements for a campus food-ordering app.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
options: The user can reset their password by email
The search results appear within 2 seconds for 95 percent of requests
The admin can add a new product
The system sends an SMS receipt after payment
quiz.explain: It describes how well the system performs, not what function it provides.

quiz.q: Why is 'The system shall be user friendly' a poor requirement?
options: It is not measurable or testable
quiz.explain: Without numbers and conditions, a tester cannot check whether it is met.

quiz.q: What does a traceability matrix show?
options: Links between requirements and the design items or tests that cover them
The salary of each team member
The list of programming languages used
quiz.explain: It maps each requirement to design, code and tests, and back to its source.

quiz.q: Which standard originally defined a common SRS structure?
quiz.explain: IEEE 830-1998 described SRS structure; it was later superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.

quiz.q: In Given-When-Then acceptance criteria, what does the 'Then' part describe?
quiz.explain: Given sets the context, When is the action, Then is the expected result.

lessons.title: UML Overview and Use Case Modeling
lessons.content:
When an architect designs a house, she does not describe it in a 50-page essay. She draws: a floor plan, an elevation, an electrical layout, a plumbing diagram. Each drawing shows one view of the same house, and every builder in the world can read these drawings because they follow shared symbols. Software engineers wanted the same thing: a standard set of drawings that any developer anywhere could read. That standard is UML, and the first drawing most projects make with it is the use case diagram.

What modeling is: A model is a simplified representation of something, focusing on what matters for a purpose and hiding the rest. A map of Dhaka's metro rail shows stations and lines but not every building. In software, models help us understand requirements, communicate with customers and teammates, explore design options before coding, and document the system for future maintainers. A model is cheaper to change than code, so it is a good place to find mistakes early.

What UML is: UML, the Unified Modeling Language, is a standard visual language for specifying, visualising, constructing and documenting the parts of a software system. It is a language of diagrams, not a programming language and not a process. You can use UML with waterfall, with the Unified Process or with agile; it simply gives you standard notation.

A short history: In the early 1990s there were many competing object-oriented modeling notations. Three of the best known were Grady Booch's method, James Rumbaugh's OMT (Object Modeling Technique) and Ivar Jacobson's OOSE (Object-Oriented Software Engineering), which introduced use cases. The three, sometimes called the "three amigos", joined at Rational Software and merged their ideas into UML. The Object Management Group (OMG) adopted UML as a standard in 1997. UML 2.0 brought major changes in the 2000s, and the current version, UML 2.5, defines 14 diagram types. UML is also published as an ISO standard.

Two families of diagrams: UML diagrams are divided into structure diagrams, which show the static parts of a system (what exists), and behaviour diagrams, which show dynamic behaviour (what happens). Structure diagrams include class, object, component, deployment, package, composite structure and profile diagrams. Behaviour diagrams include use case, activity and state machine diagrams, plus the interaction diagrams: sequence, communication, timing and interaction overview diagrams. That makes 7 structure and 7 behaviour diagrams.

Which diagrams really matter: You do not need all 14 in a typical project. In practice and in most university courses, the most used are use case diagrams (what the system offers to whom), class diagrams (the main structure), sequence diagrams (how objects interact over time), activity diagrams (workflows) and state machine diagrams (how one object changes state). Component and deployment diagrams are useful for architecture. We cover use cases in this lesson, class diagrams in the next, and the behaviour diagrams in the one after.

How UML is used: Martin Fowler famously described three ways people use UML. As a sketch: quick, informal drawings on a whiteboard to discuss ideas, the most common use today. As a blueprint: detailed, complete diagrams that programmers follow to write code. As a programming language: models detailed enough to generate executable code automatically, used mainly in some model-driven engineering settings. Knowing which mode you are in tells you how much detail to include.

Use case modeling: A use case describes a goal that a user achieves by interacting with the system, written from the user's point of view. Use cases were introduced by Ivar Jacobson. A use case diagram gives a bird's-eye view: who uses the system and what they can do with it. It does not show the order of steps or the internal design. Its main value is communicating scope with customers, who can understand it without technical training.

Actors: An actor is a role played by someone or something outside the system that interacts with it. Actors are drawn as stick figures with a name below. An actor can be a human role (Student, Teacher, Admin), another system (Payment Gateway, SMS Service) or even time (a Timer that triggers a monthly report). Important: an actor is a role, not a specific person. One person can be both a Teacher and a Student in different contexts. Primary actors start a use case to achieve their goal; secondary (supporting) actors help the system, like a payment gateway.

Use cases and the system boundary: A use case is drawn as an oval (ellipse) with a verb-phrase name, such as "Register for Course" or "Pay Fees". All use cases of the system are placed inside a rectangle called the system boundary, with the system's name at the top. Actors stand outside the rectangle. A plain line, called an association, connects an actor to each use case they take part in. Use case names should describe a goal, not a screen or a button: "Withdraw Cash", not "Click Withdraw Button".

The include relationship: Sometimes several use cases share a common piece of behaviour. Instead of repeating it, we put it in a separate use case and connect with an include relationship: a dashed arrow labelled with the keyword include in guillemets, pointing from the base use case to the included one. The included behaviour always happens. For example, in an ATM, both "Withdraw Cash" and "Check Balance" include "Authenticate Customer" (insert card and enter PIN). Every withdrawal always performs authentication.

The extend relationship: Extend describes optional or conditional behaviour added to a base use case under certain conditions. It is drawn as a dashed arrow labelled extend, pointing from the extending use case to the base use case (the opposite direction to include). For example, "Print Receipt" extends "Withdraw Cash", because a receipt is printed only if the customer asks for it. In an online shop, "Apply Discount Coupon" extends "Checkout". The base use case is complete without the extension; the extension adds something in specific situations, at points called extension points.

Remembering include vs extend: Include: always, arrow points to the shared part, like a function call the base use case always makes. Extend: sometimes, arrow points to the base use case, like an optional add-on. A handy check: if the base use case makes no sense without the other, it is include; if the base works fine alone and the other adds optional behaviour, it is extend.

Generalization: Actors and use cases can be generalised, drawn with a solid line and a hollow triangle arrowhead pointing to the more general element. Actor generalization: a "Premium Customer" is a kind of "Customer" and inherits all its use cases, plus maybe extra ones like "Access Priority Support". Use case generalization: "Pay by Card" and "Pay by Mobile Wallet" are specialised kinds of "Make Payment". Use generalization carefully; too much makes diagrams hard to read.

Use case descriptions: The diagram alone is not enough. Each important use case needs a written description, often in a template. Typical fields: use case name, ID, primary actor, stakeholders and interests, preconditions (what must be true before it starts), postconditions or success guarantee (what is true after success), main success scenario (numbered steps of the normal flow), alternative flows or extensions (what happens in other cases, like errors), and sometimes frequency of use and special requirements. Alistair Cockburn's book Writing Effective Use Cases popularised this style.

Worked example, Withdraw Cash: Primary actor: Customer. Precondition: the ATM is working and has cash. Main success scenario: 1. Customer inserts card. 2. System asks for PIN (include Authenticate Customer). 3. Customer enters PIN; system verifies it with the bank. 4. Customer selects Withdraw and enters 5,000 Taka. 5. System checks the balance and daily limit with the bank. 6. System dispenses cash and returns the card. 7. System records the transaction. Alternative flows: 3a. Wrong PIN: system asks again; after 3 wrong attempts, the card is retained. 5a. Insufficient balance: system shows a message and returns to the menu. 6a. Customer requests a receipt: system prints it (extend Print Receipt). Postcondition: the account is debited by exactly the amount dispensed.

Finding use cases: Start by listing actors: who uses the system, who maintains it, which external systems talk to it, and whether time triggers anything. For each actor, ask: what goals does this actor want to achieve with the system? Each goal that gives the actor something of value is a candidate use case. Then check: is the use case at the right level? "Log in" is often a sub-goal rather than a real user goal, so many modelers include it rather than show it as a main use case.

Real life example 1, an online exam portal: Actors: Student, Teacher, Admin, and Email Service (secondary). Student use cases: Take Exam, View Result. Teacher: Create Exam, Grade Answers, Publish Result. Admin: Manage Users. Both Take Exam and Create Exam include Log In. "Request Re-evaluation" extends View Result, since only some students use it. Publish Result uses the Email Service actor to notify students. This one diagram lets the department head see the whole scope on one page and ask, "where is the use case for uploading question banks?" before any code is written.

Real life example 2, a pharmacy point-of-sale: Actors: Salesperson, Pharmacist, Store Manager, Payment Gateway. Use cases: Sell Medicine, Return Item, Check Stock, Order Stock, View Daily Report. Sell Medicine includes Scan Barcode. "Verify Prescription" extends Sell Medicine, applying only when the medicine requires a prescription, and is performed by the Pharmacist. Store Manager is a specialised Salesperson via actor generalization, so a manager can also sell. Seeing this, the client says the cashier also needs "Close Day and Count Cash", which was missing.

Common mistakes: Drawing the order of steps in a use case diagram as if it were a flowchart; it shows only who can do what. Naming use cases after screens or buttons. Making actors specific people rather than roles. Reversing include and extend arrows. Putting internal system parts, like "Database", as actors; actors are outside the system. Too many tiny use cases that clutter the diagram, or a single giant one like "Manage System".

What exams ask: What is UML and why is it used? Name the structure and behaviour diagrams. Who created UML and when was it standardised? Draw a use case diagram for a given system (library, ATM, online shopping, hospital) with actors, system boundary, include and extend. Differentiate include and extend with examples. Write a use case description with main and alternative flows.

Recap: UML is a standard visual modeling language created by merging the work of Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson and adopted by the OMG in 1997; UML 2.5 has 14 diagrams in structure and behaviour families. A use case diagram shows actors (roles outside the system) and use cases (goals) inside a system boundary, linked by associations, with include for always-shared behaviour, extend for optional behaviour, and generalization for specialised actors or use cases. Written use case descriptions capture main and alternative flows. Next lesson: class diagrams for design.
key_points: UML is a standard visual modeling language, not a programming language or a process.
Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson merged their methods into UML; the OMG adopted it in 1997; UML 2.5 has 14 diagram types.
Structure diagrams show what exists (class, component, deployment...); behaviour diagrams show what happens (use case, activity, state, sequence...).
A use case diagram shows actors outside a system boundary and use cases (goals) inside it.
An actor is a role (human, external system or time), not a specific person.
Include: always-performed shared behaviour, arrow from base to included use case.
Extend: optional or conditional behaviour, arrow from extension to base use case.
Use case descriptions list actor, preconditions, main success scenario, alternative flows and postconditions.
lessons.tip: When unsure between include and extend, read the base use case aloud without the other one. If it still makes complete sense, the other one is an extend.
lessons.task: Draw a use case diagram for your university library: at least three actors, six use cases, one include and one extend. Then write a full description for the 'Borrow Book' use case with at least two alternative flows.

quiz.q: Who adopted UML as a standard in 1997?
quiz.explain: The OMG adopted UML in 1997 after Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson merged their notations.

quiz.q: In an ATM, 'Withdraw Cash' always performs 'Authenticate Customer'. Which relationship is this?
quiz.explain: Shared behaviour that always happens is modelled with include.

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid actor for an online shop?
quiz.explain: An actor is a role outside the system, and an external payment gateway qualifies.

quiz.q: Which is a behaviour diagram in UML?
quiz.explain: Sequence diagrams are interaction diagrams, which belong to the behaviour family.

quiz.q: 'Print Receipt' happens only if the customer asks for it during 'Withdraw Cash'. How should it be modelled?
quiz.explain: Optional, conditional behaviour is an extend pointing to the base use case.

lessons.title: Class Diagrams for Design
lessons.content:
Think about a family tree drawn on a big sheet for a wedding album. Each box is a person with a few details: name, birth year. Lines show relationships: married to, child of. You can see the whole family structure at a glance, without reading anyone's life story. A UML class diagram does the same for software. Each box is a class with its data and operations, and lines show how classes are related. It is the most used UML diagram, and it is the bridge between requirements and code.

What a class diagram shows: A class diagram is a structure diagram that shows the classes of a system, their attributes (data) and operations (behaviour), and the relationships between classes. It describes the static structure: what kinds of things exist and how they are connected, not what happens step by step. Class diagrams are used at different levels: a conceptual or domain model shows real-world concepts for discussion with customers; a design model shows software classes with types and visibility, close to code.

Class notation: A class is drawn as a rectangle with three compartments. The top holds the class name, written in singular and starting with a capital letter, like Student or Order. The middle holds attributes. The bottom holds operations (methods). Only the name compartment is required; in early sketches you may show just names. An abstract class name is written in italics or marked with the abstract keyword. An interface is shown with the keyword interface in guillemets above its name.

Attributes: The UML format for an attribute is: visibility name : type [multiplicity] = default value. For example: - balance : double = 0.0, or - phoneNumbers : String [0..3]. Static (class-level) attributes are underlined. A derived attribute, which can be calculated from others, is marked with a slash, like / age : int derived from dateOfBirth. You do not need to show every field; show what helps understanding.

Operations: The format for an operation is: visibility name(parameter : type, ...) : return type. For example: + deposit(amount : double) : void, or + getBalance() : double. Abstract operations are written in italics. Static operations are underlined. Constructors are often shown with the class name or a create stereotype, depending on the tool.

Visibility: UML uses four visibility symbols. Plus (+) means public: anyone can access it. Minus (-) means private: only the class itself. Hash (#) means protected: the class and its subclasses. Tilde (~) means package: classes in the same package. Good design usually makes attributes private and exposes behaviour through public operations, following encapsulation, which you studied in OOP.

Relationships overview: Classes rarely live alone. UML has several relationship types, each with its own line style. Association: a structural link between objects of two classes. Aggregation: a weak whole-part association. Composition: a strong whole-part association where parts cannot live without the whole. Generalization: inheritance, an is-a relationship. Realization: a class implements an interface. Dependency: a weak, temporary use relationship. Learning to choose the right one is a key skill.

Association: An association is drawn as a solid line between two classes. It means objects of one class are connected to objects of the other for some period, for example a Teacher teaches Course. You can add a name to the line (teaches) with a small arrow showing the reading direction, and role names at each end (instructor, course). An arrowhead on one end shows navigability: from an Order you can find its Customer, but the Customer class might not keep a list of orders. Without arrowheads, navigability is unspecified or both ways.

Multiplicity: Multiplicity says how many objects can be linked at each end. Common values: 1 (exactly one), 0..1 (zero or one), * or 0..* (zero or more), 1..* (one or more), and specific ranges like 2..5. Read it carefully: in Customer 1 --- 0..* Order, each Order belongs to exactly 1 Customer, and each Customer has 0 or more Orders. The number written next to a class tells how many of that class are linked to one object at the other end. Multiplicity becomes foreign keys and collections in code and databases.

Aggregation: Aggregation is a special association representing a whole-part relationship where the part can exist independently of the whole. It is drawn with a hollow (white) diamond at the whole's end. Example: a Department has Teachers. If the department is closed, the teachers still exist and can move to another department. Another: a Playlist contains Songs; deleting the playlist does not delete the songs. UML's specification leaves the precise meaning of aggregation fairly loose, so some modelers simply use plain association instead.

Composition: Composition is a strong whole-part relationship: the part belongs to only one whole at a time, and if the whole is destroyed, its parts are destroyed too. It is drawn with a filled (black) diamond at the whole's end. Example: an Order is composed of OrderLines. Delete the order and its lines disappear; an OrderLine makes no sense alone. A House and its Rooms, or an Invoice and its InvoiceItems, are classic composition examples. In code, the whole usually creates and owns its parts.

Generalization: Generalization shows inheritance: a subclass is a specialised kind of its superclass. It is drawn as a solid line with a hollow triangle arrowhead pointing to the superclass. Example: SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount both generalise to Account. The subclasses inherit attributes and operations of Account and add their own, like interestRate in SavingsAccount and overdraftLimit in CurrentAccount. Use the is-a test: a SavingsAccount is an Account, so generalization fits. A Car is not an Engine, so that would be wrong.

Realization and interfaces: Realization means a class implements the contract defined by an interface. It is drawn as a dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing to the interface. Example: an interface PaymentMethod with operation pay(amount); classes CardPayment, MobileWalletPayment and CashOnDelivery realise it. Code that depends on PaymentMethod can work with any of them, which is a powerful design idea used in later lessons on principles and patterns. A shorthand "lollipop" notation, a small circle on a stick, can also show a provided interface.

Dependency: A dependency is a weaker "uses" relationship: a change in one class may affect another, but they are not structurally linked. It is drawn as a dashed line with an open arrowhead pointing to the class being used. Typical cases: a class uses another as a method parameter, a local variable, or calls its static method. Example: ReportGenerator depends on PdfWriter because its generate method creates a PdfWriter temporarily. Too many dependencies make a design fragile, which links to coupling in the design lesson.

Association classes and enumerations: Sometimes an association itself has data. For a Student enrolled in a Course, where do we store the grade? Not in Student (a student has many grades) and not in Course (a course has many students). The grade belongs to the link, so we use an association class Enrollment with attribute grade, attached by a dashed line to the association. An enumeration is a type with a fixed set of values, like OrderStatus with PENDING, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, shown as a class box with the enumeration keyword.

Finding classes from requirements: A classic beginner technique is noun-phrase analysis. Read the requirements and underline nouns and noun phrases. Many become candidate classes or attributes. Verbs often become operations or associations. Then filter: remove duplicates (customer and client), vague words (system, information), things outside the scope, and nouns that are really attributes (name, price). Example: "A customer places an order for one or more products. Each order has a date and a delivery address. Payment is made by card or mobile wallet." Candidate classes: Customer, Order, Product, Payment, CardPayment, MobileWalletPayment. Attributes: date, deliveryAddress. Associations: Customer places Order; Order contains Product.

Worked example, a small library: Classes: Member (memberId, name, phone), Book (isbn, title, author), BookCopy (copyNumber, status), Loan (loanDate, dueDate, returnDate), Librarian. Relationships: Book 1 --- 1..* BookCopy, often drawn as composition, because a copy record makes no sense without the book record it belongs to. Member 1 --- 0..* Loan; Loan * --- 1 BookCopy; Librarian 1 --- 0..* Loan (processes). Operations: Member.borrow(copy), Loan.isOverdue() : boolean, Loan.calculateFine() : double. This diagram translates almost directly into Java classes and database tables.

From diagram to code: A class diagram maps naturally to object-oriented code. Each class becomes a class; private attributes become private fields; operations become methods; generalization becomes extends; realization becomes implements; an association with multiplicity 0..* becomes a collection field such as List of Order; composition often means the whole creates its parts in its own methods. Many tools can generate skeleton code from diagrams (forward engineering) or draw diagrams from existing code (reverse engineering).

Object diagrams: An object diagram is a snapshot of objects and links at one moment. Objects are drawn as boxes with an underlined name in the form objectName : ClassName, and attribute values instead of types, like rahim : Customer with name = "Rahim". Object diagrams help check a class diagram with concrete examples: if you cannot draw a realistic object diagram, the class diagram may be wrong.

Real life example 1, a ride-sharing domain model: Classes: Rider, Driver, Vehicle, Trip, Payment, Rating, Location. Rider 1 --- 0..* Trip; Driver 1 --- 0..* Trip; Driver 1 --- 1..* Vehicle (aggregation, vehicles can be re-registered to another driver); Trip composes two Locations (pickup and drop-off) which only matter as part of that trip; Trip 1 --- 0..1 Payment; Payment is abstract with subclasses CashPayment and WalletPayment; Trip 1 --- 0..2 Rating (one from each side). Discussing this diagram with the business team reveals questions early: can a trip have multiple stops? Can two riders share a trip?

Real life example 2, a hospital appointment system: Patient, Doctor, Appointment, Department, Prescription, Medicine. Appointment links one Patient and one Doctor with date, time and status (an enumeration). Doctor belongs to a Department (aggregation). Prescription is composed of PrescriptionItems, each referring to a Medicine with dose and duration. When the team draws this, they notice that one appointment may produce one prescription, so Appointment 1 --- 0..1 Prescription, which later becomes a foreign key in the database.

Common mistakes: Making every relationship a composition. Reversing the diamond: it always sits at the whole's end. Pointing the generalization triangle at the subclass instead of the superclass. Using inheritance where association fits (Car extends Engine). Forgetting multiplicities. Putting database IDs and every getter and setter in a conceptual diagram, which hides the important ideas. Modeling attributes as classes or classes as attributes without thinking.

What exams ask: Draw a class diagram for a given scenario (library, banking, online shop, hospital) with attributes, operations, visibility and multiplicities. Differentiate association, aggregation and composition with examples and notation. Explain generalization vs realization. What is an association class? Convert a class diagram into Java or C++ skeleton code, or the reverse.

Recap: A class diagram shows classes with attributes and operations, visibility (+, -, #, ~), and relationships: association (solid line, with multiplicity and roles), aggregation (hollow diamond, weak whole-part), composition (filled diamond, strong whole-part), generalization (hollow triangle, is-a), realization (dashed line with hollow triangle, implements) and dependency (dashed arrow, uses). Classes can be found from nouns in requirements and map closely to code. Next lesson: sequence, activity and state diagrams.
key_points: A class box has name, attributes and operations; only the name is required.
Visibility: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package.
Association is a solid line with multiplicities like 1, 0..1, 0..* and 1..* at each end.
Aggregation (hollow diamond) is weak whole-part; composition (filled diamond) means parts die with the whole.
Generalization (solid line, hollow triangle to superclass) is inheritance; realization (dashed line, hollow triangle) implements an interface.
Dependency (dashed arrow) is a weak, temporary 'uses' relationship.
Association classes hold data belonging to a link, like a grade in Enrollment.
Noun-phrase analysis finds candidate classes; class diagrams map directly to OOP code and database tables.
lessons.tip: Always say the relationship aloud: 'an Order HAS-A list of OrderLines that die with it' (composition), 'a SavingsAccount IS-AN Account' (generalization). If the sentence sounds wrong, the line is wrong.
lessons.task: Read this text and draw a class diagram: 'A university has departments. Each department offers many courses. A student enrols in several courses and receives a grade for each. A teacher belongs to one department and teaches one or more courses.' Include multiplicities and one association class.

quiz.q: What does a filled (black) diamond represent?
quiz.explain: A filled diamond at the whole's end shows composition: parts cannot exist without the whole.

quiz.q: Which visibility symbol means private?
quiz.explain: Minus is private, plus is public, hash is protected, tilde is package.

quiz.q: In 'Customer 1 --- 0..* Order', what does the 0..* mean?
options: Each customer has zero or more orders
Each customer has exactly one order
quiz.explain: The multiplicity next to Order says how many orders one customer can have.

quiz.q: A class CardPayment implements the interface PaymentMethod. Which relationship is this?
quiz.explain: Implementing an interface is realization: dashed line with a hollow triangle.

quiz.q: Where should a student's grade in a course be stored in a class diagram?
options: In an association class such as Enrollment
quiz.explain: The grade belongs to the link between one student and one course.

lessons.title: Sequence, Activity and State Diagrams
lessons.content:
A class diagram is like a photo of a cricket team lined up before the match: you see who is in the team and their positions. But it does not show the match itself: who bowled to whom, how a run-out happened, how the innings moved from powerplay to death overs. For that you need the replay, the scorecard and the commentary. UML's behaviour diagrams are the replay of software: sequence diagrams show who talks to whom and in what order, activity diagrams show the flow of a process, and state machine diagrams show how one thing changes over its life.

Why behaviour diagrams: Structure alone does not tell you whether a design works. Many bugs come from the wrong order of calls, a forgotten branch in a workflow, or an object reaching a state it should never be in (like shipping an order that was never paid). Drawing behaviour before coding helps you spot these problems on paper, discuss complex flows with teammates, and later explain the system to new developers.

Sequence diagrams: A sequence diagram shows how a group of objects interact to carry out one scenario, usually one use case flow, with messages arranged in time order from top to bottom. It is the most popular interaction diagram. It answers questions like: when a customer places an order, which object is called first, what does it call next, and what comes back?

Lifelines: Each participant is drawn at the top as a box, named like objectName : ClassName or just : ClassName, with a dashed vertical line going down called the lifeline. The lifeline represents the participant's existence over time. Actors can also appear at the top as stick figures. Time flows downward: a message lower on the page happens after a message higher up. Horizontal position has no meaning except to keep things readable.

Messages: A message is a horizontal arrow from the sender's lifeline to the receiver's. A synchronous message, drawn with a solid line and a filled arrowhead, means the sender waits for the receiver to finish, like a normal method call. An asynchronous message, drawn with a solid line and an open arrowhead, means the sender continues without waiting, like sending an event or a message to a queue. A return message is a dashed line with an open arrowhead going back, often labelled with the returned value. A message to oneself (a self-call) loops back to the same lifeline. A create message (often dashed, with the create keyword) points to a new participant's box, placed lower down where it is created; a destroyed participant's lifeline ends with a large X.

Activation bars: A thin rectangle on a lifeline, called an execution specification or activation bar, shows the period during which the participant is actively doing something, such as executing a method. When a synchronous call arrives, an activation starts; when the method returns, it ends. Nested activations show calls within calls.

Combined fragments: Real scenarios have conditions and loops. UML shows them with combined fragments: a rectangle around part of the diagram with an operator in the top-left corner. The alt fragment shows alternatives, like if-else, divided by dashed lines, each with a guard condition in square brackets, such as [balance >= amount] and [else]. The opt fragment shows an optional part that happens only if its guard is true, like if without else. The loop fragment repeats its content, for example loop [for each item in cart]. Other operators exist, such as par for parallel and ref to refer to another diagram, but alt, opt and loop are the ones you will use most.

Worked example, checkout: Participants: Customer (actor), :CheckoutPage, :OrderService, :PaymentGateway, :InventoryService. 1. Customer clicks Pay on CheckoutPage. 2. CheckoutPage calls placeOrder(cart) on OrderService (synchronous). 3. Inside a loop [for each item], OrderService calls reserve(item) on InventoryService, which returns ok. 4. OrderService calls charge(amount) on PaymentGateway. 5. alt [payment success]: OrderService marks the order PAID and returns a confirmation; CheckoutPage shows "Order placed". [else]: OrderService calls release(items) on InventoryService and returns failure; the page shows "Payment failed". 6. opt [customer opted for SMS]: OrderService sends an asynchronous message to an SMS service. Drawing this reveals an important design question: what if the payment gateway does not answer at all?

Communication diagrams briefly: A communication diagram shows the same kind of interaction as a sequence diagram, but focuses on links between objects rather than time. Objects are placed freely, connected by lines, and messages are numbered (1, 1.1, 1.2, 2) to show order. It is useful when the structure of connections matters more than timing. Sequence diagrams are far more common in practice.

Activity diagrams: An activity diagram shows a flow of actions, like an advanced flowchart. It is used to model business processes, workflows, the steps of a use case, or the logic of a complex operation. Unlike sequence diagrams, it does not focus on which object does what, unless you add partitions. It is easy for non-technical stakeholders to understand, which makes it great for discussing processes with clients.

Activity diagram notation: The initial node is a filled black circle where the flow starts. An action is a rounded rectangle with a short verb phrase, like "Check Stock". Arrows called control flows connect actions. A decision node is a diamond with one incoming flow and several outgoing flows, each with a guard in square brackets, like [in stock] and [out of stock]. A merge node, also a diamond, brings alternative paths back together. The activity final node, a filled circle inside a ring (a bull's-eye), ends the whole activity. A flow final node, a circle with an X, ends just one path while others continue.

Fork and join: Activity diagrams can show parallel work, which flowcharts cannot easily do. A fork is a thick bar with one incoming flow and several outgoing flows: all outgoing actions start in parallel. A join is a thick bar with several incoming flows and one outgoing flow: it waits until all incoming flows have finished. Example: after an order is confirmed, fork into "Pack Items" and "Generate Invoice", which happen in parallel; join before "Hand to Courier", which must wait for both.

Swimlanes: Partitions, commonly called swimlanes, divide the diagram into vertical or horizontal lanes, one per actor, department or system component. Each action is placed in the lane of whoever performs it. Swimlanes show responsibility and handovers clearly. Example lanes for an online order: Customer, Online Shop System, Warehouse, Courier. Seeing arrows cross lanes repeatedly can reveal too many handovers, a common source of delays in real businesses.

Worked example, leave application: Lanes: Employee, Line Manager, HR System. Start. Employee: Fill Leave Form. HR System: Check Leave Balance. Decision: [insufficient balance] goes to HR System: Notify Rejection, then to the end. [sufficient balance] goes to Line Manager: Review Request. Decision: [rejected] goes to Notify Rejection. [approved] forks into HR System: Update Balance and HR System: Notify Employee in parallel; join; end. This single diagram can be shown to HR and managers to confirm the real process before building it.

State machine diagrams: A state machine diagram shows the states an object goes through during its life, and the events that move it from one state to another. It is used for objects whose behaviour depends strongly on their current state: orders, bank accounts, user sessions, traffic lights, ATM machines, documents in an approval process. It describes one class's lifecycle, not the interaction of many objects.

State machine notation: A state is a rounded rectangle with a name, like Pending or Shipped. The initial pseudostate is a filled circle with an arrow to the first state. The final state is a bull's-eye. A transition is an arrow from one state to another, labelled in the form event [guard] / action. The event triggers the transition, the guard is a condition that must be true, and the action is something done during the transition. Example: from Pending to Paid with label paymentReceived [amount == total] / sendReceipt. A state can also have internal activities: entry / (done on entering), do / (ongoing while in the state) and exit / (done on leaving). Composite states can contain sub-states.

Worked example, an order lifecycle: Initial to Created. Created to Pending Payment on checkout. Pending Payment to Paid on paymentSuccess / reserveStock. Pending Payment to Cancelled on paymentTimeout [after 30 minutes]. Paid to Shipped on dispatch / notifyCustomer. Shipped to Delivered on deliveryConfirmed. Paid to Cancelled on cancelRequest / refund. Delivered to Returned on returnRequest [within 7 days]. Delivered, Cancelled and Returned lead to the final state. Drawing this makes illegal transitions obvious: there is no arrow from Created directly to Shipped, so the code must reject that.

From state diagrams to code: A state machine diagram translates well into code, for example an enumeration of states plus a method that checks the current state and the event, and either changes state or rejects the event. The State design pattern is another way to implement it, which we meet in the patterns lesson. Testing can also be derived from it: each transition, and each invalid event in each state, becomes a test case. This idea, state transition testing, returns in the black-box testing lesson.

Component and deployment diagrams briefly: Two structure diagrams are worth knowing for architecture. A component diagram shows the major software components (like Web App, Order Service, Payment Service, Database) and the interfaces they provide and require. A deployment diagram shows the physical setup: nodes (servers, phones, cloud machines, drawn as 3D boxes), the artifacts deployed on them (like an app file or a jar), and the communication paths between nodes (such as HTTPS). They help teams plan where software runs and how parts connect.

Real life example 1, a mobile recharge: A sequence diagram for a mobile recharge in a payment app: User enters number and amount on :RechargeScreen; it calls requestRecharge on :WalletService; the service checks balance; alt [enough balance]: it calls the operator's :TopUpAPI, receives success, debits the wallet and returns a success message; [else]: returns "insufficient balance". A state diagram for the same transaction shows Initiated, Processing, Successful, Failed and Reversed (for when the operator fails after the wallet was debited). Thinking about the Reversed state early prevents customers from losing money.

Real life example 2, a university admission workflow: An activity diagram with swimlanes Applicant, Admission Office, Department and Accounts: submit online form, verify documents, decision [incomplete] back to applicant, [complete] schedule test, publish merit list, decision [selected] fork into pay admission fee and choose courses, join, issue student ID. Admission staff can check this on paper and say "you missed the waiting list step", saving a change after deployment.

Common mistakes: Drawing sequence diagrams for the whole system at once instead of one scenario. Mixing up synchronous and asynchronous arrowheads. Forgetting return messages where values matter. In activity diagrams, using a diamond where parallel work needs a fork bar, or forgetting the join. In state diagrams, writing actions as states ("Send Email" is an action, not a state) and forgetting guards. Also confusing an activity diagram (flow of actions) with a state diagram (states of one object).

What exams ask: Draw a sequence diagram for a given scenario (ATM withdrawal, online order, login) with lifelines, synchronous and return messages, and an alt or loop fragment. Draw an activity diagram with decision, fork/join and swimlanes. Draw a state machine diagram for an object such as an order, a bank account or a traffic light. Differentiate activity and state diagrams. Explain combined fragments.

Recap: Sequence diagrams show interactions in time order with lifelines, synchronous (filled arrowhead) and asynchronous (open arrowhead) messages, return messages, activation bars and fragments like alt, opt and loop. Activity diagrams show workflows with actions, decisions, merges, forks, joins and swimlanes. State machine diagrams show one object's states and transitions labelled event [guard] / action. Component and deployment diagrams show software parts and where they run. Next lesson: the fundamentals of software design.
key_points: Sequence diagrams show participants' lifelines and messages in time order from top to bottom.
Synchronous messages use a filled arrowhead; asynchronous use an open arrowhead; returns are dashed.
Combined fragments: alt (if-else), opt (optional), loop (repetition), each with guard conditions.
Activity diagrams model workflows with actions, decision/merge diamonds, fork/join bars and swimlanes.
Fork starts parallel flows; join waits for all incoming flows to finish.
State machine diagrams show one object's lifecycle: states and transitions labelled event [guard] / action.
State diagrams reveal illegal transitions and give direct test cases.
Component diagrams show software parts and interfaces; deployment diagrams show nodes and what runs on them.
lessons.tip: Before drawing a sequence diagram, write the scenario as numbered sentences. Each sentence 'A asks B to do X' becomes one arrow. The diagram then almost draws itself.
lessons.task: Pick your phone's alarm clock app. Draw a state machine diagram for one alarm (states such as Off, Set, Ringing, Snoozed) with events and at least one guard. Then draw a small activity diagram of your morning routine with one fork and join.

quiz.q: In a sequence diagram, what does a filled arrowhead on a solid line usually mean?
options: A synchronous message where the sender waits
quiz.explain: Synchronous calls use a filled arrowhead; the caller waits for the result.

quiz.q: Which combined fragment models an if-else choice?
quiz.explain: alt holds alternative operands, each with a guard such as [else].

quiz.q: In an activity diagram, what does a join bar do?
options: Waits for all incoming parallel flows before continuing
quiz.explain: A join synchronises parallel flows; a fork starts them.

quiz.q: What is the standard label format of a transition in a state machine diagram?
quiz.explain: Event triggers it, guard must be true, action happens during the transition.

quiz.q: Which diagram is best for showing the lifecycle of an Order from Created to Delivered?
quiz.explain: State machine diagrams show one object's states and the events that change them.

lessons.title: Software Design Fundamentals: Modularity, Coupling and Cohesion
lessons.content:
Look at a desktop computer. If the keyboard breaks, you unplug it and plug in a new one; you do not replace the whole computer. If you want more storage, you add a drive. Each part has a clear job, connects through a standard port (USB, SATA, HDMI), and hides its internal details. You do not need to know how the keyboard's circuit works to use it. Good software design follows the same idea: split the system into parts with clear jobs, connect them through simple interfaces, and hide the messy details inside each part.

What design is: Software design is the activity of deciding how the system will be built to meet its requirements. Requirements say what the system must do; design says how it will be organised to do it. Design produces a model or blueprint: the components, their responsibilities, their interfaces, the data structures and the algorithms. Good design makes the system easier to build, test, understand and change. Bad design may still work today, but every change tomorrow becomes slow and risky.

Levels of design: Design happens at different levels. Architectural design (high-level design) decides the major components or subsystems and how they communicate, for example a mobile app, a web server, a database and a payment service. Detailed design (low-level design) decides the inside of each component: classes, methods, data structures and algorithms. Interface design defines how components talk to each other and to users. Data design defines how information is structured and stored. Architecture is covered in the next lesson; here we focus on principles that apply at every level.

Abstraction: Abstraction means focusing on the essential features of something while ignoring unnecessary details. When you call sort(list), you care that the list becomes sorted, not whether it uses quicksort or mergesort. Procedural abstraction hides how an operation is carried out behind a name, like a function sendSms(number, text). Data abstraction hides how data is stored behind operations, like a Stack with push and pop, whatever is inside. Abstraction lets people think about large systems without being overwhelmed.

Decomposition and modularity: Decomposition is breaking a big problem into smaller sub-problems. Modularity is the result: the software is divided into separately named and addressable modules (functions, classes, packages, services) that together satisfy the requirements. Smaller modules are easier to understand, to assign to different developers, to test and to replace. A 50,000-line program written as one huge file is nearly impossible to maintain; the same code in well-designed modules can be maintained by a team.

How many modules: Is it always better to split more? No. Pressman describes this with a simple picture: as the number of modules grows, the cost of building each module drops, but the cost of integrating them (interfaces, communication) rises. Total cost is lowest somewhere in the middle. Too few modules means huge, tangled ones; too many tiny modules means a confusing web of connections. The goal is meaningful modules with clear responsibilities.

Information hiding: Information hiding, introduced by David Parnas in a famous 1972 paper, says each module should hide a design decision that is likely to change, behind a stable interface. Other modules use only the interface and know nothing about the internals. For example, a module that stores student records might use a file today and a database next year. If other modules only call saveStudent and findStudent, the change stays inside one module. In object-oriented code, private fields and public methods are one way to do this, but information hiding is a broader design principle: hide what may change.

Encapsulation vs information hiding: The two words are related and often mixed. Encapsulation means bundling data and the operations that work on it together, such as in a class. Information hiding means keeping the internal details secret behind an interface. Encapsulation is a mechanism that helps you achieve information hiding. A class with all fields public is encapsulated in the sense of bundling, but it hides nothing.

Functional independence: Two qualities measure how well a system is modularised: coupling and cohesion. Pressman calls the goal functional independence: each module should do one well-defined job (high cohesion) and have minimal, simple interaction with other modules (low coupling). Independent modules are easier to develop, test and maintain, and errors spread less from one module to another. Remember the slogan: high cohesion, low coupling.

Coupling: Coupling is the degree of interdependence between modules. Low (loose) coupling means a change in one module rarely forces changes in others. High (tight) coupling means modules are tangled: change one and many others break. Classic types, from best (loosest) to worst (tightest), are: data coupling, stamp coupling, control coupling, external coupling, common coupling and content coupling. Some lists also mention "no coupling" at the very top, when modules do not interact at all.

The coupling types explained: Data coupling: modules communicate only by passing simple data as parameters, like calculateTax(income). Stamp coupling: a whole data structure is passed but only part of it is used, like passing the whole Student record to a function that only needs the date of birth. Control coupling: one module passes a flag that controls the other's logic, like print(report, mode) where mode = 1 means summary and 2 means detailed. External coupling: modules share an externally imposed format, protocol or device, such as a specific file format or hardware interface. Common coupling: modules share global data; any of them can change it, and bugs become hard to trace. Content coupling: one module directly modifies or depends on the internal data or code of another, like jumping into the middle of another module or changing its private variables. Content coupling is the worst.

Worked coupling example: Suppose module A calculates a bill and module B prints it. Version 1: A and B both read and write a global variable totalAmount; this is common coupling, and if a third module changes totalAmount by mistake, the bill is wrong and the bug is hard to find. Version 2: A returns the total and B receives it as a parameter, printBill(total, items); this is data coupling. Version 2 is easier to test (call printBill with any numbers) and safer to change.

Cohesion: Cohesion is the degree to which the elements inside one module belong together and work toward a single purpose. High cohesion means a module does one thing well. Low cohesion means a module is a grab bag of unrelated tasks. Classic types, from worst to best: coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential and functional cohesion.

The cohesion types explained: Coincidental: elements are grouped for no real reason, like a Utils module with sendEmail, calculateGPA and resizeImage.
