Logical: elements do similar kinds of things and one is chosen by a flag, like handleInput(type) that reads from keyboard, file or network. Temporal: elements are grouped because they run at the same time, like a startup function that opens files, sets counters and shows a splash screen. Procedural: elements follow a certain order of steps, but work on different data. Communicational: elements operate on the same data, like functions that all read and update one customer record. Sequential: the output of one element is the input to the next, like read data, then validate it, then format it. Functional: every element contributes to one single, well-defined task, like computeSquareRoot or calculateMonthlyInstalment. Functional cohesion is the best.

Worked cohesion example: A class StudentManager has methods addStudent, deleteStudent, printPayslip, backupDatabase and sendBirthdayGreetings. That is low, almost coincidental cohesion. A better design splits it: StudentRepository (add, delete, find students), PayrollService (payslips), BackupService (backups) and NotificationService (greetings). Each class now has one clear reason to exist, and changes to payroll no longer risk breaking student registration.

Coupling and cohesion together: They usually move in opposite directions. When you group related things together (raising cohesion), fewer messages need to cross module boundaries (lowering coupling). When a module does many unrelated jobs, other modules end up depending on it for many reasons, which increases coupling. This is why design reviews often ask two questions about every module: does it do one thing, and how many other modules does it depend on?

Other design concepts: Refinement (stepwise refinement, from Niklaus Wirth) means starting with a high-level statement of a function and gradually adding detail until it can be coded; it is the partner of abstraction. Separation of concerns means keeping different concerns, like user interface, business rules and data storage, in different parts of the system. Design for change means anticipating what is likely to change, like tax rates or payment providers, and isolating it. Simplicity means choosing the simplest design that meets the requirements.

Measuring design quality: Some simple signals help. Fan-out is the number of modules a module calls; very high fan-out suggests it does too much. Fan-in is the number of modules that call a module; high fan-in for a well-designed utility is good, because it is being reused. Very long functions, classes with dozens of methods, and long parameter lists are warning signs that cohesion is low. We meet these again as code smells in the code quality lesson.

Real life example 1, a mobile banking app: In a well-designed banking app, the module that talks to the core banking server is separated from the screens. If the bank changes its server API, only that module changes. The interest calculation is a function that takes principal, rate and time and returns interest: data coupling and functional cohesion, easy to test with many values. A poorly designed version where each screen directly builds server requests and calculates interest itself would need dozens of changes for one API update.

Real life example 2, an exam result processor: A university's old result program is one 3,000-line function that reads marks, calculates GPA, prints transcripts and emails parents, all using global variables. Every rule change, such as a new grading scale, risks breaking printing or email. A redesign splits it into MarksReader, GradeCalculator, TranscriptPrinter and ParentNotifier, passing data as parameters. When the grading scale changes, only GradeCalculator changes, and it has its own unit tests to prove the new scale works.

Common mistakes: Mixing up the order of coupling or cohesion types; remember data coupling is best and content worst, functional cohesion is best and coincidental worst. Thinking low coupling means zero communication; modules must communicate, just through simple, narrow interfaces. Believing private fields alone guarantee good design. Creating a giant "manager" or "utils" class that does everything. Splitting code into many tiny modules with no clear purpose.

What exams ask: Define abstraction, modularity and information hiding with examples. What is functional independence? Define coupling and cohesion, list their types in order and explain each with an example. Why is high cohesion and low coupling desirable? Identify the coupling or cohesion type in a given code fragment. Differentiate architectural and detailed design.

Recap: Software design decides how to build the system. Abstraction hides details, decomposition splits problems, modularity creates manageable parts, and information hiding protects decisions likely to change behind stable interfaces. Coupling measures dependence between modules (data is best, content is worst); cohesion measures how focused a module is (functional is best, coincidental is worst). Aim for high cohesion and low coupling. Next lesson: software architecture styles.
key_points: Design decides how the system will be organised to meet its requirements, at architectural and detailed levels.
Abstraction hides unnecessary detail; decomposition and modularity split the system into manageable parts.
Information hiding (Parnas, 1972) hides decisions likely to change behind stable interfaces.
Functional independence: aim for high cohesion and low coupling.
Coupling, best to worst: data, stamp, control, external, common, content.
Cohesion, worst to best: coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, functional.
Global data (common coupling) and modifying another module's internals (content coupling) make bugs hard to trace.
Too few or too many modules both raise cost; aim for meaningful modules with one clear responsibility.
lessons.tip: Memorise coupling with 'Dear Students, Come Early, Classes Commence' (Data, Stamp, Control, External, Common, Content) and cohesion from best to worst with 'Fat Sheep Come Past The Little Cottage' (Functional, Sequential, Communicational, Procedural, Temporal, Logical, Coincidental).
lessons.task: Find an old program you wrote (any language). Pick its longest function and write down what cohesion type it has and which global variables or flags it uses. Then sketch how you would split it into smaller functions with data coupling only.

quiz.q: Which is the most desirable type of coupling?
quiz.explain: Data coupling passes only the needed simple data as parameters.

quiz.q: A module groups sendEmail, calculateGPA and resizeImage for no real reason. What cohesion is this?
quiz.explain: Unrelated elements grouped together show coincidental cohesion, the worst kind.

quiz.q: Passing a flag that tells another module which logic to run is:
quiz.explain: The flag controls the receiver's internal flow, which is control coupling.

quiz.q: Who introduced the principle of information hiding?
quiz.explain: Parnas described information hiding in a 1972 paper on decomposing systems into modules.

quiz.q: What is the design goal summarised as functional independence?
options: One module for the whole system
quiz.explain: Each module should do one job well and depend little on others.

lessons.title: Software Architecture Styles
lessons.content:
Think of different kinds of buildings in Dhaka. A shopping mall has floors stacked on each other: parking at the bottom, shops above, food court on top. A hospital is organised around departments that send patients to each other. A garment factory is a production line: cloth enters at one end, passes through cutting, sewing, washing and packing, and shirts come out the other end. Each building has a different overall shape because it serves a different purpose. Software systems also have an overall shape, called the architecture, and there are well-known shapes, called architectural styles, that solve common problems.

What software architecture is: Software architecture is the high-level structure of a system: the major components, their responsibilities, how they relate to and communicate with each other, and the principles guiding their design and evolution. A widely quoted definition from Bass, Clements and Kazman describes it as the set of structures needed to reason about the system, comprising software elements, the relations among them, and properties of both. Architecture decisions are the ones that are expensive to change later, like choosing between one big application and many small services.

Why architecture matters: Architecture largely decides the system's quality attributes: performance, scalability, security, availability, maintainability, testability. Two systems with the same features can behave very differently under load or under change because of their architecture. Architecture also shapes the team: Conway's law observes that organisations tend to design systems that mirror their own communication structure. A good architecture lets several teams work in parallel without stepping on each other.

Architectural styles and patterns: An architectural style (or pattern) is a reusable, named solution for organising a system, describing the kinds of components, the connectors between them and the rules for combining them. Knowing styles gives you a vocabulary: saying "it is a layered system with an MVC web front end" tells an experienced engineer a lot in one sentence. Real systems often combine several styles.

Layered architecture: In a layered architecture, the system is organised into horizontal layers, each providing services to the layer above and using services of the layer below. A common example for business applications: presentation layer (user interface), business logic layer (rules and processing), data access layer (talking to the database) and the database itself. In a strict layered system a layer may only call the layer directly below it. The OSI and TCP/IP network models, which you meet in networking courses, are also layered designs.

Layered: pros and cons: Strengths: clear separation of concerns, each layer can be developed and tested separately, a layer can be replaced (for example a web UI added next to a desktop UI) without changing the business logic, and the structure is easy to understand. Weaknesses: requests may pass through several layers, adding some overhead; changes that affect all layers, like adding one new field shown on screen and stored in the database, touch every layer; and teams sometimes let layers skip each other, which breaks the benefits.

Client-server architecture: In client-server, the system is split into servers that provide services (data, computation, files) and clients that request them over a network. Your web browser is a client; the website's machine is a server. Mobile apps are clients of their backend servers. In a two-tier system, the client talks directly to a database server. In a three-tier system, a middle application server sits between the client and the database, holding business logic. Three-tier is common because it keeps rules and security on the server, not on every client.

Model-View-Controller: MVC separates an interactive application into three parts. The Model holds the data and the business rules. The View presents the data to the user. The Controller handles user input, updates the model and selects the view. When the model changes, the view is refreshed. Example in an online shop: the Model has Product and Cart objects; the View is the product page; the Controller handles "add to cart", updates the Cart model and tells the view to refresh. MVC lets designers change the look without touching business rules, and lets the same model have several views, such as a web page and a mobile screen. Many web frameworks use MVC or close variants such as MVP and MVVM.

Pipe-and-filter architecture: In pipe-and-filter, data flows through a sequence of processing components called filters, connected by pipes. Each filter takes input, transforms it and passes it on, without knowing about other filters. Classic examples: Unix command pipelines such as cat log.txt | grep ERROR | sort | uniq -c, compilers (lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, code generation) and data processing pipelines. Strengths: filters are simple, reusable and can be rearranged or run in parallel. Weaknesses: not good for interactive systems, and passing data in a common format between every step can add overhead.

Event-driven architecture: In an event-driven (or publish-subscribe) architecture, components communicate by producing and reacting to events, instead of calling each other directly. A publisher announces "OrderPlaced" without knowing who is listening; subscribers like the Inventory, Email and Analytics services each react in their own way. A message broker or event bus often sits in the middle. Strengths: very loose coupling, easy to add new subscribers, good for scaling and real-time updates. Weaknesses: the overall flow is harder to follow and debug, and the order and delivery of events must be handled carefully.

Repository (shared data) architecture: In a repository style, many components share a central data store and communicate through it rather than directly. An integrated development environment, where the editor, compiler, debugger and version control all work on the same project repository, is a classic example. A data-centred business system where many applications read and write one database is another. The repository makes sharing large amounts of data efficient, but it is a single point of failure and makes changing the data structure hard, since many components depend on it.

Monolithic architecture: A monolith is an application built and deployed as one unit: one codebase, one build, one running process (or several copies of it), usually with one database. Internally it may be well structured in layers and modules. Monoliths are simple to develop, test and deploy at the start, and calls between parts are fast in-process calls. Problems grow with size: the codebase becomes huge, one bug can crash everything, the whole application must be redeployed for any small change, and scaling means copying the entire application even if only one part is busy.

Microservices architecture: In microservices, the application is built as a set of small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and usually its own data, communicating over the network through APIs or messages. For an e-commerce system: User Service, Product Catalogue Service, Cart Service, Order Service, Payment Service, Notification Service. Each team can develop, deploy and scale its service independently and even use a different technology. But microservices bring the complexity of distributed systems: network failures, data consistency across services, monitoring many services, and more complex testing and deployment.

Choosing monolith or microservices: Many experienced engineers advise starting with a well-structured monolith (sometimes called a modular monolith) and extracting services only when there is a clear need, such as independent scaling or many teams blocking each other. Splitting into microservices too early adds network complexity before the business domain is well understood. A team of five building a new product rarely needs twenty services.

Service-oriented architecture and APIs: Service-oriented architecture (SOA) is an older, broader idea in which systems are composed of services that communicate through well-defined interfaces, often in large enterprises and often through an enterprise service bus. Microservices can be seen as a lighter, more independent evolution of the service idea. Today services commonly expose REST APIs over HTTP: resources identified by URLs (like /orders/42), standard methods (GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove) and data usually in JSON. A clear, versioned API is itself an architectural contract between teams.

Quality attributes drive the choice: Architecture is about trade-offs. If the main need is high availability during huge traffic spikes, you might choose stateless servers behind a load balancer, caching and asynchronous processing with events. If the main need is strict consistency of money, you might keep payment logic in one strongly consistent service with careful transactions. If the main need is fast development by a small team, a simple layered monolith is often best. The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) from the Software Engineering Institute is one formal way to evaluate such trade-offs.

Documenting architecture: Architecture is usually described from several views, because no single diagram shows everything. Philippe Kruchten's 4+1 view model uses a logical view (key abstractions such as classes), a process view (run-time behaviour and concurrency), a development view (organisation of code into modules and packages), a physical view (mapping to hardware, like a deployment diagram) and scenarios (use cases that tie the views together). Teams also record important decisions and their reasons in short architecture decision records, so future developers understand why things are the way they are.

Real life example 1, a national e-commerce platform: An online marketplace may start as a monolith: one web application with layers for UI, business logic and data. As it grows to millions of users and big sale days, the busiest parts, like product search and checkout, may be separated into services that can scale independently. Order events are published so that inventory, delivery and SMS notification services react without slowing checkout. The mobile app and website both act as clients of the same backend APIs.

Real life example 2, a hospital management system: A mid-sized hospital uses a three-tier layered system: a web interface for doctors, nurses and the front desk; an application server with rules for appointments, billing and pharmacy; and one central database. Lab machines produce results in a standard format, processed through a small pipe-and-filter pipeline (read, validate, convert units, attach to patient record). For this hospital, the simplicity of a layered monolith is a strength: a small IT team can understand and maintain the whole system.

Common mistakes: Believing microservices are always better or more modern. Confusing layers (logical separation in code) with tiers (physical separation on machines). Thinking MVC is a complete architecture for the whole system; it is mostly a pattern for the user interface part. Ignoring non-functional requirements when choosing a style. Drawing beautiful architecture diagrams that the code does not follow.

What exams ask: Define software architecture and explain why it matters. Explain layered, client-server, MVC, pipe-and-filter, event-driven and repository styles with diagrams, advantages and disadvantages. Compare monolithic and microservices architectures. Differentiate two-tier and three-tier client-server. Choose an appropriate architecture for a given scenario and justify it.

Recap: Software architecture is the high-level structure of a system and decides most of its quality attributes. Common styles: layered (stacked responsibilities), client-server (requesters and providers), MVC (model, view, controller), pipe-and-filter (data transformed step by step), event-driven (publish and subscribe), repository (shared data store), monolith (one deployable unit) and microservices (many small independent services). Choose by trade-offs among quality attributes, team size and change needs. Next lesson: design principles, starting with SOLID.
key_points: Architecture is the high-level structure: major components, their relationships and the principles guiding them.
Architecture largely determines quality attributes like performance, scalability, availability and maintainability.
Layered: presentation, business logic and data access layers, each using the one below.
Client-server: clients request services from servers; three-tier adds an application server between client and database.
MVC separates Model (data and rules), View (presentation) and Controller (input handling).
Pipe-and-filter passes data through independent transforming filters; event-driven components publish and subscribe to events.
Monoliths are simple to start; microservices allow independent deployment and scaling but add distributed-system complexity.
Choose an architecture by its trade-offs against the system's most important quality attributes.
lessons.tip: For each style, remember one everyday picture: layered = a multi-storey mall, pipe-and-filter = a garment production line, event-driven = a mosque's loudspeaker announcement that anyone interested can act on, client-server = a restaurant counter.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use (a ride-sharing app, a food delivery app or your university portal). Draw boxes for what you think its main components are and label the architecture styles you see (client-server, layered, event-driven...). Write one quality attribute that probably drove each choice.

quiz.q: In MVC, which part handles user input and updates the model?
quiz.explain: The Controller receives input, updates the Model and selects the View.

quiz.q: Which style best describes a Unix command like cat file | grep ERROR | sort?
quiz.explain: Each command is a filter and the | symbols are pipes passing data along.

quiz.q: What is a main disadvantage of microservices compared with a monolith?
options: It is impossible to scale parts separately
Every team must use the same language
It adds distributed-system complexity like network failures and data consistency
quiz.explain: Independence comes at the cost of network calls, monitoring and consistency challenges.

quiz.q: In a three-tier client-server system, where does the business logic usually live?
quiz.explain: The middle tier holds business rules between the client and the database.

quiz.q: Components announce events like OrderPlaced without knowing who listens. Which style is this?
quiz.explain: Publishers emit events; any number of subscribers react independently.

lessons.title: Design Principles: SOLID, DRY, KISS and YAGNI
lessons.content:
Think of a good kitchen. The knives are in one drawer, spices on one shelf, plates in one rack. If the gas stove is replaced with an induction cooker, you do not have to rebuild the cupboards. If a guest brings a new kind of pot, it fits on the stove because the stove accepts any flat-bottomed pot. Nobody designed this kitchen with a rulebook, but it follows principles that make it easy to use and easy to change. Software design also has principles, short rules of thumb collected from decades of experience, that help code stay easy to change. The most famous set is called SOLID.

Why principles: In the last lessons we learned the big ideas: abstraction, information hiding, high cohesion and low coupling. Principles turn those ideas into practical guidance for everyday decisions: should this class do this job? Should I add an if-else here or a new class? Should I write this feature now or later? Principles are not laws; they are heuristics. Applied with judgement, they keep code flexible. Applied blindly, they can make simple code complicated.

Where SOLID comes from: SOLID is an acronym for five object-oriented design principles promoted by Robert C. Martin (often called Uncle Bob) in the early 2000s. The acronym itself was coined by Michael Feathers. The five are: Single Responsibility Principle, Open/Closed Principle, Liskov Substitution Principle, Interface Segregation Principle and Dependency Inversion Principle. Your OOP course introduced them briefly; here we look at each with the problem it solves and a concrete example.

Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change. Martin later phrased it as: a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor (one group of people who might request changes). Example of a violation: a class Invoice with methods calculateTotal(), printInvoice() and saveToDatabase(). The accounts team may change tax rules, the design team may change the printed layout, and the database team may change storage. Three different reasons to change, all in one class, so a change for one group can break something for another. Fix: Invoice (calculation), InvoicePrinter (formatting) and InvoiceRepository (storage). SRP is high cohesion stated at the class level.

Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. The idea, first stated by Bertrand Meyer in 1988, is that you should be able to add new behaviour without editing existing, tested code. Violation: a function calculateDiscount(customer) containing if type == "regular" return 0; else if type == "student" return 10; else if type == "premium" return 20. Every new customer type means editing this function and retesting everything. Fix: an interface DiscountPolicy with method discountPercent(), and classes RegularDiscount, StudentDiscount and PremiumDiscount. Adding an EidSpecialDiscount means writing a new class, not changing old ones.

Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Barbara Liskov introduced this idea in a 1987 talk. In simple words: objects of a subclass must be usable wherever objects of the superclass are expected, without breaking the program's correctness. A subclass must keep the promises of its parent. The classic violation is Square extends Rectangle. A Rectangle lets you set width and height independently. Code like r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert r.area() == 20 works for a Rectangle. But a Square must keep both sides equal, so setting height also changes width, and the area becomes 16. The subclass broke the parent's behaviour, so it should not inherit this way.

More LSP warning signs: A subclass method that throws "not supported" for an operation the parent promised, a subclass that requires stronger preconditions (for example accepting only positive amounts when the parent accepted any amount), or one that weakens the results (returning null where the parent guaranteed a value) all break substitutability. A common example: a class Bird with method fly(), and a subclass Penguin whose fly() throws an exception. Better: separate FlyingBird from Bird, so penguins are not forced to promise flight. LSP is what makes polymorphism safe.

Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Violation: an interface Worker with work(), eat() and sleep(). A RobotWorker class must implement eat() and sleep() even though they make no sense for it, usually with empty or exception-throwing bodies. Another example: a huge interface MultiFunctionDevice with print(), scan(), fax() and staple(), implemented by a simple printer that cannot scan. Fix: split into small, focused interfaces such as Printer, Scanner and Fax, and let each class implement only what it supports. Small interfaces mean fewer unnecessary dependencies and fewer forced changes.

Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. And abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions. Violation: an OrderService class that directly creates new MySqlDatabase() and new SslCommerzGateway() inside its code. The high-level business logic is now glued to specific technologies; switching the database or payment provider means editing the business logic, and testing it requires a real database. Fix: OrderService depends on interfaces OrderRepository and PaymentGateway; concrete classes implement them. The concrete objects are passed in from outside, for example through the constructor.

Dependency injection: Passing dependencies into a class from outside, instead of the class creating them itself, is called dependency injection. Example: new OrderService(new MySqlOrderRepository(), new MobileWalletGateway()) in production, and new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepository(), new FakePaymentGateway()) in tests. Dependency injection is a technique that helps achieve DIP; many frameworks provide containers that wire objects together automatically. DIP and dependency injection are closely related but not the same: one is a principle, the other a technique.

SOLID together, a worked example: Suppose a school app must send result notifications. A first version: class ResultNotifier with method notify(student) that formats the message, then has if-else branches for SMS, email or push, each creating its own provider object. Problems: several responsibilities (SRP), editing the class for every new channel (OCP), and direct dependence on concrete providers (DIP). Refactored: an interface NotificationChannel with send(to, message); classes SmsChannel, EmailChannel, PushChannel; a MessageFormatter class; and ResultNotifier receives a list of channels through its constructor and calls send on each. Adding WhatsApp means one new class. Testing uses a fake channel that just records messages.

DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself, from the book The Pragmatic Programmer by Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas, says every piece of knowledge should have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. If the VAT rate of 15 percent is written in twelve places and the rate changes, you must find all twelve, and you will probably miss one. Put it in one constant or configuration. DRY is about knowledge, not just identical-looking text: two pieces of code that look similar but represent different business rules may need to change independently, and merging them would be a mistake.

KISS: Keep It Simple, Stupid (often softened to Keep It Short and Simple) says most systems work best if kept simple rather than made complicated. Prefer the straightforward loop to the clever one-liner nobody can read; prefer a plain function to a framework when a function is enough. Simple code has fewer bugs, is easier to review and easier for a new teammate to understand. Brian Kernighan's famous remark fits here: debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place, so if you write code as cleverly as possible, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it.

YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It, from Extreme Programming, says do not add functionality until it is actually needed. Developers often build "flexible" systems for imagined future needs: a plugin system for a feature that will only ever have one plugin, configuration options nobody asked for, support for five databases when one is used. These cost time now, add complexity, and are often wrong because the future turns out differently. Build what is needed now, keep the code clean, and add flexibility when a real need appears. YAGNI and OCP balance each other: design for change where change is likely, not everywhere.

Law of Demeter: Also called the principle of least knowledge, it says a method should talk only to its close friends: its own object, its parameters, objects it creates, and its direct fields, not to strangers reached through long chains. A violation looks like order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity().getName(). This code depends on the internal structure of four classes; if Address changes, this breaks. Better: ask the order directly, order.getDeliveryCityName(), and let each class handle its own internals. The informal slogan is "only talk to your immediate friends" or "tell, don't ask".

Composition over inheritance: The Gang of Four design patterns book advises favouring object composition over class inheritance. Inheritance creates a strong, compile-time link between parent and child; changes in the parent ripple into every child, and deep hierarchies become rigid. Composition means building behaviour by holding other objects and delegating to them. Example: instead of classes FlyingDuck, QuackingDuck, FlyingQuackingDuck and so on, a Duck holds a FlyBehaviour object and a QuackBehaviour object that can be swapped. Use inheritance for true is-a relationships with substitutable behaviour; use composition for has-a and for mixing capabilities.

Separation of concerns and principle of least surprise: Keep different concerns, like UI, business rules, data access, logging and security, in different places, so each can change independently. And design code so it behaves the way a reader would expect: a method called getBalance should not also send an email. Code that surprises readers causes bugs because people make wrong assumptions about it.

Real life example 1, a payment integration: A Bangladeshi e-commerce site first integrated one payment gateway, with gateway-specific code scattered across checkout, refunds and reports. When the business added card payments, mobile wallets and cash on delivery, every change touched many files. Refactoring with DIP and OCP introduced a PaymentGateway interface with pay, refund and status methods, and one class per provider. Adding a new wallet later took days instead of weeks, and the checkout tests used a fake gateway that never charged real money.

Real life example 2, a ride fare calculator: A ride-sharing fare function grew to 400 lines of if-else: bike or car, peak hour or not, rain surcharge, promo codes, airport pickup. Each new rule broke an old one. The team applied SRP and OCP: a base fare calculator, plus a list of FareRule objects (PeakHourRule, RainRule, PromoRule, AirportRule) applied in order. KISS reminded them not to build a general rules engine with its own scripting language, which nobody needed (YAGNI). The result was smaller, tested rule classes that product managers could reason about.

Common mistakes: Treating principles as laws and creating an interface for every class even when there will only ever be one implementation. Splitting classes so much that following one feature means opening twenty files. Confusing DRY with "never write similar code", leading to wrong abstractions that couple unrelated rules. Thinking LSP is about syntax; code can compile perfectly and still violate LSP by breaking behaviour. Mixing up DIP (a principle) with dependency injection (a technique).

What exams ask: Expand SOLID and explain each principle with an example of a violation and its fix. Explain the Square-Rectangle problem. What is dependency injection and how does it relate to DIP? Explain DRY, KISS and YAGNI. What is the Law of Demeter? Why favour composition over inheritance? Identify which principle a given code fragment violates.

Recap: SOLID gives five object-oriented principles: one reason to change (SRP), extend without modifying (OCP), subclasses must be substitutable (LSP), small focused interfaces (ISP), and depend on abstractions, not details (DIP). DRY removes duplicated knowledge, KISS keeps designs simple, YAGNI avoids building for imagined needs, the Law of Demeter limits knowledge of other objects' internals, and composition is often more flexible than inheritance. Use principles with judgement. Next lesson: design patterns.
key_points: SRP: a class should have only one reason to change (one responsible actor).
OCP: add behaviour by extension (new classes) rather than modifying tested code.
LSP: subclasses must be usable wherever the parent is expected without breaking correctness (Square/Rectangle problem).
ISP: prefer small, focused interfaces so clients do not depend on methods they don't use.
DIP: high-level and low-level modules both depend on abstractions; dependency injection is a technique to achieve it.
DRY: one authoritative place for each piece of knowledge; KISS: keep it simple; YAGNI: don't build for imagined needs.
Law of Demeter: talk only to immediate friends, avoid long call chains like a.getB().getC().getD().
Favour composition over inheritance for flexibility; apply all principles with judgement, not blindly.
lessons.tip: For any class you write, finish the sentence 'This class changes only when ...'. If you need the word 'or', you probably have more than one responsibility.
lessons.task: Write (on paper or in any language) a function that calculates delivery charges with if-else for inside Dhaka, outside Dhaka and express. Then redesign it using an interface and one class per charge type, and explain which SOLID principles your new design follows.

quiz.q: A class Invoice calculates totals, prints itself and saves to the database. Which principle does it violate most directly?
quiz.explain: It has several reasons to change, owned by different groups.

quiz.q: Adding a new discount type requires editing a long if-else chain in existing code. Which principle is being violated?
quiz.explain: OCP says new behaviour should be added by extension, not by modifying tested code.

quiz.q: Why does Square extending Rectangle break LSP?
options: Square cannot be compiled in Java
Setting width and height independently no longer behaves as Rectangle promises
quiz.explain: Code that relies on independent sides gets wrong results when given a Square.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: Low-level classes should call high-level classes
Every class must have an interface
High-level and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions
Dependencies should be created inside each method
quiz.explain: Business logic depends on interfaces; concrete details implement them.

quiz.q: A developer builds a plugin system and five configuration options that nobody asked for. Which principle is ignored?
quiz.explain: You Aren't Gonna Need It: build features only when they are actually needed.

lessons.title: Design Patterns
lessons.content:
Every experienced cook knows certain recipes by heart: how to make a basic gravy, how to cook rice so it does not stick, how to marinate meat. These are not complete dishes; they are proven solutions to problems that come up again and again in many dishes. When one cook tells another "start with a bhuna", both know exactly what that means. Design patterns are the same for software: proven, named solutions to design problems that keep coming back. Knowing them saves you from reinventing solutions and gives your team a shared vocabulary.

What a design pattern is: A design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring problem in software design, described in a way that you can adapt to your own situation. It is not finished code you copy and paste; it is a template for how to arrange classes and objects to solve a kind of problem. The idea was inspired by the architect Christopher Alexander, who wrote about patterns in buildings and towns in the 1970s.

The Gang of Four: In 1994, Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides published the book Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. The four authors became known as the Gang of Four (GoF). The book describes 23 patterns, grouped into three categories: 5 creational, 7 structural and 11 behavioural. Each pattern is described with a name, the problem it solves, the solution (the structure of classes and their collaboration) and the consequences (trade-offs).

Elements of a pattern description: Name: a short handle, like Observer, that becomes part of the team's vocabulary. Problem: when to apply the pattern, including the context and the forces. Solution: the elements, their relationships, responsibilities and collaborations, usually with a class diagram. Consequences: the benefits and costs, such as flexibility gained and complexity added. Thinking in these four parts helps you judge whether a pattern really fits your problem.

The three categories: Creational patterns deal with how objects are created, hiding the creation logic so the system is not tied to specific classes; examples are Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder and Prototype. Structural patterns deal with how classes and objects are composed into larger structures; examples are Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight and Proxy. Behavioural patterns deal with how objects communicate and divide responsibilities; examples include Observer, Strategy, Command, State, Iterator, Template Method, Chain of Responsibility, Mediator, Memento, Visitor and Interpreter.

Singleton: Problem: you need exactly one instance of a class with a global point of access, for example one configuration object or one connection pool. Solution: make the constructor private, keep a static field holding the single instance, and provide a static method like getInstance() that creates the instance the first time and returns the same one afterwards. Consequences: easy shared access, but Singleton is often criticised because it acts like a global variable, hides dependencies, makes unit testing harder and needs care in multithreaded programs. Many teams today prefer creating one instance and passing it in with dependency injection.

Factory Method: Problem: a class needs to create objects but should not be tied to their concrete classes. Solution: define a method for creating the object, and let subclasses (or a separate factory) decide which concrete class to instantiate. Example: a NotificationFactory with createNotification(type) that returns an SmsNotification, EmailNotification or PushNotification, all implementing Notification. Client code asks the factory and works with the Notification interface. Adding a new type touches the factory, not every client. The related Abstract Factory pattern creates whole families of related objects, such as light-theme and dark-theme button, menu and dialog objects.

Builder: Problem: an object has many parts or optional parameters, and constructors with ten arguments become unreadable and error-prone. Solution: a separate Builder object collects the parts step by step and then builds the final object. Example: new PizzaBuilder().size("large").addCheese().addTopping("chicken").build(). The code reads clearly, optional parts can be skipped, and the final object can be made immutable. Builders are common for constructing complex requests, documents and test data.

Adapter: Problem: you want to use an existing class, but its interface does not match what your code expects. Like a travel plug adapter that lets a Bangladeshi two-pin plug fit a UK socket. Solution: an Adapter class implements the interface your code expects and, inside, translates calls to the existing class. Example: your app uses an interface SmsSender with send(phone, text), but a new SMS provider's library offers deliverMessage(MessageRequest). Write ProviderSmsAdapter implements SmsSender, which builds a MessageRequest and calls deliverMessage. Your app code does not change at all.

Decorator: Problem: you want to add responsibilities to individual objects dynamically, without creating a subclass for every combination. Solution: a Decorator wraps an object that has the same interface, adds behaviour before or after forwarding calls, and can itself be wrapped by another decorator. Example: a Coffee interface with cost(); a basic Coffee costs 100 Taka; MilkDecorator adds 20, SugarDecorator adds 5, ExtraShotDecorator adds 40. new ExtraShot(new Milk(new BasicCoffee())) costs 160 Taka. Without decorators you would need classes like MilkSugarExtraShotCoffee for every combination. Java's I/O streams, such as wrapping a FileInputStream in a BufferedInputStream, use this pattern.

Facade: Problem: a subsystem has many classes and complex steps, and clients only need a simple way to use it. Solution: a Facade class provides one simple interface that hides the complexity. Example: placing an order requires checking stock, reserving items, charging payment, creating an invoice and scheduling delivery across five services. An OrderFacade with one method placeOrder(cart, customer) coordinates them all. Clients become simpler and less coupled to the subsystem. Think of a hotel reception desk: you ask one person, who coordinates housekeeping, kitchen and maintenance behind the scenes.

Observer: Problem: when one object changes state, many other objects need to be notified automatically, but you do not want the object to depend on all of them. Solution: the subject keeps a list of observers that implement an interface such as update(event). Observers register and unregister themselves; when the subject changes, it notifies all registered observers. Example: when a cricket match score changes, the scoreboard display, a mobile notification service and a statistics module all update. The subject does not know what they do with the news. Observer is the foundation of event handling in user interfaces and the publish-subscribe style from the architecture lesson.

Strategy: Problem: you have several algorithms for the same task and want to choose between them at run time without long if-else chains. Solution: define a Strategy interface, put each algorithm in its own class, and give the context object a strategy field that can be set or changed. Example: a delivery app calculates charges with InsideCityStrategy, OutsideCityStrategy or ExpressStrategy, all implementing DeliveryChargeStrategy. The Order object calls strategy.calculate(weight, distance). Adding a new strategy needs no change to Order, which is the Open/Closed Principle in action.

State: Problem: an object's behaviour changes depending on its state, and the code is full of if-else or switch statements on a state field. Solution: represent each state as a class implementing a common interface, and let the object delegate behaviour to its current state object, which can switch the state. Example: an Order with states Pending, Paid, Shipped and Delivered; calling cancel() on Pending cancels freely, on Paid triggers a refund, and on Shipped is rejected. Each rule lives in its state class. This is a natural way to implement the state machine diagrams from lesson 11.

Command and Template Method briefly: Command turns a request into an object, with a method like execute(), so requests can be queued, logged, scheduled or undone; undo and redo in editors are classic uses. Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class method, with certain steps left as abstract methods that subclasses fill in; for example, a ReportGenerator with generate() that always calls fetchData(), formatData() and export(), where subclasses define how each step works for PDF or Excel reports.

Patterns in MVC and frameworks: Larger structures often combine patterns. Classic MVC uses Observer (views observe the model), Strategy (the view can use different controllers) and Composite (nested view components). Frameworks you use every day contain patterns: GUI event listeners use Observer, iterators over collections use Iterator, logging libraries often use Decorator or Chain of Responsibility, and dependency injection containers use Factory ideas. Recognising patterns helps you learn new frameworks faster.

Anti-patterns: An anti-pattern is a commonly used solution that looks reasonable but causes more problems than it solves. Examples: the God Object (one huge class that knows and does everything), Spaghetti Code (tangled control flow with no clear structure), Copy-Paste Programming (duplicating code instead of reusing it), Golden Hammer (using one favourite tool or pattern for every problem), and Lava Flow (dead or mysterious code nobody dares to delete). Naming anti-patterns, like naming patterns, helps teams discuss and fix them.

When not to use patterns: Patterns add classes and indirection. If a problem is simple, a pattern can make code harder to read; a Strategy for a single algorithm that will never change, or a Factory that only ever creates one class, is over-engineering. Remember YAGNI and KISS from the last lesson. A good rule: first write simple code, notice the problem the pattern solves when it actually appears (for example, a growing if-else on types), then refactor toward the pattern.

Real life example 1, a payment app: A mobile wallet app uses several patterns. Strategy chooses the fee calculation for send money, cash out and merchant payment. Adapter wraps different banks' APIs behind one BankConnector interface. Observer notifies the balance screen, the SMS service and the fraud detection module whenever a transaction completes. Facade offers a simple TransferService.transfer() to the screens while coordinating limits, fees, ledgers and notifications. Each pattern solves a real, recurring pain point.

Real life example 2, a news portal: A Bangla news website lets editors publish articles that go to the website, the mobile app and social media. Observer: publishing an article notifies all channels. Decorator: an article view can be wrapped with "breaking news" banners or sponsored labels without changing the article class. Builder: constructing complex article objects with optional images, videos, tags and related links. Template Method: each export channel follows the same steps of fetch, format and send, with channel-specific formatting.

Common mistakes: Memorising class diagrams without understanding the problem each pattern solves. Confusing similar patterns: Adapter changes an interface to match another, Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour, Facade simplifies a whole subsystem. Mixing Strategy and State: in Strategy the client usually chooses the algorithm; in State the object changes its own state internally. Overusing Singleton as a convenient global variable.

What exams ask: Define design pattern and explain its four elements. Who are the Gang of Four and how are the 23 patterns classified? Explain Singleton, Factory Method, Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Observer and Strategy with class diagrams and examples. Differentiate Adapter and Decorator, or Strategy and State. What is an anti-pattern? Identify the pattern used in a given scenario.

Recap: Design patterns are named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems, popularised by the Gang of Four's 1994 book of 23 patterns in creational, structural and behavioural categories. Singleton, Factory Method and Builder manage object creation. Adapter, Decorator and Facade organise structure. Observer, Strategy, State, Command and Template Method organise behaviour and communication. Use patterns when the problem is real, avoid anti-patterns, and keep designs simple. Next lesson: writing quality code, code reviews and refactoring.
key_points: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem, not copy-paste code.
The Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, 1994) catalogued 23 patterns: 5 creational, 7 structural, 11 behavioural.
Creational: Singleton (one instance), Factory Method (subclasses or factory decide which class), Builder (step-by-step construction).
Structural: Adapter (convert an interface), Decorator (add behaviour by wrapping), Facade (simple front for a complex subsystem).
Behavioural: Observer (notify subscribers of changes), Strategy (swappable algorithms), State (behaviour changes with state).
Command turns requests into objects (undo/redo); Template Method fixes an algorithm's skeleton with overridable steps.
Anti-patterns like God Object and Spaghetti Code are common 'solutions' that cause more harm.
Apply patterns only when the problem actually appears; over-using them adds needless complexity.
lessons.tip: For each pattern, learn one sentence: 'Use X when ...'. For example, 'Use Adapter when the interface you have is not the interface you need.' Exam scenarios become easy to match.
lessons.task: Look at your phone's apps and find one real example each for Observer (something that notifies you when data changes), Strategy (choosing between methods, like payment options) and Facade (one button that triggers many hidden steps). Write two lines for each.

quiz.q: How many patterns are in the Gang of Four book?
quiz.explain: The 1994 book catalogues 23 patterns in three categories.

quiz.q: Which pattern lets incompatible interfaces work together, like a travel plug converter?
quiz.explain: Adapter converts the interface of an existing class into the one the client expects.

quiz.q: Adding milk, sugar and an extra shot to a coffee object by wrapping it is an example of:
quiz.explain: Decorators wrap an object with the same interface and add behaviour dynamically.

quiz.q: A score object notifies the scoreboard, a notification service and statistics whenever it changes. Which pattern?
quiz.explain: Observers register with the subject and are notified of changes.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of the Singleton pattern?
options: It always creates too many objects
It acts like a global variable and makes testing harder
It cannot be used in Java
It requires an interface for every class
quiz.explain: Hidden global state and hidden dependencies make code harder to test and change.

lessons.title: Code Quality, Code Review and Refactoring
lessons.content:
Imagine two notebooks from the same class. One is neat: headings, dates, clear handwriting, each topic on a new page. The other is a mess: notes squeezed in margins, arrows everywhere, half-erased formulas. Both may contain the same information, but a week before the exam, only the first one helps you. Code is the same. Programs are read far more often than they are written: by teammates, by reviewers, by the person fixing a bug at 2 a.m., and by you six months later. Software construction is not just making code run; it is making code that others can read, trust and change.

What construction means: Software construction is the detailed creation of working software through coding, verification, unit testing, integration testing and debugging. It is where design becomes real. The book Code Complete by Steve McConnell is a classic guide to this stage. Construction quality matters because most of a system's lifetime cost is in maintenance, and code that is hard to read is slow and risky to maintain.

Coding standards: A coding standard (or style guide) is a set of rules a team agrees to follow: naming conventions, indentation, line length, file organisation, how to handle errors, which language features to avoid. Examples include PEP 8 for Python, the Google Java Style Guide and the Effective Dart guidelines. The goal is not that one style is perfect, but that all code looks consistent, so readers can focus on logic, not formatting. Automatic formatters like Prettier, Black or dart format apply the style mechanically, which ends many pointless arguments.

Meaningful names: Names are the most important documentation. Compare int d; // elapsed time in days with int elapsedDays. Good names reveal intent: calculateMonthlyInstalment, isEligibleForScholarship, customerAddress. Avoid single letters except for short loop counters, avoid abbreviations only you understand (cstAdrLn2), avoid misleading names (a list called accountMap), and use one word per concept (do not mix fetch, retrieve and get for the same idea). Classes are usually nouns (Invoice), methods usually verbs (sendInvoice), and booleans read like questions (isPaid, hasStock).

Functions and structure: Small functions that do one thing are easier to understand, test and reuse. A function named validateAndSaveAndEmailUser is doing three jobs. Keep the number of parameters small; if you need many, maybe they belong together in an object. Avoid deep nesting: instead of four levels of if inside if, return early for invalid cases (guard clauses). Avoid magic numbers: write if (age >= ADULT_AGE) rather than if (age >= 18) repeated across the code, so the meaning is clear and the value is in one place.

Comments and documentation: Good code explains what it does through names and structure; comments should explain why. A useful comment: // The bank API rejects amounts above 50,000 in one call, so we split large transfers. A useless comment: i++; // increment i. Outdated comments are worse than none, because they lie. Public APIs deserve documentation comments (Javadoc, docstrings) describing parameters, return values and errors. Larger decisions belong in README files or architecture decision records.

Error handling and defensive programming: Construction includes deciding what happens when things go wrong. Validate inputs at boundaries (user input, files, network). Handle exceptions where you can do something meaningful, and do not silently swallow them with an empty catch block. Fail fast with a clear message rather than continuing with corrupted data. Assertions can document assumptions that must always be true. Defensive programming means not trusting inputs from outside your control, while avoiding paranoid checks everywhere inside trusted code.

Build in small steps: Experienced developers write a little code, compile and run it, test it, and only then write more. Writing 500 lines before running anything means that when it fails, the bug could be anywhere. Small steps keep each problem small and easy to locate. The same idea applies to commits: small, focused commits with clear messages are easier to review and, if needed, to undo.

Code smells: A code smell, a term popularised by Kent Beck and Martin Fowler, is a surface sign that usually indicates a deeper design problem. Common smells: long method (a function of hundreds of lines), large class (a class with too many responsibilities), duplicated code, long parameter list, feature envy (a method that uses another class's data more than its own), data clumps (the same group of variables always appearing together, like street, city, postcode), switch statements on type codes repeated in many places, primitive obsession (using strings and ints for things that deserve their own type, like money or phone numbers), shotgun surgery (one change requires small edits in many classes) and dead code. A smell is not always a bug, but it tells you where to look.

What refactoring is: Martin Fowler defines refactoring as a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behaviour. The key words are "without changing behaviour". Refactoring is not adding features and not fixing bugs; it is cleaning. It is done in small, safe steps, each followed by running the tests. Fowler's book Refactoring catalogues many named refactorings.

Common refactorings: Extract Method: move a block of code into a new, well-named function. Rename: give a variable, method or class a clearer name. Extract Class: split a class with two responsibilities into two. Move Method: move a method to the class whose data it uses most. Replace Magic Number with Named Constant. Introduce Parameter Object: replace a long parameter list with an object. Replace Conditional with Polymorphism: replace a type-based switch with subclasses or strategies. Inline: remove a pointless indirection. Modern IDEs automate many of these safely.

A worked refactoring: Original: a 60-line function printReport(orders) that loops over orders, sums totals, applies a 5 percent discount if total > 10,000, formats each line and prints. Step 1: extract calculateTotal(orders), run tests. Step 2: extract applyDiscount(total) with a named constant DISCOUNT_THRESHOLD = 10000, run tests. Step 3: extract formatLine(order), run tests. Now printReport is five readable lines, each helper can be unit tested, and when the discount rule changes there is one obvious place to edit. Behaviour never changed at any step.

When to refactor: The "rule of three": the first time you do something, just do it; the second time, wince at the duplication; the third time, refactor. Refactor before adding a feature if the current structure makes the feature hard to add ("make the change easy, then make the easy change", a saying attributed to Kent Beck). Refactor when fixing a bug if confusing code caused the bug. Refactor during code review. Do not refactor code that is about to be thrown away, and do not start big refactorings without tests to protect you.

Tests make refactoring safe: Without automated tests, you cannot be sure that refactoring did not change behaviour, so developers become afraid to touch old code, and it decays further. With a good test suite, you can restructure confidently: if all tests still pass, behaviour is very likely unchanged. This is why test-driven development and refactoring go together in XP.

Technical debt: Ward Cunningham coined the metaphor of technical debt. Taking shortcuts (skipping tests, copy-pasting, hacky fixes) is like borrowing money: you move faster now, but you pay "interest" later as every future change takes longer. Some debt is deliberate and reasonable, like a quick prototype to meet a demo deadline, as long as it is repaid. Unmanaged debt grows until the team spends most of its time fighting the code. Teams track debt items in the backlog and reserve time to pay them down.

Code review: A code review is when one or more developers examine code written by someone else before it is merged. Benefits: finding defects early, spreading knowledge of the codebase, keeping consistent style, mentoring juniors, and sharing responsibility. Today most reviews happen through pull requests on platforms like GitHub or GitLab, which we see in the Git lesson. A good reviewer checks correctness, readability, tests, security and design, and writes respectful, specific comments ("This loop runs the query once per order; can we fetch all orders in one query?") rather than vague criticism.

Formal inspections: Michael Fagan developed a formal inspection process at IBM in the 1970s. A Fagan inspection has defined roles (moderator, author, reader, inspectors, recorder), defined steps (planning, overview, individual preparation, inspection meeting, rework, follow-up), checklists, and measures such as defects found per hour. Formal inspections find many defects but cost time; they are common in safety-critical work. Lighter forms include walkthroughs (the author leads colleagues through the code or design) and pair programming, which is continuous review.

Static analysis and linters: Static analysis tools examine source code without running it, to find likely bugs, security problems and style violations. Linters such as ESLint, Pylint or the Dart analyzer flag unused variables, unreachable code, suspicious comparisons and style issues. Larger tools like SonarQube measure duplication, complexity and code smells across a project. Compilers' warnings are a basic form of static analysis; treating warnings seriously prevents many bugs. These tools are cheap reviewers that never get tired, but they do not replace human review of design and logic.

Real life example 1, a startup's growing app: A Dhaka startup built its delivery app quickly, with one 2,000-line file for order handling. After a year, every new feature broke something, and new developers needed weeks to understand the code. The team introduced a style guide and automatic formatting, required pull request reviews, added tests around the order flow, and then refactored step by step: extracting pricing, delivery assignment and notification into separate classes. Feature development speed recovered within a few months.

Real life example 2, a student group project: Four students build a hostel management system for a course. Without rules, one names variables in Bangla transliteration, another in English abbreviations, and two copy the same fee calculation into different screens with different bugs. Agreeing on a style guide in week one, reviewing each other's pull requests, and extracting the fee calculation into one tested function makes the final demo smooth and makes it easy for any member to explain any part during the viva.

Common mistakes: Confusing refactoring with rewriting or with adding features. Refactoring without tests. Writing comments that repeat the code instead of explaining why. Treating code review as a personal attack, or as a rubber stamp. Ignoring linter warnings until there are thousands. Thinking clean code is only about formatting; structure, naming and responsibility matter more.

What exams ask: What is software construction? Why are coding standards important? List and explain common code smells. Define refactoring and give examples of refactoring techniques. What is technical debt? Explain the benefits of code reviews, and describe the Fagan inspection process and its roles. Differentiate walkthrough and inspection. What is static analysis?

Recap: Construction turns design into working code. Coding standards, meaningful names, small functions, useful comments and careful error handling make code readable. Code smells point to deeper problems; refactoring improves structure without changing behaviour, in small steps protected by tests. Technical debt is the interest paid for shortcuts. Code reviews, formal inspections, walkthroughs and static analysis find defects early and spread knowledge. Next lesson: version control with Git.
key_points: Code is read far more than it is written, so readability is a core quality of construction.
Coding standards and automatic formatters keep a codebase consistent.
Meaningful names, small single-purpose functions, guard clauses and named constants make code clearer.
Comments should explain why, not repeat what; outdated comments mislead.
Code smells (long method, large class, duplication, feature envy, shotgun surgery...) signal deeper design problems.
Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour, in small steps protected by tests.
Technical debt is the future cost of shortcuts; track it and pay it down.
Code reviews, Fagan inspections, walkthroughs and static analysis catch defects early and spread knowledge.
lessons.tip: Before you push code, read it once as if you were a stranger seeing it for the first time. Rename anything you had to think twice about.
lessons.task: Take a function you wrote that is longer than 30 lines. Apply three refactorings: rename at least two unclear variables, extract one helper function, and replace one magic number with a named constant. Check it still gives the same output for three test inputs.

options: Adding new features to existing code
Rewriting the whole system in a new language
Improving internal structure without changing observable behaviour

quiz.explain: Shotgun surgery means one change forces many small edits spread across the code.

quiz.q: Which comment is most useful?
options: // The bank API rejects amounts above 50,000 per call, so we split transfers
quiz.explain: Good comments explain why, which the code alone cannot show.

quiz.explain: Fagan inspections have defined roles, steps and checklists.

options: The future cost of shortcuts taken now
The salary of the testing team
The price of a compiler licence
quiz.explain: Shortcuts speed you up now but make every later change slower, like interest on a loan.

lessons.title: Version Control with Git
lessons.content:
Have you ever had a folder like this: report.docx, report_final.docx, report_final2.docx, report_final_REAL.docx, report_final_REAL_sir_comments.docx? Now imagine five people editing the same report at the same time and emailing copies to each other. Soon nobody knows which version is the latest, whose changes were lost, or when a mistake crept in. Software teams faced this with thousands of files changing every day. Version control systems were invented to solve exactly this problem, and today the most used one in the world is Git.

What version control is: A version control system (VCS) records changes to files over time, so that you can recall specific versions later, see who changed what and why, compare versions, undo mistakes, and let many people work on the same project without overwriting each other's work. It is a time machine and a collaboration tool at once. It belongs to the umbrella activity called software configuration management, which we revisit in the last lesson.

Why it matters: Without version control, a bad change can destroy days of work with no way back. With it, you can return to yesterday's working version in seconds. You can see exactly which line changed when a bug appeared. Many developers can work in parallel on different features. Releases can be tagged and rebuilt exactly. And the history itself becomes documentation: each change carries a message explaining why it was made.

Centralized version control: Older systems such as CVS and Subversion (SVN) are centralized. There is one central server holding the full history; developers check out a working copy, and commit changes back to the server. It is simple to understand and gives central control. But if the server is down, nobody can commit or see history, and if the server's disk is lost without backup, the history is gone. Most operations need a network connection.

Distributed version control: In a distributed system such as Git or Mercurial, every developer has a complete copy of the repository, including the full history, on their own machine. Commits, history browsing, branching and comparing all work offline and are very fast. Developers share changes by pushing to and pulling from other repositories, usually a shared remote on a service like GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket. If any server dies, any clone can restore it.

A little history of Git: Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage the development of the Linux kernel, after the free use of the proprietary system the kernel developers had been using ended. Its design goals included speed, support for thousands of parallel branches, a distributed model and strong protection against corruption. Each commit is identified by a hash computed from its content, so any change to history is detectable. Git quickly became the standard tool for open-source and commercial software.

The basic concepts: A repository (repo) is the project folder together with its complete history, stored in a hidden .git directory. A commit is a snapshot of the project at a point in time, with an author, a date, a message and a link to its parent commit or commits. Commits form a chain (more precisely, a graph) that is the project's history. A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, letting you develop a line of work separately. HEAD is a pointer to the branch or commit you currently have checked out.

The three areas: Git has three main places for your files. The working directory is the files you see and edit. The staging area (also called the index) holds the changes you have selected for the next commit. The repository holds the committed history. The basic cycle is: edit files in the working directory; git add selects changes into the staging area; git commit records the staged snapshot into the repository. The staging area lets you commit only some of your changes, keeping each commit focused.

Your first commands: git init creates a new repository in the current folder. git clone URL copies an existing repository, with its full history, from a remote. git status shows which files are modified, staged or untracked. git add file.dart stages a file. git commit -m "Add fee calculation for siblings" records a commit with a message. git log shows the history. git diff shows unstaged changes line by line. A .gitignore file lists files Git should ignore, such as build outputs, secret keys and editor settings.

Writing good commit messages: A good commit message has a short summary line (around 50 characters, in imperative mood like "Fix crash when cart is empty"), and if needed a blank line followed by an explanation of what and why. Each commit should contain one logical change. "Fixed stuff" or "update" tells future readers nothing. Good messages make git log a readable story of the project and help reviewers and bug hunters.

Branches: Creating a branch is cheap and fast in Git. git branch feature/login creates a branch; git switch feature/login (or the older git checkout feature/login) moves to it; git switch -c feature/login does both. Work on the branch does not affect the main branch until you merge it. This lets one developer build a login feature, another fix a payment bug, and a third experiment with a new design, all in parallel, each on their own branch.

Merging: When a feature is ready, you merge its branch back. If the main branch has not moved since you branched, Git can do a fast-forward merge: it simply moves the main pointer forward to your latest commit. If both branches have new commits, Git performs a three-way merge using the two branch tips and their common ancestor, and records a merge commit with two parents. An alternative is rebase, which replays your commits on top of the latest main branch to produce a straight, linear history. A common rule: do not rebase commits that others have already pulled, because it rewrites history they depend on.

Merge conflicts: A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file differently, or one edited a file the other deleted. Git cannot decide which version is right, so it stops and marks the conflicting area in the file with markers: <<<<<<< HEAD, then your version, then =======, then the other version, then >>>>>>> branch-name. You edit the file to the correct final content, remove the markers, git add the file and complete the merge with a commit. Conflicts are normal; small, frequent merges keep them small.

Remotes, push and pull: A remote is another copy of the repository, usually on a server, conventionally named origin. git push origin feature/login uploads your branch's commits to the remote. git fetch downloads new commits from the remote without changing your files. git pull is fetch followed by merge (or rebase) into your current branch. Before pushing, pull the latest changes so you integrate others' work first. If someone else pushed in between, Git will refuse your push until you integrate their changes.

Pull requests and code review: On platforms like GitHub and GitLab, a pull request (GitLab calls it a merge request) is a proposal to merge one branch into another. Teammates review the changes line by line, comment, request changes, and approve. Automated checks (builds, tests, linters) usually run on every pull request, connecting to continuous integration. Many teams protect the main branch so that changes can only arrive through reviewed pull requests with passing tests.

Branching strategies: Teams agree on how to use branches. Git Flow, described by Vincent Driessen in 2010, uses long-lived main and develop branches plus feature, release and hotfix branches; it suits products with planned, versioned releases. GitHub Flow is simpler: main is always deployable, every change happens on a short-lived feature branch, reviewed in a pull request, merged and deployed. Trunk-based development has developers integrating small changes into the main branch (the trunk) at least daily, often hiding unfinished features behind feature flags; it supports continuous integration and frequent releases.

Undoing things safely: git restore file discards uncommitted changes in a file. git restore --staged file unstages it. git revert commit-id creates a new commit that undoes an earlier commit, which is safe for shared history because it does not rewrite anything. git reset moves the branch pointer back and can rewrite history, so use it only on commits that are not yet shared. git stash temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches and come back later.

Tags and semantic versioning: A tag marks a specific commit, usually a release, with a name like v2.3.1. Semantic versioning (SemVer) gives version numbers a meaning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase MAJOR when you make incompatible changes (for example removing an API endpoint), MINOR when you add functionality in a backward-compatible way, and PATCH when you make backward-compatible bug fixes. So going from 2.3.1 to 2.3.2 is a safe bug fix, to 2.4.0 adds features, and to 3.0.0 warns users that something may break.

Real life example 1, a team building a bus ticket app: Five developers work on a bus ticket booking app. Each feature, such as seat selection or SMS tickets, gets its own branch. Developers push their branches and open pull requests; a teammate reviews, and the CI server runs tests. One day two developers both edit the fare calculation, creating a conflict; they sit together, resolve it, and add a test so the combined logic is verified. Before Eid, the team tags v1.4.0 and deploys exactly that commit. When a bug appears in production, they create a hotfix branch, release v1.4.1, and merge the fix back.

Real life example 2, a thesis with Git: A student writing a thesis keeps the LaTeX source and analysis scripts in a private GitHub repository. Every evening she commits with a message like "Add results table for experiment 3". When her laptop crashes a week before submission, she clones the repository on a lab computer and loses nothing. When her supervisor asks "what did you change since last Monday?", git diff answers in seconds. Git is not only for big teams.

Common mistakes: Committing secrets such as passwords or API keys; once pushed, assume they are leaked and rotate them. Committing huge generated files or build folders instead of using .gitignore. Making one giant commit for a week of work. Working directly on main without branches in a team. Force-pushing over shared history. Confusing Git (the tool) with GitHub (a hosting service built around Git). Panicking at conflicts instead of reading the markers calmly.

What exams ask: What is version control and why is it needed? Compare centralized and distributed version control. Explain repository, commit, branch, merge, HEAD and remote. Describe the three areas of Git and the add-commit workflow. What is a merge conflict and how is it resolved? Explain pull requests and a branching strategy such as Git Flow or trunk-based development. Explain semantic versioning with examples.

Recap: Version control records history, enables safe undo and lets teams collaborate. Centralized systems keep one server; distributed systems like Git give everyone the full history. Git's cycle is edit, add to staging, commit; branches allow parallel work; merges and rebases integrate it; conflicts are resolved by editing marked regions. Remotes, push, pull and pull requests connect a team, and branching strategies and semantic versioning keep releases orderly. Next lesson: the fundamentals of software testing.
key_points: Version control records file history, enables undo, shows who changed what and why, and supports parallel teamwork.
Centralized VCS (CVS, SVN) depend on one server; distributed VCS (Git, Mercurial) give every clone the full history.
Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for Linux kernel development.
Git's three areas: working directory, staging area (index) and repository; the cycle is edit, git add, git commit.
Branches are cheap pointers to commits; merging integrates them, and conflicts are resolved by editing the marked lines.
Remotes, push, fetch/pull and pull requests connect a team's repositories and enable code review.
Branching strategies: Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development.
Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking changes, new compatible features, compatible bug fixes.
lessons.tip: Commit small and often with clear messages. If you cannot describe a commit in one short sentence, it probably contains more than one change.
lessons.task: Install Git (or use an online Git playground), create a repository for a small text file, make three commits, create a branch, change the same line on both branches, and merge to create and resolve a conflict yourself.
