options: Every clone has the full history, so most operations work offline and any clone can restore the server
Only one person can work at a time
quiz.explain: In Git each developer's repository is complete, not just a working copy.

quiz.q: Which command moves changes from the working directory into the staging area?
quiz.explain: git add stages changes; git commit then records them.

quiz.q: Who created Git and when?
quiz.explain: Torvalds wrote Git in 2005 to manage Linux kernel development.

quiz.q: A library goes from version 2.3.1 to 3.0.0. According to semantic versioning, what does this signal?
quiz.explain: Increasing MAJOR means changes that are not backward compatible.

quiz.q: Which command safely undoes a commit that others have already pulled?
quiz.explain: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the old one without rewriting shared history.

lessons.title: Software Testing Fundamentals
lessons.content:
Before a new bus goes on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway, many checks happen. Each part is tested at the factory: brakes, engine, lights. Then the assembled bus is tested on a track. Then the whole bus is tested with a full load of passengers on a real road. Finally the bus company's own drivers try it and say whether it suits their routes. If any test fails, the problem is found before passengers are in danger. Software testing works the same way: test small parts, then parts together, then the whole system, then let real users confirm it.

What testing is: Software testing is the process of executing a program, or examining its artifacts, to find defects and to gain confidence that it meets its requirements. Glenford Myers, in his classic book The Art of Software Testing, defined testing as the process of executing a program with the intent of finding errors. A good test is one that has a high chance of finding a problem not yet discovered. Testing also gives information to decision makers: is this release good enough to ship?

Testing cannot prove correctness: Edsger Dijkstra famously observed that program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence. Even a small function with two 32-bit integer inputs has 2 to the power 64 possible input combinations, far too many to try. So testing is about choosing a small, clever set of test cases that is most likely to reveal defects, and about managing risk, not about proving perfection.

Error, fault and failure: These three words have precise meanings. An error (or mistake) is a human action that produces an incorrect result, like a programmer misunderstanding a requirement or typing < instead of <=. A fault (also called a defect or bug) is the resulting flaw in the code or document. A failure is when the system, while running, behaves differently from what is expected, because a fault was executed. Example: the programmer makes an error and writes if (marks > 80) for an A grade instead of if (marks >= 80); that is the fault; when a student with exactly 80 gets a B, that is the failure. A fault can sit unnoticed for years if the code path is never run.

Verification and validation again: Recall from the V-model lesson: verification asks "are we building the product right?" and checks each work product against its specification, often through reviews, inspections and static analysis without running code. Validation asks "are we building the right product?" and checks the final system against the user's real needs, usually by running it. Testing contributes to both. Static techniques (reviews, analysis) and dynamic techniques (executing tests) complement each other.

Quality assurance vs quality control vs testing: Quality assurance (QA) is process-oriented: it aims to prevent defects by improving how software is built, through standards, reviews and process audits. Quality control (QC) is product-oriented: it finds defects in the product, and testing is the main QC activity. In many companies the job title "QA engineer" is used for testers, but in theory QA is broader than testing. We return to QA in the quality lesson.

The seven testing principles: The ISTQB, an international software testing certification body, lists seven principles. One: testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence. Two: exhaustive testing is impossible, so prioritise using risk and test techniques. Three: early testing saves time and money; start testing activities as early as possible, even on requirements. Four: defects cluster together; a small number of modules usually contain most of the defects, so focus there. Five: the pesticide paradox; repeating the same tests stops finding new bugs, so tests must be reviewed and updated (newer ISTQB versions phrase this as tests wearing out). Six: testing is context dependent; testing a banking system differs from testing a mobile game. Seven: absence-of-errors is a fallacy; a system with no known bugs can still be useless if it does not meet user needs.

Test levels: Testing is organised into levels that match the development stages. Unit (component) testing checks individual functions, methods or classes in isolation, usually by developers. Integration testing checks that units or components work together correctly, focusing on interfaces and data passed between them. System testing checks the complete, integrated system against the requirements, both functional and non-functional, in an environment close to production. Acceptance testing checks whether the system satisfies the users and the business, and decides whether to accept it.

Unit testing in detail: A unit test calls one small piece of code with specific inputs and checks the output. Example for a function calculateGrade(marks): calculateGrade(85) should return "A", calculateGrade(80) should return "A", calculateGrade(79) should return "A-" (depending on the grading table), and calculateGrade(-5) should raise an error. Unit tests are fast, run hundreds of times a day, and pinpoint exactly where a problem is. We look at writing and automating them in the test automation lesson.

Integration testing strategies: How do you combine units? In big-bang integration, all modules are joined at once and tested together; it is simple but when something fails, finding the cause is hard. In top-down integration, testing starts with the top-level modules (like the user interface or main controller), and lower modules not yet ready are replaced by stubs, simple fake modules that return fixed answers. In bottom-up integration, testing starts with the lowest-level modules, and higher modules are simulated by drivers, small programs that call the module under test. Sandwich (hybrid) integration combines top-down and bottom-up. Incremental strategies localise faults much better than big-bang.

Stubs and drivers example: You are testing a ResultService that calls a DatabaseModule, which is not finished. A stub DatabaseModule returns fixed marks for student 101, so ResultService can be tested now (top-down). Conversely, the DatabaseModule is ready but the user interface is not; you write a driver, a tiny program that calls DatabaseModule.getMarks(101) and prints the result, to test it from below (bottom-up).

System testing: System testing treats the whole system as one product. Functional system tests check end-to-end features: register, log in, add to cart, pay, receive confirmation. Non-functional system tests check qualities: performance (response times under normal load), load and stress (behaviour at and beyond expected peak), security (attacks such as SQL injection or broken access control), usability, compatibility (different phones and browsers), recovery (what happens after a crash) and installation. These come from the non-functional requirements in the SRS.

Acceptance testing: User acceptance testing (UAT) is performed by customers or users, often with business scenarios, to decide whether the system is acceptable. Contract acceptance testing checks the system against the criteria in a contract. Operational acceptance testing checks things like backup, recovery and maintenance procedures. Alpha testing is done by potential users or an independent test team at the developer's site, in a controlled environment. Beta testing is done by real users in their own environments before the final release; many apps release beta versions through app stores to a limited group.

Regression testing and retesting: When code changes, previously working features can break. Regression testing re-runs existing tests after a change to check that nothing that used to work has broken. Retesting (confirmation testing) runs the specific test that previously failed, to confirm that a reported bug is fixed. Because regression suites grow large and run often, they are prime candidates for automation.

Smoke and sanity testing: A smoke test is a quick, broad check that the most important functions work after a new build, such as the app opens, login works and the main screen loads, before spending time on deeper testing. A sanity test is a quick, narrow check that a specific fix or feature works as expected. If the smoke test fails, the build is rejected immediately.

Black-box and white-box: Test design techniques fall into two big families. Black-box (specification-based) techniques design tests from requirements and specifications, without looking at the code; examples are equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis. White-box (structure-based) techniques design tests from the internal structure of the code, aiming to cover statements, branches or paths. Grey-box testing uses partial knowledge of the internals. The next two lessons cover each family in depth.

Anatomy of a test case: A test case is a set of conditions and steps used to check one specific behaviour. Typical fields: test case ID, title, related requirement, preconditions, test data, steps, expected result, actual result, and status (pass or fail). Example: TC-07, "Login fails with wrong password", requirement REQ-3; precondition: user rahim exists with password Secret123; steps: open login page, enter rahim and wrong123, press Login; expected: message "Incorrect username or password", user stays on login page, failed attempt counter increases by 1. A good test case is clear enough that another tester can run it and get the same result.

Bug reports and the defect life cycle: When a test fails, the tester writes a defect report: a short, specific title, steps to reproduce, expected vs actual result, environment (device, OS, browser, app version), severity (how bad the impact is, from critical to trivial), priority (how urgently it should be fixed), and screenshots or logs. A defect moves through a life cycle: New, Assigned, Open, Fixed, Retest, and then Closed if the fix works or Reopened if not; it may also be Rejected or Deferred. Severity and priority differ: a spelling mistake in the company name on the home page is low severity but high priority.

Test planning and documentation: A test plan describes the scope, approach, resources, schedule, environments, entry and exit criteria, risks and deliverables of testing. The IEEE 829 standard, now superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119, defined common test documents. Exit criteria might be: all high-priority test cases executed, 95 percent pass rate, no open critical defects. Test reports summarise results so managers can decide whether to release.

Real life example 1, a mobile banking release: Before releasing a new "pay utility bill" feature, developers write unit tests for bill amount calculation. Integration tests check the app talking to the bill provider's API, using a stub when the provider's test server is down. System testers run end-to-end scenarios on several Android phones, including slow 3G networks, and a load test simulates thousands of payments on the last day before a due date. A beta version goes to staff members first. Regression tests confirm that send money and recharge still work.

Real life example 2, a university result system: Unit tests check GPA calculation for edge cases such as all F grades, retakes and exactly 4.00. Integration tests check that marks entered by teachers reach the result module correctly. System tests check that 8,000 students can view results within the first hour. In UAT, the exam controller's office compares the system's results for last semester with the manually prepared results; any difference is investigated before going live.

Common mistakes: Thinking testing starts only after coding. Believing that if all tests pass, the software is bug-free. Confusing error, fault and failure. Mixing up severity and priority. Testing only the "happy path" with valid inputs. Confusing stubs (replace called modules) with drivers (replace calling modules). Treating alpha and beta testing as the same.

What exams ask: Define testing and explain why exhaustive testing is impossible. Differentiate error, fault and failure with an example. State and explain the seven testing principles. Explain the levels of testing. Compare top-down, bottom-up and big-bang integration, and explain stubs and drivers. Differentiate alpha and beta testing, regression and retesting, smoke and sanity testing, severity and priority. Write a test case for a given feature.

Recap: Testing executes or examines software to find defects and build confidence, but can never prove there are none. A human error creates a fault that may cause a failure. Seven principles guide testing. Levels are unit, integration, system and acceptance; integration can be big-bang, top-down with stubs, bottom-up with drivers, or sandwich. Alpha, beta, regression, smoke and sanity tests serve different purposes. Clear test cases and defect reports make testing effective. Next lesson: black-box test design techniques.
key_points: Testing executes or examines software to find defects; it can show bugs exist but never prove their absence (Dijkstra).
Error (human mistake) leads to a fault (defect in code) that may cause a failure (wrong behaviour when run).
Seven principles: defects not absence, exhaustive testing impossible, test early, defect clustering, pesticide paradox, context dependent, absence-of-errors fallacy.
Test levels: unit, integration, system and acceptance.
Integration strategies: big-bang, top-down (uses stubs), bottom-up (uses drivers) and sandwich.
Alpha testing is at the developer's site; beta testing is by real users in their own environment.
Regression testing checks nothing old broke; retesting confirms a specific fix; smoke tests check a build's basic health.
Severity is the impact of a defect; priority is how urgently to fix it.
lessons.tip: For every feature you test, ask three questions: what should happen with normal input, what should happen with wrong input, and what happens at the edges? Most bugs live in the last two.
lessons.task: Pick the login screen of any app. Write five complete test cases (ID, precondition, steps, expected result) covering a correct login, a wrong password, an empty field, a very long input and three wrong attempts in a row.

quiz.q: A programmer types > instead of >= and a student with exactly 80 marks gets the wrong grade. What is the wrong grade on screen?
quiz.explain: The failure is the observable wrong behaviour; the fault is the wrong code; the error is the human mistake.

quiz.q: Which principle says repeating the same tests eventually stops finding new bugs?
quiz.explain: Tests must be reviewed and updated, like changing pesticides.

quiz.q: In top-down integration testing, missing lower-level modules are replaced by:
quiz.explain: Stubs stand in for modules that are called but not yet ready.

quiz.q: Testing done by real users in their own environment before final release is called:
quiz.explain: Beta testing happens at the users' sites; alpha happens at the developer's site.

quiz.q: A spelling mistake in the company name on the home page is usually:
quiz.explain: It does little functional harm but is very visible, so it should be fixed quickly.

lessons.title: Black-Box Testing Techniques
lessons.content:
Imagine checking a new vending machine without opening it. You do not look at its circuits. You simply try things: put in a 10 Taka note, a 20 Taka note, a torn note, a coin, no money at all; press a button for a drink that is sold out; press two buttons together. You judge the machine only by what goes in and what comes out. That is black-box testing: designing tests from what the software is supposed to do, without looking inside the code. The trick is choosing a small number of clever inputs instead of trying everything.

What black-box testing is: Black-box testing, also called specification-based or behavioural testing, derives test cases from requirements, specifications, user stories and use cases. The tester treats the software as a box whose inside is hidden and focuses on inputs, outputs and behaviour. It can be applied at every level, from unit to acceptance testing, and testers do not need to know the programming language. Its weakness is that it cannot tell you which parts of the code were never exercised; white-box testing, in the next lesson, fills that gap.

The core problem: Consider a field that accepts an age from 18 to 60. Valid integer inputs alone are 43 values, and invalid ones are endless: 17, 61, -1, 1000, 0, 25.5, "abc", empty. Testing all of them is impossible or wasteful. Black-box techniques give systematic rules for picking a few representative values that are most likely to reveal defects. The main techniques are equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing and use case testing.

Equivalence partitioning: Equivalence partitioning (EP), also called equivalence class partitioning, divides the input (or output) domain into groups, called partitions or classes, where the system is expected to behave the same way for every value in the group. If one value in a partition reveals a bug, others in the same partition probably would too; if one passes, others probably pass. So we test one representative value from each partition, both valid and invalid.

EP worked example: Requirement: an online form accepts an applicant's age from 18 to 60 inclusive. Partitions: invalid low (age less than 18), valid (18 to 60), invalid high (greater than 60). Pick one representative from each: 10, 35 and 75. Three tests cover the main behaviour instead of dozens. We can add partitions for other kinds of invalid input: non-numeric text like "abc", empty input, and decimals like 25.5 if only whole numbers are allowed. A useful rule: test valid partitions together where possible, but test each invalid partition in a separate test case, so one error message does not hide another.

EP for multiple inputs and outputs: Partitions can also be found from outputs. For a grading function where 80 to 100 gives A, 70 to 79 gives B, 60 to 69 gives C, 0 to 59 gives F, there are four valid output partitions plus invalid partitions below 0 and above 100. Representatives might be 90, 75, 65, 30, -5 and 105. Each different behaviour described in the specification usually suggests a partition.

Boundary value analysis: Experience shows that many defects occur at the edges of partitions, where programmers mix up < and <=, start loops at 1 instead of 0, or forget the last element. Boundary value analysis (BVA) designs tests at and around the boundaries of each partition. It is usually used together with equivalence partitioning: EP finds the partitions, BVA tests their edges.

BVA worked example: For the age range 18 to 60, the boundaries are 18 and 60. In two-value BVA, for each boundary we test the boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition: 17 and 18, and 60 and 61. That gives four tests: 17, 18, 60, 61. In three-value BVA, we also test the value just inside: 17, 18, 19 and 59, 60, 61, giving six tests. Classic textbooks also describe testing min, min+, nominal, max-, max, and robust testing that adds min- and max+. If the programmer wrote if (age > 18) instead of if (age >= 18), the test with 18 will catch it, while an EP-only test with 35 would never notice.

Boundaries everywhere: Boundaries are not only numeric ranges. Think about string lengths (a password of 7, 8, 16 and 17 characters if 8 to 16 are allowed), list sizes (an empty cart, one item, the maximum number of items, one more than maximum), dates (the last day of a month, 29 February in a leap year, the day a deadline ends), money (exactly the daily transaction limit), and time (a promo valid until 11:59 pm). Grading example: test 79 and 80, 69 and 70, 59 and 60, 0 and -1, 100 and 101.

Decision table testing: When behaviour depends on combinations of conditions, a decision table lists all combinations and the expected action for each. Conditions go in rows at the top, actions in rows at the bottom, and each column is a rule (a test case). With N boolean conditions, the full table has 2 to the power N columns. Some columns can be merged when a condition does not affect the outcome; a dash is used for "does not matter".

Decision table worked example: A bank gives a loan only if the applicant is a customer for at least one year (C1) and has a monthly income of at least 30,000 Taka (C2); if they also have a good credit history (C3), the interest rate is lower. Three conditions give 8 rules. Rule 1: C1 yes, C2 yes, C3 yes: approve with low rate. Rule 2: yes, yes, no: approve with normal rate. Rules 3 and 4: C1 yes, C2 no, C3 any: reject. Rules 5 to 8: C1 no: reject. After merging, we have four meaningful columns: (Y, Y, Y), (Y, Y, N), (Y, N, -), (N, -, -), and we write one test case for each. The table also exposes missing requirements: what if the applicant is a customer for exactly 12 months? That becomes a boundary test.

Cause-effect graphing briefly: Cause-effect graphing is a related, more formal technique. Causes (input conditions) and effects (outputs) are drawn as a graph with logical connections such as AND, OR and NOT, and the graph is then converted into a decision table. It is useful for complex logic and helps detect contradictions in specifications, but in everyday practice testers often go straight to decision tables.

State transition testing: Some systems behave differently depending on their current state and past events: ATMs, login systems, order workflows, traffic lights, vending machines. State transition testing uses a state diagram or state table (like those in lesson 11) to design tests that exercise valid transitions and attempt invalid ones. Coverage levels range from visiting every state, to exercising every valid transition (0-switch coverage), to sequences of two transitions (1-switch coverage), and testing invalid transitions.

State transition worked example: A login system allows three attempts. States: Start, Second Try, Third Try, Logged In, Locked. Events: correct PIN, wrong PIN. Transitions: Start with correct PIN goes to Logged In; Start with wrong PIN goes to Second Try; Second Try with wrong goes to Third Try; Third Try with wrong goes to Locked; correct PIN from Second Try or Third Try goes to Logged In. Test cases: correct on first try; wrong then correct; wrong, wrong, correct; wrong, wrong, wrong leading to Locked; and an invalid transition, entering the correct PIN while Locked, which must still be rejected. That last test catches a very common security bug.

State tables: A state table lists every state against every event, showing the next state or marking the combination as invalid. For 5 states and 2 events there are 10 cells. Empty or invalid cells are where bugs hide, because developers often forget to handle "impossible" events, such as a cancel request arriving after an order is already delivered.

Use case testing: Use case testing derives tests from use case descriptions. Each main success scenario becomes at least one test, and each alternative flow and exception becomes another. For the ATM Withdraw Cash use case from lesson 9: one test for the normal withdrawal, one for a wrong PIN, one for three wrong PINs and card retention, one for insufficient balance, one for exceeding the daily limit, one for requesting a receipt. These tests are close to how users actually use the system, so they are excellent for system and acceptance testing.

Other black-box ideas: Error guessing uses the tester's experience to guess likely mistakes: empty input, very long text, special characters like quotes, zero, negative numbers, leap years, duplicate submissions, pressing the back button during payment. Exploratory testing means simultaneously learning, designing and running tests, guided by a mission and a time box. Pairwise (all-pairs) testing reduces combinations when there are many parameters by ensuring every pair of parameter values appears in at least one test, based on the observation that many defects are triggered by the interaction of just two parameters.

Choosing techniques: Use EP and BVA for any input with ranges or classes. Use decision tables when rules combine several conditions. Use state transition testing when history and state matter. Use use case testing for end-to-end user flows. Add error guessing and exploratory testing to find what the formal techniques miss. Most real test suites combine all of these.

Real life example 1, a mobile recharge screen: Requirements: amount from 20 to 1,000 Taka; number must be 11 digits starting with 01. EP: amount partitions below 20, 20 to 1,000, above 1,000, non-numeric; number partitions valid, wrong length, wrong prefix, letters. BVA: amounts 19, 20, 1,000 and 1,001; number lengths 10, 11 and 12. Error guessing: pasting a number with spaces or a +88 country code, pressing confirm twice quickly (which must not double-charge). A dozen well-chosen tests cover what hundreds of random tries would miss.

Real life example 2, a university course registration rule: A student may register only if fees are paid (C1), prerequisites are completed (C2) and the section is not full (C3); advisers can override a full section (C4). A decision table with 16 combinations is simplified to the meaningful rules, revealing a missing requirement: can an adviser override unpaid fees? The team asks the registrar before coding. State transition tests cover a registration moving from Pending to Approved to Dropped, and confirm that a Dropped registration cannot be re-approved without a new request.

Common mistakes: Testing only valid inputs. Picking several values from the same partition, which adds cost but not coverage. Forgetting boundaries of non-numeric things like lengths and dates. Combining several invalid inputs in one test, so you cannot tell which one triggered the error. Building decision tables without checking that all combinations are covered. Ignoring invalid transitions in state testing.

What exams ask: Define black-box testing and give its advantages and limitations. Apply equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis to a given input range and list the test values. Build a decision table for given business rules and derive test cases. Draw a state transition diagram for a given system and derive tests, including invalid transitions. Explain use case testing and error guessing. Compare black-box and white-box testing.

Recap: Black-box testing designs tests from specifications without looking at code. Equivalence partitioning picks one value per class of similar behaviour; boundary value analysis tests the edges where many bugs live; decision tables cover combinations of conditions; state transition testing checks behaviour that depends on state, including invalid transitions; use case testing follows real user flows. Error guessing, exploratory and pairwise testing complement them. Next lesson: white-box testing and cyclomatic complexity.
key_points: Black-box testing derives tests from specifications, treating the code as hidden.
Equivalence partitioning splits inputs into classes with the same expected behaviour and tests one value from each.
Test each invalid partition in its own test case so one error does not hide another.
Boundary value analysis tests at and next to partition edges, e.g. 17, 18, 60, 61 for 18 to 60.
Decision tables list combinations of conditions (2^N rules for N boolean conditions) and expected actions.
State transition testing covers valid transitions and attempts invalid ones, such as logging in while Locked.
Use case testing turns each main and alternative flow into test cases.
Error guessing, exploratory and pairwise testing find what formal techniques can miss.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a range in a requirement, immediately write six numbers: just below, at and just above each end. That habit alone catches a surprising number of bugs.
lessons.task: A cinema gives a 50 percent discount to children under 12 and people aged 65 or more, and charges full price otherwise; ages above 120 are invalid. List the equivalence partitions and the boundary values you would test, then write the expected price result for each.

quiz.q: A field accepts values from 1 to 100. Using two-value boundary value analysis, which set of values should be tested?
quiz.explain: Test each boundary and its nearest neighbour outside: 0, 1, 100, 101.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of equivalence partitioning?
options: Inputs in the same partition are expected to behave the same, so one value per partition is enough
Tests are designed from the source code
quiz.explain: One representative value stands for the whole class.

quiz.q: How many rules does a full decision table have for 4 boolean conditions?
quiz.explain: 2 to the power 4 equals 16 combinations.

quiz.q: In a login system that locks after three wrong PINs, which test checks an invalid transition?
options: Entering the correct PIN on the first try
Entering the correct PIN while the account is Locked
quiz.explain: A Locked account must reject even a correct PIN; this tests an event that should not cause a transition.

quiz.q: Why should each invalid partition be tested in a separate test case?
options: To make the test suite longer
Because valid inputs are not allowed
Because black-box testing requires it by law
So one error message does not hide another defect
quiz.explain: If two invalid values are combined, the first rejection can mask whether the second is handled.

lessons.title: White-Box Testing and Cyclomatic Complexity
lessons.content:
Imagine a building inspector checking a new apartment block in Mirpur. A visitor only checks what they can see: do the lights turn on, does the tap give water? But the inspector also opens panels and follows every wire and pipe, making sure each one is connected and none is left hanging. If one pipe is never used by any tap, a leak in it would go unnoticed until it floods a wall. White-box testing is the inspector's view of software: we look inside the code and design tests so that every statement, every branch and important paths are actually exercised.

What white-box testing is: White-box testing, also called glass-box, clear-box or structure-based testing, designs test cases using knowledge of the program's internal structure: its statements, decisions, loops and paths. It is mostly used at the unit and integration levels, usually by developers. Black-box testing asks "does it do what the specification says?"; white-box testing asks "have we exercised the code we wrote?". The two are complementary: black-box finds missing features, white-box finds untested code.

Why it is needed: Black-box tests can pass while large parts of the code have never run. Hidden branches for rare cases, error handling, or special discounts may contain bugs that no specification-based test touches. Code coverage measures make this visible: if only 60 percent of statements ran during testing, then 40 percent of the code is completely untested. White-box techniques give systematic ways to raise that coverage.

Control flow graphs: White-box testing usually starts by drawing a control flow graph (CFG), also called a flow graph. Nodes represent statements or blocks of statements that run in sequence; edges represent possible transfers of control. A decision such as an if statement becomes a node with two outgoing edges (true and false). A loop becomes a cycle back to the decision node. Sequential statements with no branching can be merged into one node. The graph shows every possible route through the code at a glance.

Coverage criteria overview: Coverage criteria measure how thoroughly tests exercise the structure. The common ones, from weaker to stronger: statement coverage, branch (decision) coverage, condition coverage, condition/decision coverage, modified condition/decision coverage (MC/DC), and path coverage. Stronger criteria need more tests but catch more defects. Coverage is expressed as a percentage: covered items divided by total items, times 100.

Statement coverage: Statement coverage requires every executable statement to be executed at least once. Example: if (x > 0) { y = y + 1; } z = y * 2; One test with x = 5 executes all three statements: 100 percent statement coverage. But we never tested what happens when x is not positive. If the requirement said "when x is zero, y must be reset", that missing behaviour would never be noticed. Statement coverage is the weakest common criterion.

Branch coverage: Branch coverage (decision coverage) requires every branch of every decision, both true and false outcomes, to be taken at least once. For the example above, we need x = 5 (true) and x = -1 (false). Branch coverage includes statement coverage: 100 percent branch coverage always implies 100 percent statement coverage, but not the other way round. In many industries, branch coverage is considered a sensible minimum for unit tests.

Condition coverage and MC/DC: Decisions often have compound conditions, like if (age >= 18 && hasNid). Branch coverage only needs the whole decision to be true once and false once. Condition coverage requires each individual simple condition (age >= 18, hasNid) to be true and false at least once. Condition coverage alone does not guarantee branch coverage, so it is often combined into condition/decision coverage. Modified condition/decision coverage (MC/DC) further requires showing that each condition independently affects the decision's outcome; it is required for the most critical software in aviation standards such as DO-178C.

Path coverage: Path coverage requires every possible path from entry to exit to be executed. It is the strongest criterion, but with loops the number of paths can be enormous or infinite: a loop that can run 0 to 20 times with an if inside has an astronomically large number of paths. So complete path coverage is usually impossible. Basis path testing, described next, gives a practical, systematic subset.

Cyclomatic complexity: Thomas McCabe introduced cyclomatic complexity in 1976. It measures the number of linearly independent paths through a program, which is also the number of tests needed for basis path testing, and it is a widely used measure of a module's logical complexity. It can be computed in three equivalent ways for a single connected flow graph. One: V(G) = E - N + 2P, where E is the number of edges, N the number of nodes and P the number of connected components (P = 1 for one function, giving V(G) = E - N + 2). Two: V(G) = number of predicate (decision) nodes + 1. Three: V(G) = number of regions of the planar flow graph, counting the outside area as one region.

Worked example, the grading function: Consider this pseudo-code. Line 1: read marks. Line 2: if marks > 100, print "Invalid". Line 3: else if marks >= 80, print "A". Line 4: else if marks >= 60, print "B". Line 5: else print "F". Line 6: end. Flow graph nodes: N1 (read and first decision), N2 (print Invalid), N3 (second decision), N4 (print A), N5 (third decision), N6 (print B), N7 (print F), N8 (end). Edges: N1-N2, N1-N3, N3-N4, N3-N5, N5-N6, N5-N7, N2-N8, N4-N8, N6-N8, N7-N8, which is 10 edges. So V(G) = 10 - 8 + 2 = 4. Check with decisions: there are 3 decision nodes (N1, N3, N5), so V(G) = 3 + 1 = 4. Check with regions: the graph encloses 3 regions plus the outside region, giving 4. All three formulas agree.

Basis path testing: Basis path testing, also from McCabe, finds a set of V(G) linearly independent paths and designs one test for each. Linearly independent means each new path introduces at least one edge not covered by the previous paths. For the grading function, a basis set is: Path 1: N1, N2, N8 (marks = 120, expected "Invalid"). Path 2: N1, N3, N4, N8 (marks = 90, expected "A"). Path 3: N1, N3, N5, N6, N8 (marks = 70, expected "B"). Path 4: N1, N3, N5, N7, N8 (marks = 30, expected "F"). Four tests guarantee every statement and every branch is executed. Adding boundary values from black-box testing (100, 101, 80, 79, 60, 59) then strengthens the suite further.

Counting decisions correctly: For loops, a while or for loop contributes one decision. A switch statement with k cases contributes k - 1 decisions (or, equivalently, add the number of case branches minus one). For compound conditions with && or ||, if the flow graph is drawn with each simple condition as its own node, each simple condition counts as a decision; so if (a && b) adds 2, not 1. Different tools follow slightly different counting rules, so be consistent and state your rule in exams.

Using complexity as a warning sign: Cyclomatic complexity is used as a quality metric. McCabe suggested 10 as an upper limit for a module, and many teams and tools still use around 10 as a threshold for review or refactoring. A function with V(G) = 35 is hard to understand and needs at least 35 tests for basis path coverage; it is a strong candidate for splitting into smaller functions. Complexity also correlates with defect density in many studies: complex modules tend to contain more bugs.

Loop testing: Loops need special attention because many bugs hide in them. For a simple loop that can run at most n times, classic loop testing suggests: skip the loop entirely (0 iterations), one pass, two passes, a typical number m of passes, and n - 1, n and n + 1 passes (the last to check the loop cannot exceed its limit). Example: a function that sums at most 10 marks should be tested with empty input, 1 mark, 2 marks, 5 marks, and 9, 10 and 11 marks. For nested loops, start with the innermost loop while holding outer loops at minimum values.

Data flow testing briefly: Data flow testing focuses on how variables are defined (assigned a value) and used. It looks for paths from each definition of a variable to its uses, and for anomalies such as using a variable before it is defined, defining it twice without using it in between, or defining it and never using it. Compilers and static analysers catch some of these automatically.

Mutation testing: How good are your tests? Mutation testing answers by deliberately inserting small changes, called mutants, into the code: changing > to >=, + to -, true to false, or deleting a statement. Then the test suite is run against each mutant. If some test fails, the mutant is "killed", which is good. If all tests still pass, the mutant "survived", meaning your tests would not notice that kind of bug. The mutation score is killed mutants divided by total non-equivalent mutants. Tools exist for many languages, such as PIT for Java and mutmut for Python.

Coverage tools: In practice, nobody draws flow graphs by hand for large code. Coverage tools such as JaCoCo for Java, coverage.py for Python, Istanbul for JavaScript and the built-in flutter test --coverage for Dart measure statement and branch coverage automatically while tests run, and highlight uncovered lines in red. Teams often display coverage in pull requests and set minimum thresholds.

Coverage is not quality: High coverage means the code was executed, not that it was checked properly. A test that calls a function but asserts nothing gets coverage without testing anything. Coverage also cannot find missing code: if the requirement says "send an SMS when payment fails" and nobody wrote that code, there is nothing to cover. That is why white-box and black-box testing must go together, and why mutation testing is a useful check on test strength.

Real life example 1, a loan EMI calculator: A bank's EMI function has branches for invalid input, zero interest promotions, normal interest, and a cap on the maximum tenure. Developers run the black-box tests and the coverage report shows the zero-interest branch was never executed: no test used a 0 percent rate. They add a test, and it reveals a division by zero in that branch, which would have crashed the app during an Eid promotion. Cyclomatic complexity of the function is 6, so they write six basis path tests plus boundary tests.

Real life example 2, a legacy payroll module: An old payroll function in a garment factory's system has cyclomatic complexity 42, with nested if-else for grades, overtime, festival bonuses and deductions. Nobody dares to change it. The team first writes characterisation tests to capture current behaviour, measures branch coverage until it reaches 85 percent, then refactors the function into smaller ones (overtime, bonus, deductions), each with complexity under 10. Mutation testing shows their tests now kill 90 percent of mutants, so they trust the new code.

Common mistakes: Thinking 100 percent statement coverage means thorough testing. Forgetting that branch coverage includes the false outcome of an if with no else. Miscounting edges or nodes when computing V(G); always cross-check with the decisions + 1 formula. Treating compound conditions as one decision without stating the rule. Believing white-box testing alone is enough; it cannot detect missing requirements.

What exams ask: Define white-box testing and compare it with black-box testing. Draw a control flow graph for given code. Compute cyclomatic complexity using all three formulas. Find a basis set of independent paths and design test cases. Differentiate statement, branch, condition and path coverage, and show that branch coverage implies statement coverage. Explain loop testing and mutation testing.

Recap: White-box testing designs tests from the code's structure. Control flow graphs show all routes. Statement coverage is weakest, branch coverage is a common minimum, condition and MC/DC handle compound conditions, and full path coverage is usually impossible. McCabe's cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E - N + 2 = decisions + 1 = regions gives the number of basis paths and a complexity warning signal (around 10). Loop testing, data flow testing and mutation testing add depth, and coverage tools automate measurement. Next lesson: test automation, TDD, CI/CD and DevOps.
key_points: White-box testing designs tests from the code's internal structure, mostly at unit and integration levels.
A control flow graph represents blocks as nodes and possible transfers of control as edges.
Statement coverage is the weakest; branch coverage includes it and covers both outcomes of every decision.
Condition coverage and MC/DC handle compound conditions; full path coverage is usually impossible with loops.
Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe, 1976): V(G) = E - N + 2 = decision nodes + 1 = number of regions.
Basis path testing needs V(G) independent paths, one test per path.
Modules with V(G) above about 10 are hard to test and good refactoring candidates.
Mutation testing checks test strength by seeing whether tests kill small deliberate code changes; coverage alone is not quality.
lessons.tip: Always compute cyclomatic complexity two ways (edges and nodes, then decisions + 1). If the answers differ, you miscounted something in your graph.
lessons.task: Write a small function (any language or pseudo-code) that classifies a BMI value into underweight, normal, overweight and obese. Draw its control flow graph, compute V(G) with two formulas, list the basis paths and give one test input for each.

quiz.q: A flow graph has 11 edges and 9 nodes. What is its cyclomatic complexity?
A function has 5 simple decision nodes. What is V(G)?
quiz.explain: V(G) = number of decisions + 1 = 6.

quiz.q: Which statement about coverage is true?
options: 100 percent branch coverage implies 100 percent statement coverage
Path coverage is the weakest criterion
Coverage tools can find missing features
quiz.explain: Taking every branch runs every statement, but not the other way round.

quiz.q: In mutation testing, what does it mean when a mutant 'survives'?
options: The tests did not detect the deliberate change
quiz.explain: A surviving mutant shows a weakness in the test suite.

quiz.q: For if (x > 0) { y = y + 1; } z = y * 2;, which tests give 100 percent branch coverage?
quiz.explain: One test must make the condition true and another false.

lessons.title: Test Automation, TDD, CI/CD and DevOps
lessons.content:
Think of a rice mill. In the old days, workers checked each sack by hand: weigh it, look for stones, stitch it closed. It was slow and tired workers made mistakes. A modern mill has machines that weigh, clean and pack automatically, and a sensor stops the line the moment a sack is underweight. Humans still decide what good rice is and handle unusual problems, but the repetitive checks run by themselves every minute. Modern software teams work the same way: computers run thousands of tests automatically on every change, and a pipeline builds, tests and delivers the software, so people can focus on thinking.

Why automate tests: Manual testing is slow, expensive and error-prone when repeated. A regression suite of 500 test cases might take a tester a week by hand; automated, it may run in minutes on every change. Automated tests give fast feedback, run the same way every time, document how the code is supposed to behave, and make refactoring and frequent releases safe. Manual testing is still valuable for exploratory testing, usability and checking things that are hard to judge automatically, like whether a screen looks right.

Unit test frameworks: Most languages have a unit testing framework: JUnit for Java, pytest and unittest for Python, Jest for JavaScript, NUnit for C#, and the test package for Dart and Flutter. These frameworks let you write test functions, group them, run them all with one command, and report which passed and which failed. The xUnit family of frameworks traces back to SUnit for Smalltalk, written by Kent Beck, and JUnit, by Kent Beck and Erich Gamma.

Anatomy of an automated test: A common structure is Arrange-Act-Assert. Arrange: set up the objects and data. Act: call the code under test. Assert: check the result. Example in pseudo-code: test "fee for sibling gets 10 percent discount": arrange calculator = FeeCalculator(), student = Student(hasSiblingInSchool = true, baseFee = 2000); act fee = calculator.monthlyFee(student); assert fee == 1800. An assertion is a statement that must be true; if it is false, the test fails with a clear message. Good unit tests are fast, independent of each other, repeatable, self-checking and written close in time to the code (sometimes summarised as FIRST).

Test doubles: Units often depend on things that are slow, unpredictable or not ready: databases, payment gateways, SMS services, the current time. Test doubles replace them during tests. Gerard Meszaros's widely used terms: a dummy is passed around but never used; a stub returns fixed answers (the payment gateway always says "success"); a spy is a stub that also records how it was called; a mock is pre-programmed with expectations and verifies that certain calls happened (for example, that sendSms was called exactly once with the right number); a fake is a working but simplified implementation, like an in-memory database. Dependency injection from the design principles lesson makes it easy to pass doubles in.

Test-driven development: TDD, popularised by Kent Beck as part of XP, reverses the usual order: write a test before writing the code. The cycle is Red, Green, Refactor. Red: write a small test for the next bit of behaviour and watch it fail, which proves the test can detect the missing behaviour. Green: write the simplest code that makes the test pass. Refactor: clean up the code and tests while keeping all tests green. Then repeat with the next small behaviour. Each cycle takes minutes.

TDD worked example: Task: a function isLeapYear(year). Red: test isLeapYear(2024) is true; it fails because the function does not exist. Green: return year % 4 == 0; passes. Red: test isLeapYear(1900) is false; fails. Green: return year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0; passes. Red: test isLeapYear(2000) is true; fails. Green: return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0; all pass. Refactor: give the function a clear comment explaining the Gregorian rule. Four tests now document the exact rule and protect it forever.

Benefits and costs of TDD: TDD forces you to think about requirements and interfaces before implementation, keeps code testable and loosely coupled, gives a growing safety net for refactoring, and produces tests as executable documentation. Its costs are a learning curve and some extra time at first; studies of TDD's effect on defects and productivity show mixed results depending on context. TDD is hardest with code tightly bound to user interfaces or external systems, which is where test doubles and good design help.

BDD briefly: Behaviour-driven development (BDD), introduced by Dan North, extends TDD with language closer to the business. Scenarios are written in a Given-When-Then format, as we saw for acceptance criteria in the requirements lesson, and tools like Cucumber can run them as automated tests. BDD helps developers, testers and business people agree on behaviour using shared examples.

The test pyramid: Mike Cohn's test pyramid suggests how to balance automated tests. At the wide base: many unit tests, which are fast, cheap and precise. In the middle: fewer integration or service tests, which check components working together, such as code talking to a real database or API. At the narrow top: a small number of end-to-end UI tests, which simulate a user clicking through the app; they are valuable but slow, fragile and expensive to maintain. A common anti-pattern is the "ice-cream cone": mostly manual and UI tests, few unit tests, giving slow and unreliable feedback.

Regression automation and flaky tests: Automated regression suites run after every change to catch anything that breaks. A flaky test is one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change, often due to timing, network calls, shared state between tests or dependence on the current date. Flaky tests are dangerous because people start ignoring failures. Teams fix or quarantine them quickly, and design tests to be deterministic, for example by injecting a fixed clock instead of reading the real time.

Non-functional testing tools: Automation also covers qualities. Performance and load testing tools (such as JMeter, Gatling or k6) simulate many users to measure response times and find the breaking point. Security testing includes automated scanners for known vulnerabilities and dependency checks for libraries with known security issues, alongside manual penetration testing. Accessibility checkers flag missing labels and poor colour contrast. UI automation tools such as Selenium, Playwright, Appium or Flutter's integration_test drive real browsers and apps.

Continuous integration: Continuous integration (CI), a core XP practice described in detail by Martin Fowler, means developers merge their work into a shared main branch frequently, at least daily, and every merge is verified by an automated build and test run. A CI server (for example GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Jenkins) watches the repository; on each push or pull request it checks out the code, compiles it, runs static analysis and tests, and reports the result. If the build breaks, fixing it is the team's top priority. CI catches integration problems within minutes, not weeks.

A typical CI pipeline: Stage 1, build: fetch dependencies and compile. Stage 2, static checks: formatter, linter, security scan of dependencies. Stage 3, unit tests with coverage report. Stage 4, integration tests against a test database. Stage 5, package the artifact, such as an APK, a container image or a web bundle. If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and the pull request cannot be merged. Pipelines are usually defined as code in a file in the repository, so they are versioned and reviewed like everything else.

Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment: Continuous delivery extends CI so that every change that passes the pipeline is automatically deployed to a staging environment and is always in a releasable state; releasing to production is a business decision made with one click. Continuous deployment goes one step further: every change that passes all automated stages is released to production automatically, with no human approval. Both depend on strong automated testing, and both are often abbreviated CD, so be careful which one is meant.

Safe release techniques: Teams that deploy often reduce risk with techniques such as feature flags (code is deployed but the feature is switched on only for some users), canary releases (a new version goes first to a small percentage of users while metrics are watched), blue-green deployment (two identical environments, switching traffic from the old to the new and back if needed), and automatic rollback when error rates rise. Mobile apps also use staged rollouts through app stores.

DevOps: DevOps is a culture and set of practices that brings development and operations together, breaking down the wall between those who write software and those who run it. The term grew popular around 2009, associated with Patrick Debois and the first DevOpsDays conference. Key ideas: shared responsibility for the running system ("you build it, you run it"), automation of builds, tests, infrastructure and deployments, infrastructure as code (servers and networks defined in versioned files), continuous monitoring and logging, and fast feedback from production back to development.

Measuring DevOps performance: The DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) programme popularised four key metrics: deployment frequency (how often you release), lead time for changes (from commit to production), change failure rate (what percentage of releases cause a problem) and time to restore service after a failure. High-performing teams deploy frequently with short lead times and still keep failure rates low, showing that speed and stability can improve together when automation and testing are strong.

Real life example 1, a ride-sharing backend: A ride-sharing company's backend team merges dozens of pull requests a day. Each one runs a pipeline of about 3,000 unit tests in a few minutes, plus integration tests against a test database. Merged changes go automatically to staging; a canary release then sends the new version to 5 percent of production traffic while dashboards watch error rates and trip completion. If errors rise, the system rolls back automatically. Engineers release several times a day without overnight "release parties".

Real life example 2, a university student project with CI: A team building a Flutter app for their final project sets up GitHub Actions: on every pull request, run dart format check, flutter analyze and flutter test. They write the fee and timetable logic with TDD. Two weeks before the demo, a teammate's change breaks timetable generation; the pipeline turns red within minutes and shows the failing test, so the bug is fixed the same day instead of being discovered on stage in front of the examiners.

Common mistakes: Automating everything through the UI and ending up with a slow, flaky ice-cream cone. Writing tests with no assertions. Over-mocking until tests only check that mocks were called, not real behaviour. Ignoring a red build. Confusing continuous delivery with continuous deployment. Thinking DevOps is just a job title or a tool; it is mainly culture plus automation. Skipping the refactor step in TDD.

What exams ask: Why is test automation important? Explain the Arrange-Act-Assert structure. Define stubs, mocks and fakes. Explain TDD and its Red-Green-Refactor cycle with an example. Draw and explain the test pyramid. What is continuous integration and what does a CI pipeline contain? Differentiate continuous delivery and continuous deployment. What is DevOps and what are its key practices and metrics?

Recap: Automated tests give fast, repeatable feedback; frameworks like JUnit and pytest structure them, and test doubles isolate units. TDD writes tests first in a Red-Green-Refactor cycle; BDD writes behaviour as Given-When-Then. The test pyramid favours many unit tests, fewer integration tests and few UI tests. Continuous integration builds and tests every change; continuous delivery keeps software always releasable; continuous deployment releases automatically. DevOps unites development and operations through culture, automation and monitoring. Next lesson: software project management and scheduling.

Arrange-Act-Assert structures a test; good unit tests are fast, independent, repeatable and self-checking.
Test doubles: dummy, stub (fixed answers), spy, mock (verifies calls), fake (simplified working version).
TDD cycle: Red (failing test), Green (simplest passing code), Refactor (clean up with tests green).
Test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end UI tests.
Continuous integration merges often and runs an automated build and tests on every change.
Continuous delivery keeps every change releasable; continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically.
DevOps joins development and operations through shared responsibility, automation, infrastructure as code and monitoring.

lessons.title: Software Project Management and Scheduling
lessons.content:
Think about organising a big family wedding in Dhaka. There is a budget, a fixed date, many people with different jobs (decoration, catering, invitations, photography), and tasks that depend on each other: you cannot print cards before the venue is booked, and the caterer needs the final guest count. Somebody has to plan who does what and when, notice when things slip, and decide what to do about it. Software projects are the same, only less visible, because half-finished software looks like nothing at all. Software project management is the discipline of planning, organising, tracking and steering that work so the product arrives on time, within budget and with the agreed quality.

Why software projects are hard to manage: Software is intangible, so progress is hard to see; "90 percent done" can stay 90 percent done for months. Requirements change. Each project is somewhat unique, so past experience transfers imperfectly. Productivity varies greatly between people. And the work is highly interconnected: a change in one module ripples into others. Surveys over many years, such as the Standish Group's CHAOS reports, have repeatedly found that a large share of software projects are late, over budget or delivered with fewer features than planned. Good management does not remove these problems but makes them visible early.

The four Ps: Roger Pressman describes the management spectrum as four Ps. People: the most important factor; recruiting, training, motivating and organising the team. Product: the scope of what is to be built, understood well enough to estimate. Process: the framework of activities chosen for the project, such as Scrum or an incremental model. Project: the planning, monitoring and control that make it all happen. A project with strong people and a clear product can survive an imperfect process; the reverse is rarely true.

The project triangle: Every project balances scope (what is delivered), time (schedule) and cost (people and money), with quality often placed in the middle. If one changes, at least one other must change too. If the client adds features but keeps the deadline, either more cost, lower quality or reduced scope elsewhere must follow. Agile teams usually fix time and cost (fixed-length sprints, stable team) and let scope flex, which is why the product backlog is prioritised.

The project manager's activities: Classic textbooks list: project planning (scope, estimates, schedule, resources), risk management (next lessons), team building and people management, tracking and control (comparing actual progress with the plan), reporting to stakeholders, and closing the project with a review of lessons learned. In Scrum, these duties are shared: the Product Owner manages scope and priorities, the Scrum Master removes impediments, and the self-managing team plans its own work, so there may be no single "project manager" role.

The project plan: A project plan, sometimes called a software project management plan (SPMP), typically includes: an introduction with objectives and constraints, the project organisation and roles, the chosen process model, the work breakdown, estimates of effort and cost, the schedule with milestones, resource allocation, risk management plan, quality assurance and configuration management plans, and how progress will be monitored and reported. It is a living document, revised as the project learns more.

Work breakdown structure: A work breakdown structure (WBS) decomposes the whole project into smaller, manageable pieces, level by level, until each bottom-level item, called a work package, is small enough to estimate, assign to one person or team, and track, often between about one day and two weeks of effort. Example WBS for a hospital appointment app: 1 Requirements (1.1 interviews, 1.2 SRS); 2 Design (2.1 UI design, 2.2 database design, 2.3 architecture); 3 Implementation (3.1 patient app, 3.2 doctor dashboard, 3.3 backend API); 4 Testing (4.1 integration, 4.2 user acceptance); 5 Deployment and training. The WBS ensures nothing is forgotten; the 100 percent rule says the children of each item must cover all of its work.

Milestones and deliverables: A milestone is a significant point in the schedule with zero duration, such as "SRS approved" or "beta released", used to check progress. A deliverable is a product handed to the customer, such as the SRS document, a working build or a user manual. Milestones should be concrete and verifiable: "design 80 percent complete" is a bad milestone because nobody can check it; "design review passed" is good.

Gantt charts: A Gantt chart, named after Henry Gantt who popularised it in the 1910s, shows tasks as horizontal bars on a timeline. Each bar's start and length show when the task runs; arrows can show dependencies, and diamonds mark milestones. Gantt charts are easy for stakeholders to read and are good for tracking progress (bars can be shaded as work completes). Their weakness is that dependencies and the critical path are not always obvious, which is why they are combined with activity networks.

Activity networks: An activity network shows tasks and their dependencies as a graph. In the activity-on-node (AON) form, each node is a task with its duration and edges show "must finish before". Common dependency types are finish-to-start (the most common: B starts after A finishes), start-to-start, finish-to-finish and, rarely, start-to-finish. Before building the network, list each task, its duration estimate and its predecessors.

The critical path method: The critical path method (CPM), developed in the late 1950s, finds the longest path through the activity network. Its length is the minimum possible project duration, and tasks on it are critical: any delay to them delays the whole project. A forward pass computes the earliest start (ES) and earliest finish (EF = ES + duration) of every task; a backward pass computes the latest finish (LF) and latest start (LS = LF - duration) that would not delay the project. Slack, also called float, is LS - ES; critical tasks have zero slack.

CPM worked example, part 1: A small app project has six tasks. A: requirements, 3 days, no predecessor. B: UI design, 4 days, after A. C: database design, 5 days, after A. D: backend coding, 6 days, after C. E: frontend coding, 5 days, after B. F: integration testing, 3 days, after both D and E. Forward pass: A runs 0 to 3. B runs 3 to 7. C runs 3 to 8. D runs 8 to 14. E runs 7 to 12. F can start only when both D and E finish, so at max(14, 12) = 14, finishing at 17. The project takes at least 17 days.

CPM worked example, part 2: Backward pass from the end at 17: F has LF 17 and LS 14. D has LF 14 and LS 8. E has LF 14 and LS 9. C has LF 8 (D's LS) and LS 3. B has LF 9 (E's LS) and LS 5. A has LF equal to the smaller of B's LS and C's LS, min(5, 3) = 3, and LS 0. Slack: A 0, B 5 - 3 = 2, C 0, D 0, E 9 - 7 = 2, F 0. The critical path is A, C, D, F with length 3 + 5 + 6 + 3 = 17 days; the other path A, B, E, F is 15 days. So the database and backend work deserve the strongest people and closest tracking, while UI design and frontend can slip by up to 2 days without harm.

PERT: The Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT), developed in the late 1950s for the US Navy's Polaris programme, handles uncertainty by asking for three estimates per task: optimistic (o), most likely (m) and pessimistic (p). The expected time is te = (o + 4m + p) / 6, and the variance is ((p - o) / 6) squared. Example: o = 4, m = 6, p = 14 days gives te = (4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 42 / 6 = 7 days, and standard deviation (14 - 4) / 6 which is about 1.67 days. Summing expected times and variances along the critical path gives an estimate of the project duration and the probability of meeting a deadline.

Brooks's law: In The Mythical Man-Month (1975), Fred Brooks, who managed IBM's OS/360 project, wrote: "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." New people need time to learn the system, existing members must spend time training them, and communication overhead grows quickly: with n people there are n(n - 1) / 2 possible communication channels, so 5 people have 10 channels and 10 people have 45. He also pointed out that people and months are not interchangeable: nine women cannot make a baby in one month. Brooks's law is a strong warning, not an absolute rule; adding people early, or for well-separated tasks, can help.

Team structures: Classic structures include the democratic or egoless team, where decisions are shared and everyone reviews each other's work, good for hard problems; the chief programmer team, proposed by Harlan Mills and promoted by Brooks as the "surgical team", where a senior programmer does the key design and coding supported by specialists; and the hierarchical or controlled-decentralised team with a leader and sub-groups, common in large projects. Modern agile teams are small (Scrum suggests 10 or fewer), cross-functional and self-managing, and large organisations coordinate many such teams.

Tracking and control: Once the project runs, managers compare actual progress with the plan using tools such as burndown charts in Scrum, updated Gantt charts, milestone reviews and status meetings. Earned value analysis (EVA) is a more formal technique that compares planned value (budgeted cost of work scheduled), earned value (budgeted cost of work actually performed) and actual cost. Schedule performance index SPI = EV / PV and cost performance index CPI = EV / AC; values below 1 mean behind schedule or over budget. When slippage appears, options include reducing scope, adding time, adding people early, or improving the process, but rarely all at once.

Real life example 1, a mobile banking feature: A bank plans a new "pay utility bill" feature for its app for the start of the fiscal year in July. The PM builds a WBS with 40 work packages, an activity network and a Gantt chart. CPM shows the critical path runs through the integration with the electricity board's API. When that API team is delayed by a week, the PM sees immediately that the launch is at risk, while delays in the help-screen design do not matter because that task has 10 days of slack. They negotiate an early test environment from the electricity board instead of adding more developers to the app team.

Real life example 2, a final year project: Four students plan their project over a 14-week semester. They build a simple WBS, draw an activity network and find the critical path runs through dataset collection, model training and the report. They start dataset collection in week 1 instead of week 4, keep a shared Gantt chart, and hold a 15-minute meeting every Friday. In week 9 one member falls ill; instead of panicking, they move non-critical UI polish to later and keep the critical tasks moving, finishing on time.

Common mistakes: Planning once and never updating the plan. Milestones that cannot be verified. Ignoring dependencies, so people wait for each other. Not identifying the critical path, so attention goes to the wrong tasks. Assuming people and months are interchangeable. Adding many people late in a project. Reporting optimistic percentages instead of finished, verified work.

What exams ask: Explain the 4 Ps of project management. What does a project plan contain? Construct a WBS for a given project. Draw a Gantt chart and an activity network. Given tasks, durations and dependencies, compute ES, EF, LS, LF and slack, and identify the critical path. Compute PERT expected time and variance. State and explain Brooks's law. Compare team structures. Explain earned value analysis.

Recap: Software project management plans, organises, tracks and steers work across people, product, process and project. Scope, time and cost trade off against each other. A WBS breaks work into packages; milestones mark verifiable progress; Gantt charts show schedules; activity networks show dependencies; CPM finds the critical path and slack; PERT handles uncertainty with (o + 4m + p) / 6. Brooks's law warns that adding people late makes things later. Tracking with burndown charts and earned value keeps the plan honest. Next lesson: software estimation with LOC, function points and COCOMO.
key_points: Pressman's 4 Ps of project management: People, Product, Process, Project.
Scope, time and cost trade off; changing one forces a change in another.
A WBS decomposes the project into small, assignable work packages; the 100 percent rule covers all work.
Milestones are verifiable zero-duration checkpoints; Gantt charts show tasks as bars on a timeline.
CPM finds the longest path; critical tasks have zero slack (slack = LS - ES).
PERT expected time = (o + 4m + p) / 6, variance = ((p - o) / 6) squared.
Brooks's law: adding people to a late project makes it later; channels grow as n(n - 1) / 2.
Earned value: SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC; below 1 means behind schedule or over budget.
lessons.tip: In CPM questions, draw a small table with columns Task, Duration, ES, EF, LS, LF, Slack. Fill ES and EF top to bottom, then LS and LF bottom to top. The critical path is simply the tasks with zero slack.
