lessons.title: Software Estimation: LOC, Function Points and COCOMO
lessons.content:
Suppose you ask a contractor in Chattogram how much it will cost to build a three-storey house. A good contractor does not guess wildly. They ask the floor area, the number of rooms, the quality of fittings, and then use past experience: so many Taka per square foot, so many workers for so many months. Software estimation tries to do the same: predict how much effort, time and money a project will need before it is built. It is harder than for a house, because software size is invisible and requirements are fuzzy at the start, but there are proven methods that turn guesswork into reasoned numbers.

What is estimated: Estimation usually predicts four things. Size: how big the software is, measured in lines of code or function points. Effort: how much human work it needs, usually in person-months (one person working for one month) or person-hours. Duration: calendar time from start to finish. Cost: mostly effort multiplied by the cost of a person-month, plus hardware, licences and other expenses. The usual chain is size first, then effort from size, then duration and team size from effort, then cost.

The cone of uncertainty: Early estimates are very uncertain. Barry Boehm observed, and Steve McConnell later popularised as the "cone of uncertainty", that at the initial concept stage an estimate can be off by a factor of about four in either direction (from 0.25 to 4 times the real value), narrowing as requirements, design and code become concrete. The lesson: give early estimates as ranges, not single numbers, and re-estimate at each milestone. A single precise number on day one is false confidence.

Why estimates go wrong: Common causes include unclear or changing requirements, optimism (people estimate the happy path and forget testing, integration, meetings and rework), pressure from managers or clients to give a low number, ignoring past data, and confusing an estimate (a prediction) with a target (what the business wants) or a commitment (a promise). An honest estimate says: "with what we know today, this will probably take 4 to 6 months".

Lines of code: The simplest size measure is lines of code (LOC), often given in thousands, KLOC. It is easy to count once the code exists and is used in models like COCOMO. Its weaknesses: it depends on the programming language (the same feature may be 50 lines of Python or 200 lines of C), on coding style, and on what counts as a line (comments, blank lines); it cannot be measured directly before coding, so it must itself be estimated; and it rewards verbose code. LOC-based productivity comparisons across languages are therefore misleading.

Function points: Allan Albrecht at IBM introduced function point analysis (FPA) in 1979 to measure size from the user's point of view, independent of language. Function points count the functionality delivered, based on five component types. External inputs (EI): data or control entering the system from outside, such as an add-student form. External outputs (EO): data leaving the system with some processing, such as a report or a calculated result sheet. External inquiries (EQ): simple input-output retrievals without derived data, such as searching a student by ID. Internal logical files (ILF): groups of data maintained inside the system, such as the students table. External interface files (EIF): data referenced by the system but maintained by another system, such as the bank's exchange rate feed.

Function point weights: Each component is rated simple, average or complex, and given a weight. The standard weights (simple, average, complex) are: EI 3, 4, 6; EO 4, 5, 7; EQ 3, 4, 6; ILF 7, 10, 15; EIF 5, 7, 10. Multiplying each count by its weight and summing gives the unadjusted function points (UFP). Notice that files carry the heaviest weights, because maintaining data is a large part of a system's work.

The value adjustment factor: Fourteen general system characteristics, such as data communications, performance, heavy configuration, online data entry, complex processing, reusability, installation ease, multiple sites and facilitating change, are each rated from 0 (no influence) to 5 (essential). Their sum, called total degree of influence, ranges from 0 to 70. The value adjustment factor is VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 times the sum, so it ranges from 0.65 to 1.35. Finally, FP = UFP times VAF.

Function point worked example: A small library system has 3 external inputs of average complexity (add book, add member, issue book), 2 average outputs (overdue report, fine receipt), 2 simple inquiries (search book, check member), 2 average internal files (books, members) and 1 simple external interface file (the university's student database). UFP = 3 x 4 + 2 x 5 + 2 x 3 + 2 x 10 + 1 x 5 = 12 + 10 + 6 + 20 + 5 = 53. Suppose the 14 characteristics sum to 42. Then VAF = 0.65 + 0.42 = 1.07, and FP = 53 x 1.07 = 56.71, about 57 function points. If the team's history shows about 8 function points per person-month, the effort is around 7 person-months.

Using function points: Function points can be counted from requirements, before code exists, and are language-independent, so they suit early estimation and productivity comparisons. Counting rules are standardised by the International Function Point Users Group (IFPUG), and other methods such as COSMIC exist. Weaknesses: counting needs training and some judgement, the 14 factors are subjective, and it fits data-centric business systems better than algorithm-heavy or embedded software. Function points can be converted into approximate LOC using language-specific tables when a model needs KLOC.

COCOMO: The Constructive Cost Model (COCOMO) was published by Barry Boehm in 1981 in his book Software Engineering Economics, based on data from 63 projects. It estimates effort and duration from size in KLOC. Basic COCOMO uses E = a x (KLOC) to the power b, in person-months, and D = c x E to the power d, in months. Average team size is E divided by D. The constants depend on the project type.

The three project modes: Organic projects are relatively small, with an experienced team, familiar environment and flexible requirements, such as a payroll system for a company that has built similar ones: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38. Semi-detached projects are medium-sized with a mixed team and some unfamiliar parts, such as a new database management system: a = 3.0, b = 1.12, c = 2.5, d = 0.35. Embedded projects are under tight hardware, software and operational constraints, such as flight control or a real-time banking switch: a = 3.6, b = 1.20, c = 2.5, d = 0.32. Note that b is greater than 1: effort grows faster than size, a diseconomy of scale caused by communication and integration overhead.

COCOMO worked example: Estimate a 32 KLOC organic project. Effort E = 2.4 x 32 to the power 1.05. Thirty-two to the power 1.05 is about 38.05, so E is about 91.3 person-months. Duration D = 2.5 x 91.3 to the power 0.38, which is about 2.5 x 5.56, about 13.9 months. Average staff = 91.3 / 13.9, about 6.6, so roughly 7 people. For comparison, the same 32 KLOC as an embedded project gives E = 3.6 x 32 to the power 1.2, about 230 person-months, with duration about 14.3 months and roughly 16 people. Same size, more than double the effort, because of the constraints.

Intermediate and detailed COCOMO: Basic COCOMO ignores many factors. Intermediate COCOMO multiplies the nominal effort by an effort adjustment factor (EAF), the product of 15 cost drivers grouped into product attributes (such as required reliability and complexity), hardware attributes (such as memory constraints), personnel attributes (such as analyst capability and language experience) and project attributes (such as use of modern tools and schedule constraints). Each driver is rated from very low to extra high with a multiplier, for example high required reliability raises effort, while highly capable analysts reduce it. Detailed COCOMO applies the drivers phase by phase.

COCOMO II: Boehm and colleagues released COCOMO II around 2000 for modern practices like reuse, object-oriented and iterative development. It has sub-models for different stages: an early prototyping stage using object points (or application points), an early design model and a post-architecture model. The exponent is computed from five scale factors (such as precedentedness, development flexibility, architecture and risk resolution, team cohesion and process maturity), and size can be KLOC or function points converted to code. For exams, basic COCOMO calculations are most common, with COCOMO II explained briefly.

Other estimation techniques: Expert judgment asks experienced people; it is fast and often reasonably accurate but can be biased. The Wideband Delphi method, developed from the RAND Corporation's Delphi technique, has several experts estimate independently, discuss the differences anonymously or in a meeting, and re-estimate until estimates converge. Estimation by analogy compares with similar past projects. Top-down estimation estimates the whole and splits it; bottom-up estimates each WBS work package and adds them up, which is detailed but can miss integration work. Using two different methods and comparing results is a good check.

Agile estimation: Agile teams often estimate in story points, a relative measure of size and complexity, rather than hours. In planning poker, popularised by Mike Cohn, each team member holds cards with numbers like 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 (a Fibonacci-like sequence that reflects growing uncertainty for larger items). For each story, everyone reveals a card at once; the highest and lowest explain their reasoning, and the team re-votes until it converges. Velocity, the story points completed per sprint, then forecasts how many sprints the backlog needs. T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL) are used for rough early sizing.

Real life example 1, a government tender: A software firm bids for a land records system for a district office. From the requirements they count about 600 function points. Their historical productivity on similar government projects is about 10 function points per person-month, giving 60 person-months. As a cross-check they convert to approximately 32 KLOC and run COCOMO as semi-detached, getting about 145 person-months: a big difference. Investigating, they realise their historical data came from smaller projects with less integration. They settle on a range of 90 to 140 person-months, price with a risk buffer, and state assumptions clearly in the proposal.

Real life example 2, a startup's sprint planning: A Dhaka startup building a grocery delivery app uses planning poker. The story "pay with mobile wallet" gets votes of 3, 5, 5 and 13. The developer who voted 13 explains that the wallet provider's sandbox is unreliable and needs retry logic and reconciliation. After discussion, the team re-votes 8. Their velocity is about 30 points per sprint, so with 180 points in the release backlog they forecast about six two-week sprints, and they update the forecast after every sprint as velocity becomes clearer.

Common mistakes: Giving a single number instead of a range. Estimating only coding and forgetting testing, reviews, deployment and meetings. Using LOC to compare productivity across languages. Mixing up FP components, for example counting a report as an inquiry when it contains calculated data. Using the wrong COCOMO mode or forgetting that E is in person-months and D in months. Treating story points as hours or comparing velocity between teams.

What exams ask: Why is software estimation difficult? Explain the cone of uncertainty. Compare LOC and function points. Compute function points for given counts, weights and characteristics. Explain the three COCOMO modes and compute effort, duration and staff for a given KLOC. Describe intermediate COCOMO's cost drivers and COCOMO II. Explain Delphi, planning poker and story points.

Recap: Estimation predicts size, effort, duration and cost, and early estimates should be ranges because of the cone of uncertainty. LOC is simple but language-dependent; function points measure user functionality with five components, weights and a VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 times the sum of 14 factors. Basic COCOMO computes E = a x KLOC to the power b and D = c x E to the power d for organic, semi-detached and embedded modes; intermediate COCOMO adds 15 cost drivers and COCOMO II modernises the model. Expert judgment, Delphi, analogy and planning poker complement the models. Next lesson: risk management and software quality.
key_points: Estimation predicts size, effort (person-months), duration and cost, usually in that order.
The cone of uncertainty: early estimates can be off by about 4 times either way, so give ranges.
LOC is easy to count but depends on language and style and is unknown before coding.
Function points count EI, EO, EQ, ILF and EIF with weights; FP = UFP x (0.65 + 0.01 x sum of 14 factors).
Basic COCOMO: E = a x KLOC^b person-months, D = c x E^d months; staff = E / D.
Intermediate COCOMO multiplies by 15 cost drivers; COCOMO II uses scale factors and stage-specific sub-models.
Expert judgment, Wideband Delphi, analogy and planning poker with story points complement the models.
lessons.tip: In COCOMO calculations, write the formula first with the right constants for the mode, then compute step by step with a calculator's power key. Most lost marks come from using organic constants for an embedded project.
lessons.task: List the features of a simple online exam system (create exam, take exam, view result, search students, etc.), classify each as EI, EO, EQ, ILF or EIF with a complexity, compute UFP, assume a total degree of influence of 35, and compute the final function points.

quiz.q: In basic COCOMO, what is the value of 'a' for an organic project?
quiz.explain: Organic uses a = 2.4 and b = 1.05.

quiz.q: If the sum of the 14 general system characteristics is 30, what is the VAF?
Which function point component represents data maintained inside the system?
quiz.explain: An ILF is a logical group of data the system itself maintains.

quiz.q: Why is the exponent b greater than 1 in COCOMO?
options: Because code is written in KLOC
Because effort grows faster than size due to communication and integration overhead
Because larger projects use better tools
quiz.explain: This diseconomy of scale makes big projects disproportionately expensive.

quiz.q: What does the cone of uncertainty tell us?
options: Estimates are most accurate at the start
Early estimates are very uncertain and narrow as the project progresses
quiz.explain: Give ranges early and re-estimate at milestones.

lessons.title: Risk Management and Software Quality
lessons.content:
Before the monsoon, a careful farmer in Sylhet thinks ahead: what if the river floods, what if the seed is bad, what if fertiliser prices jump? She cannot stop the rain, but she can raise the seedbed, keep spare seed, and buy fertiliser early. She also judges quality at every stage, from seed to harvest, rather than only looking at the rice on the last day. Software teams need both habits: risk management, which deals with what might go wrong before it happens, and quality management, which builds and checks quality throughout the process instead of hoping to inspect it in at the end.

What a risk is: A risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it happens, has a negative effect on the project. Two things characterise every risk: uncertainty (it may or may not happen) and loss (if it happens, something bad follows). A problem is a risk that has already happened. Reactive teams wait for problems and fight fires; proactive teams identify risks early and prepare. Barry Boehm, who also created the spiral model, made risk management central to software projects in the late 1980s.

Types of risks: Project risks threaten the schedule and budget: a key developer leaves, a vendor delivers late, estimates are too optimistic. Technical risks threaten quality and feasibility: a new framework is immature, performance targets cannot be met, integration with a legacy system is harder than expected. Business risks threaten the product's success even if it is built well: no market for the product, a competitor launches first, management loses interest, budget is cut. Risks can also be known (identified), predictable (expected from past experience) or unpredictable.

The risk management process: Most textbooks describe a cycle. Risk identification: list what could go wrong, using checklists, brainstorming, past project records and assumptions analysis. Risk analysis: estimate each risk's probability and impact. Risk prioritisation: rank risks so the most serious get attention. Risk planning: decide responses. Risk monitoring: watch risk indicators and reassess regularly, because new risks appear and old ones change. Boehm grouped these into risk assessment (identification, analysis, prioritisation) and risk control (planning, resolution, monitoring).

Risk exposure: To compare risks, compute risk exposure RE = P x C, where P is the probability of the risk occurring and C is the cost or impact if it does. Example: there is a 40 percent chance that the payment gateway integration will take three extra weeks, costing 600,000 Taka in team time; RE = 0.4 x 600,000 = 240,000 Taka. Another risk: a 10 percent chance that the cloud provider raises prices, costing 300,000 Taka; RE = 30,000 Taka. The first deserves far more attention. Many teams use simple scales instead: probability and impact each rated low, medium or high, shown in a probability-impact matrix with red, amber and green cells.

The risk table: Pressman suggests a risk table with columns for the risk, its category, probability, impact and a pointer to its management plan. Risks are sorted by probability and impact, and a cut-off line is drawn: risks above the line are actively managed, those below are recorded and watched. Ten well-managed risks are better than a hundred listed and ignored.

Risk response strategies: Avoidance: change the plan so the risk cannot happen, for example using a proven framework instead of a brand-new one. Mitigation (reduction): lower the probability or impact, for example pairing developers so knowledge is shared if someone leaves. Transfer: move the impact to another party, such as insurance or a fixed-price contract with a vendor. Acceptance: consciously accept the risk, often with a contingency reserve of time or money. Choosing a strategy depends on the cost of the response compared with the risk exposure.

RMMM: Pressman's RMMM stands for risk mitigation, monitoring and management. For each important risk, the RMMM plan records how to mitigate it in advance, what indicators to monitor, and what contingency actions to take if it actually happens. Example, risk "high staff turnover": mitigation: document designs, cross-train, use pair programming, reward people fairly; monitoring: watch team morale, overtime and job-market conditions; management: if someone leaves, reassign work using the documentation and prioritise the backlog.

What software quality means: Quality has several views: conformance to requirements (does it meet the specification?), fitness for use (does it satisfy users in practice?) and the absence of defects, but also internal qualities like maintainability that users never see directly. A product can meet its specification and still fail users if the specification was wrong. Quality models break the vague word "quality" into measurable characteristics.

McCall's quality model: Jim McCall and colleagues proposed one of the first quality models in 1977, with 11 quality factors in three groups. Product operation (how it behaves when used): correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity and usability. Product revision (how easy it is to change): maintainability, flexibility and testability. Product transition (how easily it adapts to new environments): portability, reusability and interoperability. Each factor is linked to measurable criteria. Boehm's 1978 model is a similar hierarchical model.

ISO 9126 and ISO/IEC 25010: ISO 9126 (1991, later revised) defined six quality characteristics: functionality, reliability, usability, efficiency, maintainability and portability, each with sub-characteristics. It was replaced by ISO/IEC 25010 (2011), part of the SQuaRE series, whose product quality model has eight characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability. Security and compatibility became top-level characteristics. ISO/IEC 25010 also defines a quality-in-use model covering effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, freedom from risk and context coverage.

Quality metrics: Some common measures: defect density, the number of defects per KLOC or per function point; defect removal efficiency (DRE), defects found before release divided by total defects (before plus after release); mean time between failures (MTBF), and availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), where MTTR is mean time to repair; customer-reported problems per month; and code metrics such as cyclomatic complexity and coverage from earlier lessons. Example: 90 defects found in testing and 10 reported by users after release give DRE = 90 / 100 = 0.9, or 90 percent.

Software quality assurance: Quality control (QC) checks products to find defects, for example testing and inspections. Quality assurance (QA) is broader: it ensures the process used is likely to produce quality, through standards, procedures, audits and training. An SQA group or function typically prepares the SQA plan, reviews activities against the defined process, audits work products, ensures deviations are documented and fixed, and reports to management. In agile teams, much of this is built into the team's practices: definition of done, code review, CI and retrospectives.

Reviews and inspections: Reviews find defects before testing, often more cheaply. Informal reviews and walkthroughs, where the author leads colleagues through the document or code, are light. Formal technical reviews and inspections are structured. Michael Fagan introduced software inspections at IBM in 1976: defined roles (moderator, author, reader, recorder, inspectors), preparation with checklists, an inspection meeting that finds but does not fix defects, then rework and follow-up. Reviews work on requirements and designs too, where catching an error is cheapest. Modern pull-request code review is a lighter descendant.

CMMI: The Capability Maturity Model (CMM) was developed at the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon University, led by Watts Humphrey, and later evolved into Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI). Its staged representation has five maturity levels. Level 1, Initial: processes are unpredictable and success depends on heroes. Level 2, Managed: projects are planned, tracked and controlled. Level 3, Defined: the organisation has standard processes tailored for each project. Level 4, Quantitatively Managed: processes are measured and controlled using statistics. Level 5, Optimizing: continuous process improvement based on data. Many outsourcing firms seek CMMI appraisal to win international contracts.

ISO 9001 and Six Sigma: ISO 9001 is a general quality management system standard for any organisation, not only software; certification shows the organisation has documented processes and follows them, with management responsibility, customer focus and continual improvement. ISO/IEC 90003 gives guidance for applying ISO 9001 to software. Six Sigma, which grew out of Motorola in the 1980s, aims to reduce variation and defects to at most 3.4 defects per million opportunities, using the DMAIC cycle: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control. Software organisations use Six Sigma ideas mainly for improving processes with data.

Cost of quality: The cost of quality includes prevention costs (training, planning, standards), appraisal costs (reviews, testing), internal failure costs (fixing defects before release) and external failure costs (fixing defects after release, support calls, lost customers, reputation). Investing in prevention and early appraisal usually reduces the expensive failure costs; this is the business case for reviews, testing and process improvement.

Real life example 1, a hospital management system: A team building a hospital system for a private medical college in Rajshahi lists its top risks: the lab equipment vendor's interface is undocumented (technical), the only developer who knows the old billing system may leave (project), and hospital staff may resist the new system (business). For the vendor risk, they build a prototype integration in the first sprint; for staff turnover, they pair a second developer on billing; for resistance, they involve senior nurses in design and plan training. They review the risk list every sprint, and two months later a new risk appears: a government regulation on patient data, which they add and plan for.

Real life example 2, an outsourcing company's quality journey: A software company in Dhaka wants European clients who require evidence of process quality. Initially, each project works differently and success depends on a few heroes, typical of maturity level 1. Over two years they introduce project planning and tracking, configuration management and QA audits (level 2), then organisation-wide standard processes, inspections and training (level 3). Defect density in delivered code falls, DRE rises from about 75 to above 90 percent, and the CMMI appraisal helps them win contracts.

Common mistakes: Listing risks once at the start and never revisiting them. Writing vague risks like "technical problems" instead of specific ones with causes. Confusing a risk with a problem. Treating QA as only testing at the end. Thinking a CMMI level or ISO certificate guarantees good software rather than good processes. Measuring defect density without consistent definitions of defects and size.

What exams ask: Define risk and classify software risks. Explain the risk management process and RMMM. Compute risk exposure and build a risk table. Explain McCall's quality factors and the ISO 9126 or ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics. Differentiate QA and QC. Describe formal technical reviews and inspections. Explain the five CMMI maturity levels. Compare ISO 9001 and CMMI. Compute DRE or availability.

Recap: Risk management identifies, analyses, prioritises, plans for and monitors risks; risk exposure is probability times impact; responses are avoidance, mitigation, transfer and acceptance, documented in an RMMM plan. Quality is captured by models like McCall's 11 factors, ISO 9126's six characteristics and ISO/IEC 25010's eight. Metrics such as defect density and DRE make quality measurable; SQA, reviews and inspections build it into the process; CMMI, ISO 9001 and Six Sigma guide organisation-wide improvement. Next lesson: software maintenance, configuration management and evolution.
key_points: A risk is uncertain and causes loss if it happens; a problem is a risk that has occurred.
Risk types: project, technical and business; the process is identify, analyse, prioritise, plan, monitor.
Risk exposure RE = probability x impact; responses are avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept.
RMMM: risk mitigation, monitoring and management plan for each important risk.
McCall (1977): 11 factors in product operation, product revision and product transition.
ISO 9126 has 6 characteristics; ISO/IEC 25010 (2011) has 8, adding security and compatibility.
DRE = defects found before release / total defects; availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
CMMI levels: Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing; Six Sigma targets 3.4 defects per million opportunities.
lessons.tip: For the CMMI levels, remember the phrase 'I Must Do Quality Over' for Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing.
lessons.task: For your next group assignment or final year project, write a risk table with at least six specific risks. Give each a probability (percent), an impact (in hours or Taka), compute the risk exposure, sort them, and write one mitigation and one monitoring action for the top three.

quiz.q: A risk has a 25 percent probability and an impact of 400,000 Taka. What is its risk exposure?
Which CMMI level is characterised by organisation-wide standard processes tailored for each project?
quiz.explain: Defined means the organisation has standard processes that projects tailor.

quiz.q: Which group of McCall's model contains maintainability, flexibility and testability?
quiz.explain: Product revision is about how easy the software is to change.

quiz.q: 90 defects were found before release and 10 after. What is the defect removal efficiency?
Pairing developers so knowledge is shared in case someone leaves is an example of which risk strategy?
quiz.explain: It reduces the impact of the staff-turnover risk.

lessons.title: Software Maintenance, Configuration Management and Evolution
lessons.content:
A Dhaka city bus might run for twenty years. Over that time it gets new tyres, a repaired engine, new seats, a fresh coat of paint, an upgraded engine to meet new emission rules, and countless small fixes. The day it left the factory was only the beginning of its life. Software is the same, only more so: the day of release is the start of a long life of fixes, changes, upgrades and growth. This final lesson covers software maintenance, the configuration management that keeps all those changes under control, and how software evolves over years. Then we will recap the whole course.

What maintenance is: The IEEE defines software maintenance as modifying a software product after delivery to correct faults, improve performance or other attributes, or adapt it to a changed environment. Unlike a bus, software does not wear out physically; its "ageing" comes from a changing world: new laws, new operating systems, new user expectations, growing data, and accumulated quick fixes. Maintenance is usually the longest and most expensive phase of a software system's life. Many studies and textbooks estimate that it accounts for well over half of total lifecycle cost, though exact figures vary widely between studies.

The four types of maintenance: Corrective maintenance fixes defects found after release, such as a bug that calculates late fines wrongly. Adaptive maintenance adapts the software to a changed environment, such as a new Android version, a new database server, or a new VAT rate set in the national budget. Perfective maintenance improves or adds functionality and performance in response to user requests, such as adding a dark mode or making reports faster. Preventive maintenance improves the software's future maintainability without changing its behaviour, such as refactoring, updating documentation or removing dead code. Classic studies by Lientz and Swanson around 1980 found that most maintenance effort was not bug fixing but enhancements requested by users.

Why maintenance is hard: Maintainers often did not write the original code, and the original developers may have left. Documentation is missing or out of date. The code has been patched repeatedly under deadline pressure, so its structure has decayed. Changing one part can break another in unexpected ways (ripple effects). Testing is difficult if there is no automated test suite. And maintenance work is often seen as less glamorous than new development, so it may attract less experienced staff. This is why the design principles, testing and documentation from earlier lessons pay off most during maintenance.

The maintenance process: A typical process: a change request or bug report arrives; it is analysed for impact (which components, how much effort, what risk); it is approved or rejected and prioritised; the change is designed, implemented and tested, including regression tests; documentation is updated; and the new version is released. Impact analysis is crucial: tools that show dependencies and good traceability from requirements to code to tests make it much faster.

Lehman's laws: Meir Lehman and László Bélády studied the evolution of large systems such as IBM's OS/360 from the 1970s onwards. Lehman formulated laws of software evolution for E-type systems, those embedded in the real world. The best-known are: continuing change, where a system must be continually adapted or it becomes progressively less useful; increasing complexity, where as a system evolves its complexity increases unless work is done to reduce it; continuing growth, where functionality must keep growing to maintain user satisfaction; and declining quality, where quality will appear to decline unless the system is rigorously maintained and adapted. Others concern self-regulation, organisational stability, conservation of familiarity and feedback. The lesson: change is inevitable, and fighting complexity must be planned work.

Technical debt: Ward Cunningham coined the metaphor "technical debt" in 1992. Taking shortcuts, like copy-pasted code, missing tests or a hard-coded configuration, is like borrowing money: you deliver faster now, but you pay interest later in the form of slower, riskier changes. Some debt is deliberate and reasonable, such as hard-coding something for a demo; the danger is never repaying it. Teams track debt in the backlog and reserve some capacity each sprint for preventive maintenance and refactoring.

Legacy systems: A legacy system is an older system that remains critical to an organisation, often built with outdated technology, poorly documented, and hard to change, but too important or risky to simply switch off. Banks, airlines and governments still run systems written decades ago, some in COBOL. Options for a legacy system include continuing to maintain it, wrapping it with modern interfaces such as APIs, re-engineering it, or replacing it, often gradually.

Reverse engineering and re-engineering: Reverse engineering analyses an existing system to recover its design and specifications, for example generating class diagrams from code, extracting database schemas, or reading code to rediscover business rules. It does not change the system. Re-engineering (or renovation) restructures or rewrites parts of a system to improve maintainability without changing its functionality: source code translation to a newer language, restructuring programs, modularisation, data re-engineering, and redocumentation. Forward engineering is the normal process of going from requirements to code; re-engineering is often reverse engineering followed by forward engineering.

Strangler fig migration: Rewriting a large legacy system all at once (a "big bang") is very risky; many such projects have failed. Martin Fowler's strangler fig pattern, named after a vine that gradually grows around a tree, suggests building new functionality around the old system and gradually routing features to the new code until the old system can be retired. For example, a bank might first move balance enquiry to a new service, then fund transfers, then statements, keeping the old core running underneath until the end.

Software configuration management: Software configuration management (SCM) is the discipline of identifying, organising and controlling changes to the items that make up a software system, so that everyone knows what the current version is, what changed, why and by whom. Software configuration items (SCIs) include source code, requirements documents, design models, test cases, build scripts, configuration files and even tool versions. SCM activities are: configuration identification, version control, change control, configuration status accounting and configuration audits.

Baselines: A baseline is a formally reviewed and agreed version of one or more configuration items that serves as the basis for further work and can be changed only through a formal change control procedure. Examples: the approved SRS is the requirements baseline; the reviewed design is the design baseline; a release candidate is a product baseline. Before a baseline, changes can be made informally; after it, they must go through change control. Baselines give everyone a stable reference point.

Version control and releases: Version control, covered in detail in the Git lesson, records every change to every file and lets teams branch, merge, and recover old versions. Release management decides what goes into a release, assigns version numbers, builds and packages it reproducibly, and records exactly which versions of each component it contains. Many teams use semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a major increment signals incompatible changes, a minor increment adds backward-compatible features, and a patch increment fixes bugs, for example moving from 2.3.1 to 2.3.2 for a bug fix and to 3.0.0 for a breaking change.

Change control: Change control ensures changes to baselined items are evaluated, approved, implemented and verified in an orderly way. A change request (CR) describes the proposed change and its reason. Impact analysis estimates effort, risk and affected items. A change control board (CCB), a group of stakeholders such as the project manager, technical lead, QA and customer representative, approves, rejects or defers the request. Approved changes are implemented, reviewed and tested, the configuration is updated, and status accounting records what happened. In agile teams, the Product Owner and backlog play much of the CCB's role for scope changes, while pull requests and CI enforce control over code.

Status accounting and audits: Configuration status accounting records and reports the state of configuration items and change requests: which CRs are open, which version of each item is in each release, what changed between releases. Configuration audits verify that a release contains exactly what it should (functional and physical audits): every approved change is included, no unapproved changes slipped in, and the documentation matches the delivered software.

Documentation: Maintenance depends on good documentation: system documentation (requirements, architecture, design decisions, API references, database schemas, deployment guides) and user documentation (user manuals, help pages, release notes). Architecture decision records, short notes explaining why an important decision was made, are especially valuable to future maintainers. Documentation should live close to the code, be versioned with it, and be updated as part of the definition of done, not left for "later".

Real life example 1, a VAT rate change: Each year the national budget may change VAT or tax rules. A retail point-of-sale company receives this as an adaptive maintenance request. Because the rates were designed as configuration data, not hard-coded, the change takes a day: a change request is raised, the CCB approves it for the July release, the developers update and test the rate tables, regression tests run in CI, the release is tagged v4.2.0, and release notes are sent to shop owners. A competitor that hard-coded rates in many places takes weeks and misses some shops' tills.

Real life example 2, modernising a university results system: A university's results system was written fifteen years ago as a desktop application by a developer who has since left. The team first reverse engineers it: they extract the database schema, read the code to document grading rules, and write characterisation tests. Then, using the strangler fig approach, they build a web portal for viewing results that reads the same database, then move result entry, then transcript printing, retiring the old application module by module over two years. Each step is a baselined release with clear rollback plans.

Course recap, part 1: We began with what software engineering is and why disciplined processes matter. We studied the SDLC and process models: waterfall and V-model, incremental, iterative and prototyping, spiral, RAD and the Unified Process, and how to choose. We learned agile values, XP practices, and Scrum and Kanban. We covered requirements essentials and pointed to System Analysis and Design for deeper elicitation and DFDs. We used UML: use case, class, sequence, activity and state diagrams.

Course recap, part 2: We studied design fundamentals like abstraction, modularity, coupling and cohesion; architecture styles; SOLID, DRY, KISS and YAGNI; and the Gang of Four design patterns. We looked at code quality, reviews and refactoring, and version control with Git. We covered testing deeply: levels and types, black-box techniques, white-box testing with cyclomatic complexity, automation, TDD, CI/CD and DevOps. Finally we studied project management, CPM and PERT, estimation with function points and COCOMO, risk and quality management, and in this lesson maintenance and configuration management.

What exams ask: Define software maintenance and explain its four types with examples. Why is maintenance expensive? State Lehman's laws. Explain legacy systems, reverse engineering and re-engineering. What is software configuration management and what are its activities? Define baselines and configuration items. Describe the change control process and the role of the CCB. Explain semantic versioning and technical debt.

Recap: Maintenance modifies software after delivery and is corrective, adaptive, perfective or preventive; it is the longest and costliest phase. Lehman's laws say systems must keep changing and complexity grows unless actively reduced. Technical debt must be repaid. Legacy systems are handled by maintenance, wrapping, re-engineering or gradual replacement such as the strangler fig. SCM identifies configuration items, sets baselines, uses version control, controls changes through a CCB, and tracks status with accounting and audits. Good design, tests and documentation make all of this easier. Congratulations on completing Software Engineering.
key_points: Maintenance modifies software after delivery and usually takes the largest share of lifecycle cost.
Four types: corrective (fix bugs), adaptive (new environment), perfective (new features or performance), preventive (improve maintainability).
Lehman's laws include continuing change, increasing complexity, continuing growth and declining quality.
Technical debt (Cunningham, 1992): shortcuts that speed delivery now but slow future change.
Reverse engineering recovers design from an existing system; re-engineering restructures it without changing functionality.
SCM activities: identification, version control, change control, status accounting and audits.
A baseline is a reviewed, agreed version that can change only through formal change control and a CCB.
Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH signals breaking changes, new features and bug fixes.
lessons.tip: To remember the four maintenance types, think of a phone: fix the cracked screen (corrective), update it for the new SIM network (adaptive), add a better camera app (perfective), clean out junk files so it stays fast (preventive).
lessons.task: Pick an app you use every day, such as a mobile banking or ride-sharing app. Read its recent update notes in the app store and classify each change as corrective, adaptive, perfective or preventive. Then guess what its version numbers suggest under semantic versioning.

quiz.q: Updating an app to work on a new Android version is which type of maintenance?
quiz.explain: Adapting to a changed environment is adaptive maintenance.

quiz.q: What is a baseline in software configuration management?
options: A reviewed, agreed version of configuration items that changes only through formal change control
